There has been an almost unexampled number of promotions from the ranks of the army since the commencement of the -year. Since theist of Jan- uary no fewer than fourteen comatissions have been conferred—almost as many as the total during 1893. The commissions include those of seven second lieu- tenants, five quartermasters, on riding master, and one lieutenant of the Coast Battalion of Royal En- gineers. 1 hear, too, that the War Office Officials have before them another list of non-commissioned officers backed for commission, and in all proba- bility another half dozen appointments will snortly be gazetted. Mr. Campbell-Bannerman has himself investigated each of the claims to promotion.

Boy, politely returning compliment, totally unconscious of sarcasm, "The same to you, air.* "Yes," remarked Fenderson, "I was pretty hard pressed for money for a while, but I am now on my feet again." " Are you r replied Fogg, glancing at Feuderson's No. ll's ; "you are lucky. Nothing, I should say, could overthrow you."

" Ah, Fogg," began Fenderson, "What did they .say of my address Last evening ?" Fogg—". It was the general remark that you were a very happy speaker." Fenclerson (delighted)—" Did they ? A FAMILY living at Cancnburf found a good thickness of cream on some milk that had been standing over-night, and when the milkman made his usual call, the pleased servant exhibited the cream, and said, "I never expected to see, this." The man looked at the cream, winked wisely and solemnly, scratched his head, and replied, " I don't know what's the matter with it, but you can throw it out, and I'll give you a fresh pint in its place." " "Oh, no, Mr. Dumley, the lady replied, "the beautiful Miss Smith to whom you refer is a cousin of mine." "Oh, that's it? I,N ell, I thought there must be ri.istae somewhere," said. the gallant Dumley. "I SWAM teach you to speak properly, and then to write as you speak," said a teacher in the public schools. "Poor Billy Willcox !" said a little voice involuntarily. " What about Billy'?" asked the schoolmistress. "Please, ma'am, he speaks through his nose; so he will have to write through his nose." - - - - -

div.p: Though tbe experiments in military ballooning carried on at Chatlasfa by Colonel Templer have conducted in comparative • secrecy, it has become known that the Colonel has succeeded in making a number of important impreveinents in the machin- ery of the balloons. He has not, so I learn, yet btien able to perfect a steering apparatus, but he haa effected euch improvements in the method of con- trol that he believes he is within- mensurabledis- tance of accomplishing what has been a distinct purpose with him for two years. The reports made by the Colonel to the War Once authorities have, I know, given considerable satisfaction.

I believe the Tories of Northampton are prepar- ing trouble for Mr. Labouchere and us colleague in that city. Two candidates will fight on behalf of the Conservatives at the ne-xt election. Mr. Drucker of Milton Abbey, got beaten before, but be means to keep on trying ; and it is freeiy stated that the directors of tne South African Company mean to put up a strong opponent to Mr. Laboucnore. The editor of "Truth" however, caa afford to view the prospect with equanitnity.

The real motives which have stimulated the Try peers to commit the grave excesses of which they are now convicted before the country io dealing with the Parish Councils Bill are variously inter- preted. Some Liberals argue that the policy is so utterly reckless that it can only be explained by the theory that the Tory wirepullers have reported that the present moment may be more favourable for a dissolution than later, and that therefore Lord Salisbury is trying to provoke Sir. Gladstone, by wrecking the two bills, into a premature appeal to the country. If so, they are reckoning without their host. I have good reason to believe' ths.t the advice given from every section of the party to members of the Government is to hold on and in no circum- stances be driven to a dissolution till a considerable number of measures have met the same fate as is no* tbreitefied to Employers' Liability' and Parish Councils*. it is believed in London flat the Cabiiet also are quite unanimously of thi4opinion. The favourite view is that the Lords are really a little intoxicated by being left alone after Home Rule and by the Hbrneastle figures. If there is any metlioa in their present madness, it may be- directed to the simple policy of asking for three times as much as they wait in order ultimately to get a little.

To the staff,a gratifying feature of hie tersinstration is his evident resolve personally to rook into substantial grievancss. I hear of two cases last week which Mr. Walpole insisted upon inquiring into, and the men themselves are said to regard the result as satis-; factory.

Playing cards is the newest medium which has been foudd to be concerned in the dissemination of tuberculosis. A bacteriologist obtained some packs of cards from the phthisical ward of a hospi- tal and submitted them to an examination for the tubercle bacillus. The bacilli were present in abun- dance on the cards, but chiefly over the thumb marks—a circumstance explained by tho bad habit of the players moistering their thumbs in the pro- cess of dealing. Clearly this statement carries a warning the obserVance of which would be useful in respect to the dissemination of other diseases. The investigations of this bacteriologist were fur- ther extended to the examination of packs of cards used skt cafés and private houses. This report is reassuring, inasmuch as although he was able to , show that bacilli were present they were not of a nature that could be considered harmful.

Year ago the Sutherland clearances shocked that section of the public which put the welfare of the people before the rights of property. Ruud' eds of Jamilies were driven from their mountain homes.so that room might be given to the wild deer to wan- drat will ; and every day saw a sad procession, coriiprising the young and cqd, tha hopeful and the despairing, wending its Nay to the seaport en route for some distant laud. It appears that the present Duke and Duchess of Sutherland are more popular .in the Highlands than was the nobleman of" Clear- ance " intamy. Dunrobin Castle, where the Duke goes in a few weeks. is near the Brora, a famons trout stream.

The Duchess will not accompany her husband. She is at present actively eng,aged in promoting the highland home indastries movement,and in u short time she means to vis.t the cottages of the pea!,,ants on the estates oh ti;utherland, and give some encour- agement and practical assi:stituce. to each. The days of the wholesale expatriation by landlords are past, and it is refreshing to find that some " owners of the soil" are awakening to a consciousness of the duties which their inherited privilege of extracting rent from the people imposes on them. But they are as yet in

A. few years ago the late Charles Bradhiugh took proceedings against certain persons in connection with the publication of a certain book purporting to be a record of his life. The proceedings ended in his favour, and the books were directed to be des. troyed. But it has since been discovered that there are copies in certain public libraries and in die hands of private persons who acquired them in a perfectly innocent way and were unaware that the work had. been condemned as libellous. Among the libraries are the British Museum and the Bodleian. A request has been made by Mr. Bradiaugh's daugh- ter for the delivery of this libellous book to her,but these libraries have decided only to place the nook beyond the reach of the public. On the other hand the National Liberal Club, in whose Gladstone Library a cony was found, resolved on Wednesday to pay respect to the memory of the deceased politician by consigning the book to the flames, as being unworthy of a place on the shelves of a library maintained by a political party that owes much to his life's service.

Mr. Gladstone has given very many proofs of his desire to honour the leaders of the literary and artistic worlds. It has already neer' remarked that Sir E.Burne-Jones is the fourth of the Art baronets. He is the third of Mr. Gladstone's creation, the others being Sir Frederic Leighton and Sir John Probably the painters will be still farther complimented by Sir Frederic Leighton's " eleva- tion ' to the peerage at a convenient opportunity. Lord Salisbury paid homage to science by giving Lord Kelvin to the peerage. Alfred Tennyson's title was bestowed by Mr. Gladstone. No statesman ever gave away so many coronets, at the same time consistently declining to accept such " nobility " tor himself.

Sir Charles Dilite has a grievance against the 1, " Morning Journal" of New York. Huge capitals , introduced a two-column article in that paper. It was an" interview" with lea Charles, in the course of which he was represented as the author of some very remarkable statements. The nature of the grievance will be understood when it is learned that Sir Charles never saw a representative of the enterprising Yankee paper, and never used the words attributed to him. Me belivesi that it must have been what 2,1 r. Stead would term a telepathic interview : bio; " the spirit interviewed by the cor- respondent must have been lying."

A city friend told Mr. Labouchere that" when i the " Pall Mall Gazette " announcing Mr. Glad- stone's intended resignation reached the Stock Exchange the priests of that temple of mammon burst forth into rapturous chews' and then sang " Rule Britannia." And yet if these people are really so strongly anti-Radical as they fancy them- selves to be, they would pass their time, when not 'bulling 'and bearing,' in offering up prapers an their bended knees to Heaven for Mr. Gladstone's indefinite leadeiship of the Liberal party, as after him there will be no Liberal party—it will become the Radical party. I think the transformation has gone on—and is going on—as quietly under Mr. Gladstone's leadership as it possioly could after he resigns.

Children's dresses form a subject which is interesting to everyone and it is a:so one which can be studied by all who take a delight in dress of any kind. A pretty suit for a boy can be made in French cloth with frilled cambric shirt; an over- coat in beaver cloth can be made to match.

An elegant mmftle is of black moir6, and this might play its part for wear in the afternoon as well as in the evening. It is set into box pleats right the way round, alternating with handsome jet ornaments, and winged sleeves are made on the same principle. Cloak of satin of a bright petunia shade, trimmed with a dust-coloured lace, striped with ribbons to match, tied into bows tap and bottom looks pretty. It is easy to realise that the lining of sheeny flowered silk adds to the general effect with elopmee.

With tlae object of training women for the various publio appointments that are now thrown open to them, it is proposed to establish a Women's Municipal Guild in London, in connection with which there will be a col- lege. The instruction will be for the most part of a technical nature, and will comprise the necessary train- ing for such posts as those of town clerks, public analysts, medical officers of health, and se forth. Whenever the Empress of the French writes about her lamented husband, she invariably 11401 the diamond pen which signed the Trinity of Paris. Each of the fourteen plenipotentiaries wanted to keep the pen which signed the Paris Treaty, as a memento of the occasion. They; however, yielded to the request of the Empress Eugenio, who begged that only one pen should be used, which should be retained by her as a souvenir. Only one pen was accordingly used; it was a quill plucked front a golden eagle's wing, and riehly mounted with diamonds and gold. Miss Sarah Jewett, New England's representative authoress, resides a portion of the year in Berwick, Nile., and spends the winter in Boston. Before Miss Jewett's day no writer depicted the phases of country life which she treats without making a burlesque of the attempt. Miss Jewett has shown that the country dialect and country habits hide some of the noblest beartliand kind- est words in the world: Contrary to the Custom of most writers, she works in the afternoon, and usually devotes four hours to a sitting. She is systemati.., and her story is usually outlined in her mind before putting it on paper.

"It sounds a funny job, perhaps, but that is what I am: a maker of misfits: 'A -thriving firm in the beot trade employs me to make boots and shoes that are not of theirxegular stock patterns. Confided by a Lady Cyclist. • "I have ridden to business in the City every day this summer excepting one or two wet ones," declared a young lady patroness of the safety bicycle to the writer the other day, and never had an accident of any kind ' amongst the traffic. As far as my experience goes, the 'busmen and cabdrivers are an extremely obliging set of men, though I must remark that nine times out of ten after they have pulled to one side they will make ramie jocular observations for the edification of their passengers, the same usually taking the form of Go it, Daisy An that song, I -should say, has this season, been the greatest drawback to the appearance in public of a lady on a bicycte. Never a 'morning goes by that as I am on my way to the City I dGn't hear it whistled or sung as 1 pass a dozen times or more. Once when the asphalt° was rather slippery, and the 'busses and other vehicles were going at only a very slow pace along a crowded street,l had to dismount and push my machine along. Just behind me came a road ear, driven by a rather smart young ,fellow. Looks just as nice on font, don't she?' I heard him remark, causing all the people on top to stare over at me. It was impossible to mount and get on ahead, so I thought I'd stop and let hisn pass. As he did so—" What a shame, Daisy, isn't it?' he called to me. Why don't you get a bicycle made for two, so as cou Could sit on the seat and let him do the walking ?' "—" Cassell's Saturday Journal."

BY LAUBA JEAN LIBBEY, Author of "lona the Pride of the Mill," ezo.,
CHAPTER 19CXVIL, 'I THRRNY THE LETTER IN THE yrf.s." Tho most intense excitement prevailed through- out the orowded room as Uldene, pale as death, drew back the folds of l.er veil and stood before
them. Ratledge Cheeter rose to his feet with an awful cry. "Am I mad, or dreaming ?" he cried, hoarse!y. "Has the grave _givoli back its dead? Do I see

Uldene betore "Hold, your honour, and gentlemen of the jury. Do no paw sentence upon the prisoner untli you. have beard what I have to say. I saw the blow str tick. Yes, I witinet;sed the cowardly assault, and I say Captain Linsibg is guiltless. The would•be as,.o...sin is at .4bizs niouitut in this"room I recogniu

him!". • A thunderbolt falling from a clear sky could not I have produced more; profound sensation than these words ; and, to add to the excitement, a tall , stranger lounging near the door, with his • hat ,ptillod low °vet' his face, made a desperate leap for tbo opon door; but ere he reached it Uldens had cried out, dtkily,ratAy : "That is the Man I Stop him ! Hold him I" Strong .hands fell upon his arm, and in a single instant the man found himself completely hedged.

• Ile Wined his dark, haughty, defiant face toward the court, who was rapping ail in vain for order. - So great was Rutledge Chester's amazement, he htt4 sunk ba-f,t utrn his seat, literally speech ss.. He triedlo cry out, but the words died On his lips. -lie tried to rise, to :cross over to where this being to see if it were really a creature of flesh and .blood—this beautiful vision who stood before biro with the face an the voice of his lost Uldene. Ali the thrilling, exciting scene transpiring around him seemed like a contused dream--..a trance—to him— lie wan to tembly, shocked, so incapable of action. " You dare accase rue—you ?" cried the stranger, fiercely, turning toward Uldene, and facing her with foa,m•fl,ched "Yes, I dare accuse you. I can tell my story, and then I can die. It will .not matter much after that," murmured Uldene, faintly, clutching her little, fluttering white hand over her heart. .i.gain there was a ca.ll.lor order, and when silence :reigned ami the breathless throng, the judge bade Uldeue proceed. "I must tell my story in my own way," she murmured ; ,and this permission granted, catching her breath with a piteous sob, she went on, slowly

an.: sobbingly : "I have the strangest and bitterest story to tell that over fell from human lips," she sobbed; "and if it had not been to save the prisoner from an unmerited fate, I would have died a thousand deaths rather than have revealed that I, the last dauehter of an accursed race, and the miserable bride of Rutledge Chester, whom he believed to bo dead, still lived." . There was a murmur of surprise in the vast court-room, but Uldene held up her hand warn- " Hear me out while I have the strength to speak," she said. "It is not a long story, and it is as bitter as it is short. "There are those among you who have known melrom childhood up, and the first part of my story will not be new to you. I can only say that 1 for long years I believed myself to be the child of Mark and Nella Sefton, and believed fair-haired Verde to be my sister. I might have had a hat py enough life of it if I had never ventured beyond the conlinea of the nar,•ow strip of island on which Black-Tor Light-House stands. "1 longed for change of scene, for gaiety and pleasure, as all young girls do ; and honest Mark consentod that Veriie and I should spend the corning holidays with an old friend's family, who spent part of their winters in Washington, dividing tueir time between there and their beautiful villa in Beaton. " In granting my prayer—v.-Hi which I often retitioned him—to sue the world, honest 2,'lark Lief ton cursed me with my heart's " Even now his parting words riog in rny ears : You shall see the gay world beyond ; Our, I waru you, give no thought to lovo or marriage, child. They Ml' 0 not tor you. There is Do lover on the le.ek a fate for you. Rcnteniber, Utciene, I warn. You.' I laughed gaily as I turned from li!In ; then, Nv!.:en I was quite alone, tears of vexa!ioti titled my eyes. Why should fate have decrre% that I should have no lover ? I asked myself, with pouting lips. Other girls iess fair had lovvr, and life seemed all sweet enough ;or them. Every girl that has a spark of human nature in her breast has her own dream of a lover who is to come to her and woo her in the blissful, golden future. My dreams v;exci quite as rosy as other girls', and I had my ideal hero. How often I had d, and sung the , words over to myself ; 'Every heart fin,is its own true mate erne time in life ; for this is fate.' "Verlie and I would never have been permitted to visit at the home of Senator Chester if honest Mark had not believed that the son was not travelling abroad in Europe, and through that error the whole course of my life was changed. 'When I met Rutledge Chester I said to myself I had aleb the hero of my dreams. I hope I may not weary your honour with this preface," faltered Uldeue, "but on this slender, tangled thread hangs the. weighty evidence which in the end will . clear the innocent prisoner, and cast the man you I are holding yonder into his place." "flub ere she reaches that point she will have spoken her own doom l" cried the stranger with mocking defiance. Uldene bowed her helpless head until the angry tumult which the man's words had evoked had died down and silence was again restored. "Let me be brief," Uldene went on, speaking with difficulty, as though the words pained her, and never taking her great dark eyes from the face of the stern judge. "Soon after, I became engaged secretly to Rutledge Chester. I was on the point of writing this home to honest Mark Sefton when , I made a startling discovery which was written in a letter from the SZftons to Rutledge's mother, and which by accident .I came across. "In it Mark. Sefton warned the lady to nip in the bud any flirtation which I—being of a very roman- tic turn of mind--might fall into if a young and handsome man should cross my path. She must never love, /or she must never marry; so ran the letter. And I, full of curiosity, read these lines, , which bad never been intended for my eyes, care- fully to the end. It was a history of my life, that read like a tragic romance. It was then I made the diseovery.that I was not Mark Sefton's child but a waif clasped close in my dying mother's arms —who had been saved from a wrecked steamer, which was drifting toward the light-house one terribly stormy night. My mother did not live long enough to tell who we were, or from whence we came. She cried out to Nella Sefton to take her hapless child—for she !-wa, dying—and rear it as her own. This child must never love—for she most never marry," sobbed my poor young mother, bitterly, for a curse most terrible hangs over her hapless head that will blast ' her life, mock her love, until death ends it all. Listen while I tell you what it is. But first you must swear never to reveal it even to the child 11.=.11-ar.il.Lflk QLJ vfU LQI Lritiala

bre,oltt) 44, t4oetwit) seereb she fell back I dead, with the bitter secret untold." "'Now, you set"; wrote Mark Sefton in conclu- sion, why you must, guard her, dear madam, more core :ally, wails she is under your roof,. than roost ,girls.' There the letter ended. I threw it in the fire, and as I watched the glowing coals I cried out to myself, Why should I care for those written words? Why should I let them rob me of love and happiness?' I could not—no, I would nob! I would brave fate itself. and marry Rutledge Cheater. . , "I was on my guard now, and I resolved Rut- ledge's mother should never know I loved her son, less she should warn him against me. In his mother's absence, one day, Rutledge and I were married. Oh, fatal day! Oh, bitter hour! In that hour I brought my own doom upon my head. I had dared fate:—l was to suffer its full vengeance. ' And ah I God help me, the penalty was worse than death. But I must not deviate. When Rutledge's mother returned and discovered that we had been suddenly married she threw up her hands with a wild cry, fell upon her face and never spoke again. The horrible secret those lips might have told died I with her. I knew what. the blow was that killed her—o I knew but too well. _

"I hurried Rutledge away as soon as possible —always in trembling, guilty fear lest he should meet the Softens and learn ail, or at least enough to make him fear the future—with me. 1 was happy a few short months, ea happy earth seemed a heaven to inc. I had its fairest, sweetest gift— love. This jay was too sweet to last, even though I fancied myself secure. There was not a day, not an hour, hut what I cried out exultantly to my own heart, I have married my love, and still no ill has befallen me.' The horrible sword which hung over my head in the warning, This child must never love, for she must never marry,' had not "I have often since cried out wildly and bitterly to Heaven: Why could I not have died then, in my youth and my happiness ? ' But I mast not digress. I must be brief while you have the patience to listen to the bitter sorrow that followed," murmured Uldene, while tears fell like rain from the beautiful dark eyes and down the marble-white cheek.,

The silence of death reigned throughout the densely packed room; no sound broke the breath- less silence save the quivering sob that broke from Üblene's white lips as she went on with her piteous story--ah, yes, surely the strangest, as she had said, that ever fell frSin mortal lips. •

THE CCESE. Rutledge Chester sprang to Uldene's aide, almost overcome by intense eFnotion, but she waved

him off. "Do not touch my hand Until you .have all," she said, piteously. "You must not I pray you let me continue while I have the strength. Across the sunlight of my happiness a- dark cloud &Med, bringing with it—my doom. All unawares the cyclone bur above my head; the volcano broke beneath my feet. , • "I was in a picture gallery one• day, with the young girl who sizo btmide, the prisoner Miss Temple will remember the odeurienCei*elti—when mu:Idol-lay I was aware—painfully aware—of the fixed, but rrihig vazo ci ,a- pair of eyes bent upon me, and 10.-,kir,g up, I beheld a str,..nger serntinislng me cioc&y, vii!ll.a k that burned down to my very son',; . that "I mOtiOnless, rooted to the spot," I oaned "too terrified to cry out or utter any Wird. Lke a flazh • the -fatal words of the letter oceto•re,i lo 'me—the wardamy young mother had utl.et o iler death-bed,l that dove was not /or

Me. "'W leae is your purpose here?' I murmured, desperately., " To eereeade you that you must leave Rut- ledge Chkee T at once and Prever, or I shall publicly at euece that which will cause on to be eiii fro;i ;; ;4 by his ov.ei commend—that will caut.e. eiety hro from you in horror and fear too gi ;!7 c words. I will telt you the first doom weiet, heegs over you, and which has fal:ee eeughter of your race for eencratiow, back ; thee you. muet cheese whether eoa will go quietly beiele to France (from where you were stolen in yeer infancy) or enter a convent here under OM oeemuted name, and where you will be shut out fA ern the world for life. " 'I will give you proof, first of all, that I am indeed whtul claim to he, your uncle and guar- dian; then I will tell you your story.' "1 examteed the portrait of my mother, which be had btought with font, which was Si) Hite m; own face it might easily have been taken for me. Berfeale it was my mother's name—Uldene. I knew he spoke the truth. I could feel it in my heart. Every pulse thrilled as I gazed at the pictured face in the white, bright moonlight. One by one I examined the papers he had brought with him ; and no doubt was left in my mind but what he was indeed my untie. "'The daughters of your race were all beautiful women,' he said, slowly; 'but none were so beautiful as you, who seem to have inherited alt the beauty of your race. You have inherited, too, their quick, passionate nature. Quick to love, and to love intensely, and quite as quick tc hate, and hate bitterly.' "I knew his words as to my disposition were quite true." " 'Some three or four generations back,' be said, thoughtfully, 'there belonged to your race a handsome, debonair, reckless fellow, who did more harm in the world than good. He owned a princely chateau and a large estate, and spent money like a prince. At the age of 30 heshad en- joyed every happiness—every pleasure that life holds. „Just as he was tiring of it all most pro- foundlir, a beautiful gipsy girl chanced to cross his path. tier dark, glowing beauty pleased him, and obeying a sudden impulse, he made her his bride. The flame so quick to light in his capricious heart, as quickly died out; and the fetters that bound him to the 13eautiful gipsy were galling to him, and a thousand times he cursed himself for wedding her; and always to the face of her who would have given her life-blood for one word, one kindly smile from him whom she idolised as a living god. About this time he met a fair-haired maiden, whom, with -him, to see was to love, and love with all the mad ardour of his passionate nature. But for the gipsy girl, he told himself, he would be free to woo and win the only wosian he could ever love. In speaking of the matter to a bosom friend, he was shown a loop-hole in the marriage bond which held him, and he was not long in availing himself of the oppo.tunity of turning the beautiful gipsy girl from his doors) "'lt was on her eighteenth birthday that the beautiful gipsy girl fled from her husban i's home back to the nomadic life of her people, whom she had foritaken, and all for love of him. "'The scene between them was fierce and terri• ble. He thrust her from the grounds; and maddened to frenzy, she attempted to draw the si;ver arrev., that caught back her long, dark hair, and bury h in his faithless heart. "'ln this she failed ; but she left with him a curse more bitter than to have been -elain by her hand would have been ; and this was her curse: "'That if he married the fair-haired maiden to whom his heart had turned, that evcry danyhter of their race should be accursed ; anti if they married young—as she, the hapless gipsy girl, had done—that their marriage should end in a broken heart, as hers had. See sank down on her knees amid the blue bells of the open glade, and prayed the great spirit of her people, who had witreseed her dethronement, to make the eighteenth birthday of the daughters of his race— should he marry again—as memorable in sorrow as hers was on that day. She prayed that they might on that day lose hope and reason. Aye, that they reieeht geleavineesnad, as slue was going ; and that

"'lt was horrible—this curse the wild, un- tuto.ed child of nature uttered; but it. has followed them,' he said, from generation down. Each daughter braved fate by marry- , ing, and on her eighteenth birthday, her doom fell ' upon her. Bereft of reason, a tragedy ensued. They lifted their white hands against him whom, in reason, they had loved beat; but they never knew the sad end, for each daughter, in turn, spent her lonely life after that in the old • stone house on the river road that had been set apart for their use. 'Your mother, Uldene,' he continued, was nearly eighteen and married, when she first heard the story, and, to avoid the curse, fled from her husband, taking you with her. The shock of the story killed her husband. Then we heard she came to America. We followed her, but found trace of " her too late.

" Now, Uldeno, you see Rutledge Chester'sa,‘ danger,' ha went on. 'lf you love him, fly from : him—a:lave him; better thAt than slay him, or, knowing yOur story, have him turn from you in horror, and seek measures to confine you in an. . insane asylum. 4 "If you ref we to fly, I will proclaim your story to the world. 'Choose. Take your fate in your own hands.' "I Went,' faltered Uldene, "although it neariy. broke my heart to part from him. "Still I meet save him from myself,' I 3-led out to my own breaking heart. In my desperation, I cried out. that I would enter a convent, and there, hidden from Rutledge and from the eyes of the World, end my miserable days. "He was to accompany me there; but on the. journey Heaven ini,crposed. There was a terrible,- - railway aceideat, and he , accompanied me— aye, the whole wor!d —fielieved that, then and there, I met my death. A 'young girl, sitting in a a seat at the. back of me, held my cloak and satchel, - stipposing I intended getting a cup of tea at a rail- way station where the train was to stop. I had conceived this idea a bile he was in the smoking- ". • car ahead. I had changed my mind about entering the convent. I aligated from the train, it thua- dered on, and you knaw the rest. "I read in the papers of my supposed death— • how I had been identified by the cloak and satehel, taad now, , afterivsad, my supposed mutilated remaine had been placed in the fa:nily vault by my grief. stric.:ken husband. "'He believes me dead !' I cried, with a bitter sob. And dead to the world atal to him I must, a ever be l'

a " What it cost me to, live ap.at from him only heaven knows, and the pit) log angels. Two . years passed, and, famishing for 00e glance at his well loved face, I dared go to Wa.ehiugtoe, where % he was. I was heavily veiled as I passed him by, - and looked at him with yearniog, wiArful eyes ; but he did not know me. IL, never drenmed the dark- robed figure he had so careic) p ..Pcd by knelt on the spot where he }lad stood, anti, with passion- ate, .burning tears, kisbed the cold pavement overvihich he had passed.'

DO TI-lOU LIKEWISE. When one s'etg a candle in a window on a dark night he never can tell how many lost and bewildered travel-

lers it may guide on their way. I one knew a dear old lady who habitually did it on every dark night. The road that passed her h7use was always forsaken and lonesome enough, and houses were far apart. So, on the general principle of goodwill to men, she placed her candle in a sort of projecting window, where it would shine both ways and do the most good. She is dead and cone now; hut let us hope that her family keeps up the custom. To be &Ire it brought her many a strange
,auest, yet she did what she could for them, and never - grumbled—pay or no pay. ,

A year or two ago a little hook was printed, contain- ing anfaccount by Mr. John Hodson, of Warboys, Hunts, of the way he was cured of a wasting disease by Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup—a complaint contracted in India, where Mr. Hodson was once a soldier in the

British Army. This candle of Hodson's beamed hopefully in all direc- tions, and among others, its rays fell upon the eyes ef a woman who needed light at that particular time. HOW it came to pass she tells in a letter, from which we quote the following "I was," she says, "always healthy up to May, 1884, when I had an attack of gastric fever, which left me low and feeble. I had a tad taste in the mouth, and after everything I ate I had great pain in my chest and sides, and also dreadful pain at the back and between ,tbe Ishoulder-blades, and a sinking feeling at the pit of the stomach. ,My legs trembled and shook under me, so I could not walk erit.. Indeed, it was as much as I could do to get across the floor, A dry, hacking cough set in and shook me very much, and I lost a deal of sheep. "As I grew weaker I was confined to my bed more and More, and mY daughter was obliged to take ray place in doing the housework. -A doctor attended me for Over a year. lie tried first one kind of medicine and, then another; but none of them helped me. At the end of the year the doctor said he couid do no more for roe.l. and recommended me as a last resort to try a change
"1 lie;d got to despair of ever getting better when book was sent to me full of statements from different

people, telling how they had been made well of variour, complaints by using Mother Curative Syrup and I read of a young man living at Warboys, near rne.s having been cured in a marvellous manner by tbiø medicine. I got a bottle from Messrs.Pahner and Sons,. chemists, liamsey,and after I had taken it a week, I felt relief and gained strength. All my pain left me, and

have never looked behind me since. I take an ocea- sionaal. dose of the Syrup and keep in excellent hea give you full permission to use this letter as you tlaini fit. Yours truly,(signed) Sarah Mason,Rainsey Heights, Ramsey Hunts, January 27th, 1892." What better use could we possibly put this lady's letter than to publish it ? In this way it has fallea into the present reader's hands, and may turn out to be 116 candle in the window to show him refuge and shelter besides some long and gloomy path. A word more on this very point. It is not a matter of choice whether we are to help one another. We are obliged and boitzti to do so by every consideration of morality and utilitY• Humanity is like the body of one man : if a single 11314 is neglected the rest must pay the penalty. TherelOre set candles in windows. If, for instance, Mother Siege' Curative Syrup has done you good, say so, publish make it known. Others near you may be groping darkness. And it is all the more a subject of rejoicing that remedy, as in the above case, conquers indigestion dyspepsia, because that complaint it is which the sun for millions on Life's hard road.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. FEBRUARY 10, 1891.
For the amendment there voted : Alderman Blackhurst G)uncillor Wilkinson „ Wright „ Shaw Councillor Hutchinson „ Da7ies

~„ .. . ~ lf Heaton ~Skelton ft Smethurst „ Shillcock f t Tinsley 11 Flood If Longton I if 11111-14. Against it there voted— Alderman Harrison Councillor Muir „ Sutton 91 Monks Cyuncillor R. T. Fairclough ~ Greening Roberts „ J. Fairclough if ii Cannel' Hepherd-11. &Amen It Councillor FIRPHERD then proposed that the salary of Mr. Doss he increased from £2OO to £250 per annum. Councillor Bovrow seconded.

Couecillor SHAW-GREEN supported the proposition. Councillor ROBERTS : I said I should move an amend- ment that the amount be £75. lam a man of my word and Jam going to move it now. Councillor Bouroe : We cannot let you. • The CHAIRMAN : We have to get the ether out of the way first. Councillor Reseals : Very well. I can speak to this amendment. There has been circulated in the town, and it has been mentioned in this Council Chamber for the first time to-night.that I am not a ratepayer in War- rington. Councillor SHAW : I object to that sir. I never said anything of the sort. I said his qualification in the borough was for a stable. Councillor ROBERTS : I want to put myself right just for a moment. It is only to this extent—that there is a firm in Warrington witea whieh lam connected and which pays a eonsiderable amount of ratesit is a limited company and, therefore, it does not appear in any name on the ratepayers' book. In that respect lam as much a ratepayer as anyone in the town de facto. Proceeding he said he would like the Council to remember that owners of property were not consequently because they were owners of property directly ratepayers. It was quite true that they paid a very large amount of money into the exchequer as rates, but except so far as their own occupation was concerned, the houses in which they lived or the busineee premises which they occupied, they were no more ratepayers than a man who lived outside Warrington. The people who paid rates were the ten- ants who oecupied the property, and the gentlemen who were se fond of posing there as large ratepayers were merely the agents of the Corporation as collectors of rates frown the tenants who occupied their property. • Councillor Heeeoez : I shall apply for an increase of , salary. (Laughter.) • Councillor ROBBRTS said Councillor Heaton got con- sideration in this way—that there was a certain amount of commission allowed to persons we collected the rates in the way he had mentioned. Something had been said by Councillor Smethurst with regard to the patent that had been brought out at Longford. He endeavoured to show that the committee were playing into the hands of the manager in an improper way for the advancement of the position of the manager without any advantage to the committee. Councillor Smethuret was a member of the committee and knew What was being done; and he (Councillor Roberts) submitted that Councillor Smet- hurst had not put a fair statement of the case before the Council. This was the first time the question of the destructor had been discussed publicly, and he wanted te put the facts before them. In the first place the minute of the committee in which they decided that a , sum not exceeding £5O should be expended an the con- struction of tile destructor had, to the beet of his belief, • come before the Council for confirmation. Councillor SMETHURST : Did it? Prove it. The TOWN CLERK on being appealed to, said. he did cot think this particular minute was printed. • Councillor ROBERTS said it was a matter that could I easily be decided on reference to the minutes. If he was wrong he would admit it. But that did not affect the issue very much. If Councillor Smethurst had chosen to object to it, he could have objected to it in committee, but he did not do so. They did grant £5O for the construction of the furnace, but they did not supply a single halfpenny towards the cost of patenting it. That had been entirely done by Mr. De.a,s and those connected with him. He believed there were certain members of the Council from whom they would not. have heard a word of opposition if they had been a party to the patenting of the furnace. Conncillor SHAW : You had better ask Councillor Bea- man. ' Councillor Roetseers : I leave Councillor Shaw to do his dirty work himself. Continuing, he said they had got' for that £5O the use of the furnace without any royalty na.yments whatever,a.nd the right to have as many more furnaces as they wanted constructed on that principle on the same terms. It was only fair to Mr. Dees and the committee that that statement should be made, to show that, there was no underhand work or anything improper being done on the part of the committee or Mr. Does. Councillor SHAW: You speak for yourself. COW-1611M' ROBERTS: If you were on the committee I should be afraid et something of the serf. Councillor Suavr (indignantly) : Mr. Roberts, it won't do for you to make that remark about me. The CHAIRMAN: Order, order. Councillor SHAW: I respect my character as mutt) as Mr. Roberts does his, or as much as you do yours Mr. Chairman, and if he makes an insinuation of that sort about me I shall " screw " him for it. I shall tell him straight. The CHAIRMAN endeavoured to interpose when Councilter SHAW shouted "I ask him to withdraw it." Councillor ROBERTS: Withdraw what? The CHAIRMAN: There is a proper time to say what you are saying and to take action. Alderman WRIGIT : It is certainly wrong, and I should not like it to go on. Such abusive language is very im- proper. Councillor ROBERTS: Abetsive language? Alderman WRIGHT: One has a right to protect himself. Couticillor ROBERTS: What did he say to me? Councillor SHAW (to Councillor Roberts) : I told you I should screw you, and it will not take much to do it. Councillor ROBERTS: We are not in the habit of talking here in the language of pigeon-flyers, and I hope we shall not have a repetition of this sort of thing. Councillor Moves: I should like to appeal to Council- lor Roberts to go on with the business. lam sorry the whole thing has happened. Ccuncillor Rouen : I was trying to show that this was done straightforwardly and above- board, oli nenmdolssy-ish to repudiate emphatically on behalf of the Committee the suggestions that have been made outside the Committee te my knowledge. Councillor Suaw : Mr. Chairman, I most interfere, and ask him to withdraw the words to the effect that something might happen if I was on that committee. The Ciseinmem : I did not hear that expression at all. I only heard you shouting in a very loud voice, and I think it would be very much better if Councillor Roberts would not keep turning out these little bits of sarcasm or spiteful words. Ido not think he mars anything by it, but somebody takes it up as if it were a terrible crime. Councillor ROBERTS : If the members of the Council will leave Couneillor Roberts alone he will leave them alone. Councillor Seuvr : No one interfered with you. Councillor ROBERTS: Yes, you did several times. A MEMBER : Are we to sit here till midnight listening to these long speeches? Councillor ROBERTS : If you like. The CHAIRMAN (to Mr. Shaw) : You will do better if you sit down and wait till he has finished, and snake your speech afterwards. Councillor SHAW: I want him to withdraw his re- marks. Councillor ROBERTS: If you repeat what I said objec- tionable I will withdraw. Councillor SHAW: You said if I were on the commit- tee "something of the sort might happen." The CHAIRMAN: Have you said that? ! Councillor Rommys : If Councillor Shaw under- -1 stands me to have said something of the sort, I have not the slightest hesitation in withdrawing it. (Hear,hear.) I won't qualify it in any way ; I will have it as it is. I should like him to understand this, and all the members of the Council too, that it has been common ' for some time past to interfere with and interrupt me. I cannot very easily stand interruptions, and if I burst out occasionally you must make the best of it. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) The CHAIRMAN hoped there would be no more inter- 1 ruptions, as it was not doing justice to the Chairman or the committee. Councillor ROBERTS: I simply wished to put that matter right and I have done so, and I will leave it' where it is. (Cries of " Vote, vote.") Councillor hioNits stated that tho amount of money spent hy the committee on the furnace was £44 1013.10 d. The committee authorised £5O for experimental pt.*, poses,and that sum had not been exceeded, while the Corporation had the benefit of the furnace. The propositiou that Mr. Dees' salary be increased from £2OO to £250 per annum was put to the meeting and carried, and the minutes as amended were accord- ingly confirmed. OAS COMMITTEE.-FURTHER ADVANCES OF SALARIES.

At a meeting of the above committee held on the 19th January, resolutions were passed to the effect that the salary of Mr. W. S. Howard, cashier, be increased to £2OO per annum, and that of Mr. E. J, Smith, chief clerk, to £llO per annum. Councillor HEPRBRD moved the confirmation of the minutes, and said he hoped the Council would be unani- mous in granting the increase of salaries recommended. He mentioned that Mr. Howard had been in the service ,of the Corporation 20 years, and that the aggregate salaries in the gas department had decreased from £1,025 In 1891 to £957 at the present Mme. Mr. Howard had• £50,000 passing each year through his hands, and he thought £2OO a year was little enough to give him (Hear, hear.) Councillor R. T. Fainclerson seconded tbe proposi- tion. Councillor FLOOD moved as an amendment that only £25 be given. Councillor SHAW seconded. Councillor Davies, Alderman Wright, Alderman Harri- son, and Councillor Roberts supported the confirmation of the minutes. „„ The mover and seconder of the amendment ultimate-

was experienced, and the anxiety of the Sanitary Com- mittee in knowing that something was wrong at the works. But there wns no necessity to repeat history or to kill a dead lion. People knew the cause of the trouble, but when Mr. Deas had a free hand, and the committee were able to exercise their judgment, the whole place was completely transformed. The new management had brought out the fact that the spending of money in the past was carried out in such a manner that the members of the committee found themselves powerless to deal with it. Money was spent ad libitum, and with- out consideration; money that should have gone to capital account was taken out of revenue. No there had been a change, and members became so infatuated with it, with such a sudden transformation of things from had to good, that they were apt to be carried away, and to say "This is an extraordinary servant, and we will pay him•sufficient to keep him here in per- petuity." But this was a course which ought not to be adopted. He was afraid that some members of the corn-- mittee were showing a disposition to deal with £lOO as they would with 100 pence. Coiincihlor SMETWURST supported the amendment, be- cause every opportunity was given in committee to settle the matter of the proposed increase, but the mem- bers rose with one voice and said " We will have £100." (A Voice : "Rubbish.") No one respected Mr. Dew; more than he did, but hi respected himself and the rate- payers equally, and believed that the present was not an opportune time to grant the increase recommended by the committee. Several questions had been asked, notably by Councillor - Longton. He (Councillor Smet- hurst) entirely disputed the facts as given OR the agenda paper, and signed by the Borough Treasurer. (" Oh, oh !") What right had any man to tax a concern, and show a profit on things of the past ? It was said that so much money had been saved, although the manure was never there. Then, again, credit had been given for £1,200, which the committee had no right to give. Let them statt the comparison when Mr. Deas started work, and make the kala,nce show from him. (Flear, hear.) Since Mr. Deas was appointed certain altera- tions had been made, They were under the impression that the refuse was do6troyed at Longford. The whole of the members of the committee, with one exception, thought it was being destroyed. He pressed the matter in committee, and the result was that a retutn was pre- sented, whin showed that stuff, the worst stuff, that ought to have been destroyed was tipped away, while the best stuff was used to produce the wonderful results to which reference had been made. It was said that Mr. Deas-would leave if the £lOO was not granted to him. Did they mean to tell him es one who understood a little about patents, that a person wko had prevailed upon the Corporation to build a furnace, and take out a patent, would leave it after an expenditure had been is- curred cf from £1,500, to £2,000. Would Mr. Deaf; be able to induce any other Corporation to take the patent up ? They had put a fortune in Mr. Deas' hands, and. he (the speaker) hoped the patent would be a success. (Hear, hear.) The members of the committee said that it had only cost the Corporation £5O for the alteration of the furnace, but lie contended that the furnace for patent purposes was started from the very foundation, from the very first brick that was put down. The fur- re.ce was built up and made ready for work, and then the front portion was pulled down, a grant of £5O was obtained to make an alteration, and now it was said to • he a patent. But a fan had'also been bought. It cost ahout £lOO, and had never been worked, the old fan still being in operation. He objected to buying fans when they were already on the premises, and he should else object to any increase whatever being made to Mr. Deas' salary. _ _ _

Councillor R. T. Peariceonen supported the adoption of the original minutes strictly from a commercial sense. The results that had been shown upon Mr.Dem' manage- ment he considered juttified the advance proposed. (Liear, hear.) Councillor GREENING said he should support the minutes as printed. He thought that a rise of £lOO was not too much to give considering the capabilities of the manager. He was a member of the old Sanitary Com- mittee, and he remembered the chaotic condition of things which existed at one time at the depot; now it was in perfect order. It was fundamental to their sani- tary work in Warrington that they should have a good man at the head of affairs. Ile advocated the proposed increase upon economical grounds, because they knew that the best men and the best machinery were the cheapest in the end. (flear,hear.) It would boa great loss to thenvas a committee if they lost Mr. Deas' services, and a rise of £5O was inadequate. The manager of the works had really done more than his duty, and the com- mittee by the proposed increase were only asking the ratepayers to pay at the rate of one,fifth of a penny in- crease in the rates. 'That also meant tkat they would ensure Mr. Deas' services for many years to come. Councillor FIEATON supported the amendment which had been submitted by Councillor Flood, although he should be willing to grant an increased £5O to make the salary £250 a year. "In anether 12 months they could give the manager another £5O. (Cries of "No, no.") Councillor Sesaw said that as am economist and as a ratepayer he shout support Councillor Flood's motion. He believed that Mr. Deas was a first-class man, but, at the same time they were paying him a first-class price— (" Question ")—inasmuch as his predecessor only received £175, and Mr. Deas received £2OO. Let Mr. Dees come before them at a more opportune time than the present. Surely the members of the Council could not shut their eyes to the fact that people were closing their houses on account of the high rates of the borough, and going into the country to live ! In the neighbourhood of Latchford alone there were no fewer than seven houses which would become empty this week owing to the circumstance he had mentioned —the exorbitant rates. It was now time that the Cor- poration understood the meaning of the word "economy.' The people who supported the motion for an increase of £lOO that night were people of wealth, and they found it "most adequate and suitable "to live out of the borough. (Hear, hear.) Let them have to pay the rates and see. Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH : I pay rates inside the borough.. Councillor SHAW: Tam not alluding to you. Councillor Rosseers : And so de I. (Laughter.) Couacillor Ssetw ; We know there is a stable that gives you a qualification ; but I don't know whether there is anything in it or not. (Renewed laughter.) Councillor 'ROBERTS rose to speak. The CHAIRMAN : Up to this point Councillor Shaw was in order.

Councillor SWAIT : I was in order, and if Councillor Roberts had not got up I should have continued to be in order. Councillor ROBERTS (Still standing) : I was going to say- Councillor Sri-kw : And I was going to say-- Councillor ROBERTS : I rise to a point of order, Councillor Silsw : There is no point of order. Councillor flosaers : I was only going to call atten- tion to a stitetnent made by Councillor Shaw. I have a Btable, and I want a donkey for it, and I shall apply to Councillor Shaw. (Loud laughter.) Councillor Slaw (who said he had not heard the re- mark) : What is that? _ _

The CHAIRMAN: I hope you will take it in good part, because if Mr. Roberts came to me, instead of a donkey I would give him a pony. (Renewed laughter.) Councd!or SHAW: Whatever he (Councillor Roberts) said I failed to hear it. If it is,howevor,anything detri- mental to me,ancl he will tell me in private,l will charge my aceount with him. (Laughter.) Councillor Moxxs : Mr. Flood has referred to a eqmpromiy,o. He said he made a compromise, but he did so attor moving his amendment. Was it likely that I should accept a comprornise until I had had an oppor- tunity of ascertaining what was the general feeling of the Council with regard to the proposed increase? I consider that my position as chairman prevented me from accepting a compromise under such circumstances. (Hear, hear.) I feel, and ether members also feel, that we should be doing as little as we ought to do if we gave Mr. Dens £lOO increase. It is my duty to Mr. Deas to make every effort ISAR to get hint that increase. lam quite prepared now, however—and I know other mem- bers will support me—to say that if the Council will give us £5O now and £5O next year--(Cries of "No, no.") The CHAIRMAN : £5O and let the matter rest as it is. (To Councillor Flood) : Will you withdraw your amend- ment and support the other one? If not we must divide the Council. Councillor FLOOD, refused to withdraw his amend- ment. _ . .

_ Councillor BEAMAN wished to say something about the manner in which the discussion had been carried out. Some of the speeches had been fair, but some had been tinged to the very root with animus; some had fairly quivered with viciousness and wickedness. ("Oh Ohrand Laughter). It had been contended that they were experi- menting at Longford. Was not sanitary science still in its experimental stage ? Had they got to that state of perfec- tion which they could term a final stage? There were no sanitary works anywhere in the kingdom where experi- mental work was not done, and Longford depot had been no exception to the rule. (Hear, hear.) Hundreds and hundreds of pounds had been spent there in experi- ments. Councillor Smethurst had said that he would give place to no one in his love for Mr. Deas. It was perfectly justifiable for him to dissemble his love for Mr. Deas, but why on earth did he kick him downstairs? (Laughter.) Mr. Deas was not only a mechanical engineer, but a chemical engineer, and he knew a great deal about machinery. In him they had a first-rate all-round man, and a man who reflected honour on the Corporation, and he contended that it would be the strictest economy to retain his services. He did not say that if he did not get the £lOO he would leave their service; he loved his work so much that they would have his services for years to come at all events. (Hear, hear.) After a little further discussion, Councillor FLOOD said he had imen asked by a large section of the Council to withdraw his amendment. In deference to them' if his seconder eonsented he would do so, and move that the salary be £250.
The CHAIRMAN: Does the seconder approve? Councillor Saw: I decline to withdraw iny seconding af the amendment, and I should like it to go to the vote.
The CHAIRMAN said Councillor Flaod's amendment read as follows :—" That the minute of the 24th January, 1894, referring to Mr. Deas' salary be not con- firmed. ' . .
ly withdrew it, and the minutes were confirmed almost unanimously.

div.head: TOWN NALL WARD
div.p: TOWN NALL WARD

At a meetinfz of the General Purposes Committee. it was resolved " that the scheme for taking down the Town Hall wall between the two existing gates, in- cluding the erection of the gates presented by Mr. F. Monks, be carried out at an expenditure estimated at £550, and that the improvement be, com- pleted to Crosfield-street as soon as practicable."— At a meeting held on the 29th January, it was resolved " That the tender of Messrs. E. and A. Eustanco to wind and keep in repair all the clocks belonging to the Cerporation,,for a period of three years at £9 per year, be accepted."
• The minutes were passed on the motion of the CHAIR- MAN, seconded by Councillor HUTCHINSON after which the Council rose, haying sat two hours and a half.

BY Mn. JOHN FREELS. (With Apologies to Laurence Sterne, M.A.) "it is all P—said my father, holding a coin edge- ways in his fingers— it is all' according to 'dastur.' It is all decided for us by the Pates of nativity," —here he dropped the coin on the table—" whether we follow the Oriental or Occidental dastur." "Mau is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upwards," interposed Mr. Yorick. "Not more truly than he makes most of the trouble that comes to him "—re- joined my father, "as did your authority for that in- terruption; for had Job not been such a Jeremiah —had he paid more attention to the needs of health and cleanliness he would have had lest,. cause to curse the day of his birth." "No, your Rever- ence, men may be born to trouble, but they show considerable thrift in the increase of the inherit- ance." "But man is born to be the creature of his surroundings," said my father," as the coin drops, it is heads or tails, whether we are destined, to fol- low the Eastern or the Western social God, dastur." We English follow the" dastur" of precedent ; the code that makes it the "thing" to commit certain sins and follies that have been committed before.

"Yea, it :is our 'skittle to have bishops who exist on a pittance of .£lO,OOO a year, more or less, to preach to us from the text: Matt. xix. 24. "And again I say unto-you, it is easiei for a camel to go through the eye Of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven." "And go sell that thou haat, and give to the :Poor." a" Ia this as in other things" said Slawkenbergius, "we follow the bishop's example rather than his precept. We get hold of all we can and stick to it as long as we can; and some of the bishops-are famous hands at this last. Near this from a London journal, "The longevity of irremovable dignitaries is proverbial, and the Church of ngland is a conspicuous in- stance of it. The following table of bishops and deans who have passed the age of threescore and ten contains the names of many who are still at ' work,itogether with a few,and those not necessarily the oldest, who are manifestly unfitted by age or infirmity for active service, ought to retire : Bishop of Chichester 91, Bishop ot Beth and Wells 45, Bishop of Liverpool 77, Bishop of Hereford 76, Bisbop of Gloucester and Bristol 74,Bishop of London 72, Bishop of Llandaff 72, Bishop of Mt.' David's 71. Bishop of Wakefield 70, Dean of St. David's (Allen) 91, Dean of Ripon (rremantle) 87, Dean of Exeter (Cowie) 774. Dean of Llandaff (Vaughan) 77, Dean of Durham (Lake) 76,Dean of Bangor (Lewis) 75,Dean 40 Rochester (Hole) 74, Dean of Lincoln (Butler) 75, Dean of St. Paul's (Gregory) 74, Dean of West- minster (Bradley) 72. Whatever (is the comment of my authority) may be their theory, the practice of the clergy is to keep, out of heaven as long as they possibly can." "And," put in my father,"to re- tain firm hold of the disqualifying lucre until death do them part." freely admit," qu.oth Yorick, "that it is an apparent anomaly for hig. ly remune- rated clergymen to be found preaching the bles- sings and advantages of a poverty so strenuously and successfully resisted bytheniselves,but it maybe, that the custom of the country has been tog strong foi them, and the dictates of this they have had to follow however much against their inclinings." "Or, again," said my father, with a twinkle in his eye, "it may be that they think the narrow way will be too crowded, and so give place to those not so heavily handicapped in the race for Heaven." "But even a bishop," said my Uncle Toby, " cannot carry heaven by assault,"And besides "—this was Slawkenbergius— a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush."" Yes, the long and short of it is," said my father," that it is far easier to get a needle through the eye of a camel than it is to get a rich man to give up his blessings 'in esse' in exchange for hypothetical blessings in posse: He's afraid of making a bankrupt of himself in this world for fear there might be no assets in the next. You kno fir one's never sure.

".Your honour," said the Corporal," I have beard say that parsons are like finger posts, pointing the way they go not themselves • what would happen them to us were all these indicators to take it into their heads to leave us and go the way instead of pointing it out to us ?" "I see no danger of that,"said sty father. " God forbid I" Said my Uncle Tohy. " A prayer, which, if it flies in the face of scripture and logic is more likely to be answered than many we hear," whispered Hasen Slawkenbergius in my father's ear.

"Here," said my father looking up from the book whose leaves he had been turning over, "is a strange custom of a curious people, who not only make the elements pray for them in shape of wino anti water turned praying wheels, but so contrive that the very walls shall intercede for them ; a kind of mural supplication :—` Our late Joint Commissioner, Mr. Ramsey, has greatly improved the road between Leh and Dras,, and for the last five miles from Pitik to the gates of the city. But the Ladakis, fantastic as usual, loving zig-zags and tortuous ways and abhorring regularity,often avoid this easy route to take a longer and rougher. There, is, however, some reason for this eccentric conduct: there are manes by the side of the new road, so that, to walk these five miles, though a saving of time, is an unprofitable and absolutely wasted effort so flu. as preparation for the next world is concerned ; it is therefore more advantageous to follow the rugger', old native winding road, well provided as it is with rows of prayer stones and so far superior to the new one from a theological point of dew."—" What a grand place to recruit in?" exclaimed Trim, "How so Trim, thinks thou that they would be easily en- listed ? What might not be expected of folks who expect stone walls to pray for them ?" murmured Trim.

Mr. Gladstose will return from Biarritz to London to- day (Saturday). The Prime Minister on receiving the telegrams as to his rumoured resignation expressed sur- prise that currency should be given to such a report,es- pecially as there was no ground for it other than the de- gree of uncertainty which must always attend tile con- tinuance in office of a statesman so advanced in age.

div.head: WARRINGTON CHAMBER OF COMMERCE. '
div.p: WARRINGTON CHAMBER OF COMMERCE. '
ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce, was held in the Chamber, Market Gate Chamber,on Monday afternoon. The chair as occupied by the president; Mr. Wm. Pierpoint, and there were also present, Messrs. F. Monks, J.P., C.C., John Fairclough, J.P., J. H. Fleming, J.P., R. Garnett, J.P., T. J. Hulse, and Coun- cillor Arthur Bennett (secretary). The secre- tary read the following letters of apology for abience from the meeting: "- My dear am .extremely sorry that absence from home will prevent ins' attend- ance at the annual meeting of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce on Monday. The report to be presented is an interesting one, and it is encouraging, to see that the membership has been increased during the past year. It is not so much in the actual work to be done singly by the Chamber that its usefulness lies,but it forms ofie of a large an powerful organisation whose influence is wide- spread and effective with our commercial legislation and in the general interests of commerce. No one who has attended the meeting of the associated chambers can fail to have been impressed witit the business-like character Of the proceedings, and the more our traders and manu- facturers recognise this fact, the more I trust they will see it to be their interest to support the Chamber by their presence as well as by their subscriptions.—Yours, etc.,—W. Long."—" Dear, Sir,—l have to thank you for your letter of the let inst., and I beg to assure the Coun- cil of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce that I very strongly appreciate their kindness in inviting me to be- come a member of the chamber. As lam at present situated, I regret that it is quite impossible for me to take any active part in their proceedings, and while I attach very great importance to concerted action such as Chambers of Commerce can bring to bear on ques- tions affecting the welfare of the trading community. I have always felt a 'difficulty of identifying myself with publictiusiness to which I am unable to give sufficient Cm* and attention-to justify my interference.—l am, etc.,—J. J. Blectzly.

div.head: ANNUAL REPORT.
div.p: ANNUAL REPORT.
The adoption of the annual report and accounts which appeared in our last issue, was carried on the motion of Mr. F. Monks, seconded by Mr. R. Garnett.
ELECTION OF OFFICERS.

Mr. Wm. Pierpoint expressed a wish to retire from the office of president, and proposed Mr. J. H. Fleming,,,J.P. Mi. John Fairclough seconded, and the motion was car- ried. Mr. R. Garnett, J.P., was elected vice-president on the motion of Mr. F. Monks, seconded by Mr. John Fairelough. The following officers were also elected— , treasurer, M. John Murray ; udit ors, Idessrs. Z. Armit- age, J.P., and Thomas Tonstall, F.C.A. The following gentlemen were a,ppeintecl to form the council :—The pre- sident,vice-prosident, Mayor of Warrington for the time being, member for Warrington for the time being,Messrs Wm.,Pierpoint,..l.P., Wm. Carson, Joseph Davies, John'Fairclough, J.P., Wm. Long, J.P., George McCor- qcodale, J.P., Frederick Monks. J.P.,C.C.,R. A. Naylor, H. Roberts, J.P., Peter Stubbs, J.P., Wm. Tinsley, and T. J. Mdse.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CIIURCTIPS-WARRINGTON.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CIIURCTIPS-WARRINGTON.
CAIRO STREET CHAPEL

At the Unitarian Chapel, on Sunday evening, th e Paster, the Rev. W. H. 'Drummond, delivered his monthly address to workingmen, the subject being "Joseph Mazzini, the prophet -of democracy." There was a crowded congregation, and the discourse was listened to with deep interest.

div.head: SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN CriAPEL.
div.p: SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN CriAPEL.

The Rev. G. D. Mason preached at this chapel on Sun- day morning, and in the evening a memorial service was held, conducted by Mr. W. Brough, in memory of the late Mrs. Morgan and Mrs. Cannon,members of the con- gregation of the chapel. The chapel was crowded to its utmost capacity, and the service throughout was of an impressive character. At the commencement of the ser- vice, Mr. T. Brough played " Dead March" in Saul, and during the service, Mr. Levi Richardson sang as a solo, a song appropriate to the occasion.

div.head: WYCLIFFE P.S.A.
div.p: WYCLIFFE P.S.A.

The usual P.S.A. meeting in Wycliffe Church, which Was the 49th since its inauguration, was held on Sunday afternoon. Mr. R. Atkinson was .the chairman, and gave a short address. The address for the afternoon was delivered by Mr.C.E. Parker, ot Penketh, who said that he felt it to be a great honour to be invited a second time to address that P.S.A. meeting. Mr. Parker afterwards gave an interesting bible lesson on" The Creation." Mr. R. H. Pearson contributed two solos during the service, his singing of "Comfort Ye" from the Messiah beirig particularly good, Messrs. S. W. Jeffery, and T. Haw- thorn also took part in the service. There was a very large attendance.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday night at the Town Hall. Mr. J. Pritchard presided, and there were present the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Dr. McDougall, Messrs. E. Imison, T. Handley, and G. Moss (clerk).
SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.

rho visitors reports to the School Attendance Commit- tee for the month of January showed that the number of scholareon.the rolls was 3,600, being 123 less than in the same period of last year, The average attendance was 2,982, against 2,979 list year, being an increase of 3; and the percentage of attendance was 82.8 against 80. The falling off in the number on the rolls was attributed to families having left the town owing to the completion of the Manchester Ship Canal.—Confirmed on motion of Canon Wood.

div.head: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT.
div.p: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT.

The School Management Committee held a meeting, on January 9th, when applications for the post of assistant master at Greenway-road school were read. There were 31 certificated applicants and one ex P. T. The following candidates were selected to appear before the Board at a special meeting: F. Goulden, Stockport ; J. W. Dakin, Blackpool; F. W. Shepherd, Freston; W. Blakernore, ‘Volverhampton ;J. C. Cragg, Carnforth'; E. J. Moly- neux, Kidderminster; and A. McLean, Stockport. The Committee recommended that the salary of Mr. Kennan assistant master at Greenway-road school be advanced to £BO per annum, commencing March let, 1894.—The Clerk read a circular from Mr. It P. Ward, of the Cheshire County Council, announcing a series of scholar- ships to be given to children in elementary schools. The Clerk was instructed to see that the necessary arrange- ments were made at Greenway-road school. At a fur- ther meeting of the Committee held on January 30th, it was recornmeaded that Mr. Clarke's resignation be ac- cepted on condition of his paying the expenses incurred in consequence of his not fulfilling his engagement. It was also recommended that Harristt Beatrice Smith be appointed temporary assistant teacher at Mill Brow school.—Passed on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. unison.

div.head: EDUCATION OF THE BLIND.
div.p: EDUCATION OF THE BLIND.

The Clerk drew the attention of the Board to the fact that an Act came into force at the beginning of the year called the Elementary Eilucation Blind and Deaf Child- ren Act, 1893. He pointed out that it was now the duty of the Board to see that these children were properly educated until the age of 16 years. The best plan would be to make arrangements with some school in Manches- ter or Liverpool. The parents would hare to contri- bute towaros the expense. It was decided that the Clerk cause inquiries to be made as to whether there were any such children in the town, and ascertain their names.

div.head: PROPOSED EXTENSION OF GREENWAY-ROAD SCHOOL.
div.p: PROPOSED EXTENSION OF GREENWAY-ROAD SCHOOL.

A letter from the Education Department was read- dated January 17th, stating that the plans for the exten, sion of Greeuway-road school were returned, and point- ing out that a well should be replaced by a sliding glass partition. The division between the two little classrooms would be better omitted. The windows needed complete alteration. The plan should be revised and again submitted. Enquiry was made whether the Board had considered the question of providing addi- tional accommodation for boys, the average attendance in the boys' school having during the past two years ex- ceeded the prescribed limit.—Dr. Gastaldi moved that consideration of the matter be deferred until they could sea their way clearer.—Mr.Handley seconded. He said he did not consider that the proposed plans with the altera- tions of the Education Department were worth carrying out. They would involve an expenditure of £6OO for the sake of accommodating sixty children, and he did not think the game was worth the candle at such an ex- pense. From rumours he heard he thought the Board would very soon have to take into consideration the making of larger provision than for sixty or eighty children. In another month they might have mere light on the subject. At one school in the town the managers were considering whether they should close the school.— Canon Wood said a business man had given him a very glowing view of the town as regarded indnstries and population.—Mr. Handley did not think there would be. much difference. They had a larger attendance this month than in the same month last year.—The Chair- man: There are two opinions abroad—one taking a glowing view of matters. A few months will test the whole business, and we shall see what the result will be. —Canon Wood said it was a question of work. If there wss work to do the numbers of people would increase and the Board would provide accommodation. If there was no work for them people could not stop in the town. —The Clerk said with regard to accommodation for boys, he could reply to the Department that there was accommodation in the other schools for boys, and that after the examination a less number would be admitted to the Board school.—The motion was carried.
