IMPERIAL • PARLIAMENT.
MONDAY.

-The House of Lords again went into Committee ess the Local Government (Parish Councils) Bill on Monday evening. The Marquis of Salisbury moved to omit front clause 11 words relating to the defrayal of the expenses of parish councils and perish meetings, and said his amendment raised the question of the compounder. The Earl of Kimberley opposed the amendment, contending, that if it Was adopted a large proportion of the agricul- tural labourers of the country would be prevented from taking part in the management of their own affairs. On a division the amendment was carried by 120 to 53, and a consequential amendment was then agreed to, which declared that" the said rate shall be paid directly by this i occupier." Clauses 11 and 12 having been added to the bill, a new clausa, movcsl by the Marquis of Salisbury, which his Lordship said, would furthet limit the applica- tion of the powers of compounding so far as the parish council was concerned,was carried by 140 to 37. Amend- ments expunging the proposals of the bill in regard to parish councils and the administration of charities were r moved from the Oppositien side, and were carried by majorities of 110 to 27 and 80 to 19. The House reached clause 20 before rising. The later portion of the sitting was rendered interesting by a sharp contrcversy between the Marquis of Salisbury and the Lord Chancellor on the subject of the appointment of magistrates.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

In the House of Lords on Tuesday evening the Marquis of RrPox, replying to Lord Knutsford, said the Colonial Office had received information—but nothing beyond the bare fact—that aaother collision appeared to have oc- curred between the English and French troops in Sierra Leone. The House again went into Committee on the Local Government (Parish Councils) Bill. On clause 20 the Earl of HARROWEY moved an amendment with a view t) its being followed by the insertion of a new section providing that members of a County Council should .be ex-officio guardians of the union in which they resided. The Earl of KIMBERLEY said he could not accept the amendment, and the Marquis of SALISBURY said he Could not support it. On a division the amendment was car- ried by 109 to 26, and a new sub-section to the effect above stated was added to the clause. .A proviso moved by Earl CADOGAN' that the sub-seation as to nominated guardians should not apply to guardians nominated by the Local Government Bard under a section of the Act 30 and 31 Vic., chap. 6, relating to London, was carried by 122 to 44. The Earl of ONSLOW moved a new sub- section providing that only persons separately assessed to the poor-rate should be entitled to vote as parochial electors. The Duke of DEVONSHIRE said it was undesir- able to propose so serious a measure of disfranchisement as the amendment involved, whereupon the Marquis Of SALISBURY said it was useless to pre A the amendment, and it was withdrawn. Lord liatroun of BURLEIGH moved an amendmeat excepting London unions from the operation of clause 20. The Earl oi KIMBERLEY resisted the amendment, which, after some discussion, was with- drawn. An amendm,nt moved by the Earl of CRA?../.. BROOK to omit clause 22, which provided that the chair- man of a district council should be by virtue of his MEC* a county justice was carried by 54 to 18. A new clause for the transfer of school attendance powers to district councils was, on the motion of the Earl of HARROWBY, added to the bill by 89 to 47. LOrd BaLrourt of BUR.. mon moved an amendment to leave out of clause 30 words which practically transform London vestries into urban district councils, and it was carried by 107 to ge.

div.head: TFIUtiSDAY.
div.p: TFIUtiSDAY.

In the House of Lards on Thursday; considerations of the Parish Councils Bills in Committee was vsumed,and ; clauses 30 and 35 were dealt with. On clause 36 (re- moval of disqualification of married women),the Earl of. , Caperdown moved an amendment extenriing to women for the poses of the Act of Parliamentary,lodger and ser- vice franchise. The Earl of Kimberley,the Lord Chancellor I and the Marquis of Salisbury opposed, and the amend- ment was negatived without a devision, the clause being added. The Duax of Richmond moved the omision of clause 54, which provided that no meeting of a parish council, district council, or board of guardians should be held in premises licensed for the sale of intoxicating ' liquors unless no ether suitable room was available,either free of charge or at a reasonable cost. After some dis- cussion the amendment was withdrawn,the clause being agreed to. On the motion of the Earl of Selborne it WAS decided by a majority of 46 to widen the definition of "ecclesiastical charity" so as to include, building's whole trusteeship, management, or control is vested in ministers or officers of any church or denomination. Other clauses and the schedules were agreed to with some Government amendments,and the bill was ordered to be reported on .Monday.

div.head: "WE MAY BE HAPPY YET ! "
div.p: "WE MAY BE HAPPY YET ! "

New Version, Tune—" The lass of Richmond Hill." Patrieroft ther lives a chap, Wo sez he's anusiii; An' likes to get his grog on "strap," Or at a private "still." At ev'ry change er full o'th' moon, He's trayted by a vet; An' tak's a horse-ball to the tune, " We may be happy yet ! " He poo's a face, an' looks so bad, It puts yo on the rack; He seems to say i' accents sad, "Get ready wi' yer But still, altho' he's i' sitch pain, He gets his teeth weel set, An' wobbles eaut, i' mournful strain, "We may be happy yet!" Yos't look aw reaund these roads fer miles, . Yo'le noan find one like him; Per tho' he jokes, he never smiles, • An' ne'er seems owt but grim. No matter heaw yo try to chaff, He's never i' a pet,: An' sings, —because he connot laugh— We may be happy yet ! " Jost once% a yer he guz to see A' owd chum i' Chowbent ; That s th' only time he hez a spree, An' gies his spirits vent. But even then, when " haul seas o'er," An' o'er his cigarette, He moans, (ez if his yd wuz sore,) "We may be happy yet !" "He goes on Sundays to the church," Reet opposite the trams; An' keeps the divil i' the lurch,— He never swears or d—ns An' then reawnd th' corner, dry ez chips, He sups his "heyvy wet " ; An' murmurs, wile he smacks his lips, . "We may be happy yet l" Poor Jack o' Trumps, I'm sad an' wild, To think thy doom is seal'd ; That soon thy grave-sods mun be piled Pth' village burying field. But when King Death gies th' fatal blow. An' makes tne room "To Let," Theau'l sing i'th' skies, er deavyn. idow, "We may be happy yeti" TUX 0' PEGS

THE House of Lords seems to The Lords and Parish Councils. have persuaded itself that it if§

kill a power in the land. Maul people had come to the conclusion that the dayl had gone by in this country when hereditary legis- lators could cut and carve, reject and select, lb l, their own sweet will the progressive measures which , had been endorsed by majorities in the House of commons. It would now seem that the peoplo . who have entertained an opinion of this kind have . been wofully mistaken. The House of Lords ha° , still a place in the Constitution and it is deter ~ mined to assert its power. Its special functioof ..- • judging by its recent actions, is to protect the ' privileges of the powerful and the wealthy,And to • eliminate from the legislation that is submitted te its tender mercies all those parts which are de' signed to still further enfranchise, socially sod politically, the "common people." The countrY , ill is at the present time looking with amazerneos and indignation and, so far as the more judicioilg ~ supporters of the Peers themselves are concerned; ". 1 with dismay, at the deliberate destruction of rir ...: -• forms which the present Government and HOlO9 of Commons were elected to carry out. Lass week it was the Employers Liability Biliii; this week it is the Parish Councils 13iP" In regard to . the first named of WO Bills, the . House of Lords has deterrainl ' to insist upon conditions which destroy almost - its value in the eyes of those who'' ' -(00) intended to benefit, and as for the Bill that is being mangled to sue it is almost certain the Governme abandon it altogether than adopt " amendments " which Lord SALis. dictate. As a matter of fact the have been made by the Peers havc with the intention of improving have been made in order to frus objects which the promoters of th ' piece of legislation had in view. 1 and the Opposition approach th opposite poles." This Bill,' said L in effect, "will give the villager: more direct control of their own t trel of their own stairs," retorted in one of those candid momenta oi lais ungnoista have se much -

Parish Council, 1 au extent 010 nit would rather all the so-CaiioCl 8131IRY WiSbOS aiteratiOnS th3S not been wade the Bill ; theY itrate the verl is much-needed rile Govern inetA le subject frDill ..ord Kimpnitail s of England a affairs." "C 0 Lord Salisbury If his for which to be

° control of other people's affairs, you mean." There is no need to go beyond this utterance of the Marquis of SALISBURY to find an explanation of the bitter hostility of the ory Party to the Parish Councils Bil In the opinion of the Tory Peers the villagers of England have no " affairs" of their own. The affairs of a village are the affairs of the landlord of that village, and, in the opinion of the Peers, the landlord is quite able to manage everything himself without asking any advice from the villagers or having to submit to the impertinences of a Parish Coun- cil. This is, in reality, neither more nor less than the old Tory doctrine that the common people Should be governed by their "betters," but it is, certainly, rather startling to find it enunciated so Openly by the leader of a party which appeals for suppert to the democracy of the country. The same idea is to be found in the contention of Lord SALISBURY that the cottagers of the country do llot, for the most part, pay any rates, simply because the rates are paid along with the rent to the landholder and by him handed over to the rate collector. That is a method of rate collection - which has been found from experience to bo the Inost convenient alike by those who collect and those who pay the rates. The proposal that the present system shoulg be abolished and that each individual occupier should be separately rated, . although it found favour with the Tory Peers,was toe much for the Liberal Unionist leader, ' and the Duke of DEVONSHIRE'S protest Stemmed the tide of reaction in this respect ' at all events. It can hardly be doubted that, on the whole, the debates in the House of Lords upon the Parish Councils Bill will have an admirable ! efreet upon Liberal prospects in the county con- stituencies Just as last week the Peers flouted the artisans and trades uniohists of the towns,.l 10 this week they have flouted the agricultural labourers of the country. It would almost appear that, in the opinion of these great landowners, the 'Pillage labourer is not only a mere dependent upon. their bounty but a superfluous kind of individual 41together. Ho has, in their opinion, no "affairs" 6f. his own and he does not pay rates. Yet how dnierent is the real state of things. The labourer often spends his whole life in the parish in which O was born and his happiness is largely affected 13,Y what we may call the communal life of the Village in which lie lives. The landlord, on the !ether hand, is, as often as not, a non-resident, and ni• many instances an entirely unknown figure in the locality. Then, as to the payment of rates. All imposts of this kind are deducted from the agri- cAltural wealth of the country, and who is the Prime factor its the production of this wealth P The, landlord himself, and even those powerful land- . lords who dominate the House of Lords, are, in this connection, mere rent-receivers. Take away the labourer, who is often spoken of so slightingly, and there would be very little left indeed either for rent or rates.

THE new social experiment which A Social Experiment. has been originated in Australia, and which is to he carried out in Paraguay, South America, has now been fairly entered upon. We are told that the" Royal the co-operative boat of the social pioneers, left Adelaide towards the end of December with

_ a second company of two hundred picked men for South America. It is said, too, that the Austra- lian governments are becoming alarmed by the enthusiasm with which the movement is being taken up. It threatens to deprive the by no means over-populated Antipodean colonies of a larg.,3 number of their best inhabitants. Three thousand men are already enrolled as members of the movement and are only waiting for the oppor- tunity to be wafted across the ocean to the new I.ltopa, and it is expected that many thou- sands mare will follow. This is not a case of a band of needy emigrants making a desperateeffort to escape from the hardship of their lot. Some idea may be obtained of the c lass of men who are Combining to carry out this scheme and of the resources at their command from the fact that each member throws all he, or she, possesses into the common fund, and in no case has this sum to he less than sixty pounds. In addition to this no Person who is not a total abstainer and of high character has been accepted as a ineraber. These colonists have received a free grant of four hundred and fifty thousand acres of the best land of Para- guay and upon this they are founding their settle- tcent on Communistic principles. This movement lieerns to have forced the hands of Australian 4,tatesinen in a Socialistic direction. In South 4ustralia they have passed a Village Settlement et under which any twenty or more persons may :741 a village association and receive from the r3vernment a grant of land equivalent to one hundred and sixty acres per member, and ad- nces from the colonial exchequer on all improve.

BURDENS C'N THE BATES.

At Runcorn Police Court yesterday, before Mr. Brun- drit and Mr. Norman, John Albison, chemical labourer, was charged with running away from Runcorn on the 28th November, 1892, whereby his three children became chargeable to the Union. Mr. Frodshatu prosecuted for the Guardians, and said the prisoner's family had cost the ratepayers £29 ss. 6d. The prisoner had twice served a month hard labour nuder a similar charge. He had never made the slightest inquiry about his children for two years. The prisoner was now sentencoid to a month's hard labour. Cocurs's nee over ten tons of Flou every week .—/det.

div.p: DRAT OF ONE OF RUNCORN'S OLDEST TRADESMEN.

Mr. Samuel Horton who for upwards of thirty years lived at 13, Church-st., carrying on business as pork butcher, died on January 31st at the residence of his eldest daughter, Mrs. W. Pilling, Pemberton, Wigan, at the ripe old age of 71 years. He was interred at Runcorn cemetery on Saturday. The deceased was born at Nor- ton and came to reside in Runcorn over 50 years ago. In the earlier part of his iife he was gardener to the late Mr. Jonathan Potter, at Higher Runcorn, of whom he always spoke in the highest terms. As a man of busi- ness Mr. Horton could always be trusted to deal justly with rich and poor alike. He was highly respected throughout the town. Go to PRITCHARD 'B, 51, High-st., Runcorn, for the lest FLYSGuzias WATCEI a working man can have.—A.
SHOCKING BURNING ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.

Late on Friday night,Gliarles rlaylor, provision dealer, Portland-st., Runcorn, and his wife Hannah, met with a shocking accident. Early in the evening a bottle of varnish had been placed in the oven to soften, and had been forgotten. Whilst preparing supper, Mrs. Taylor opened the oven door, when a tongue of flame shot out, followed by an explosion, which blew out the kitchen window. Bah Taylor and his wife were enveloped in flames, and Mrs. Taylor ran into the street, where two neighbours named Richardson and Rose, extinguished the flames by means of a rug. Mr. Taylor has lost one eye, and it is feared that he will now lose the other. The injured couple are in a very serious condition, suffering from shock and burns. Dr. Robinson is in attendance upon them.

SHOCKING BURNING FATALITY AT RUNCORN.

On Thursday morning, Mr. J. E. Worsley, coroner, held an inquest at Runcorn Police Court, on the body of Edith May Foster, aged three years and ten months, daughter of Wm. Forster, waterman, of 19 Robert-st, who died on Tuesday from the effects of burns received on Sunday. On the latter date the mother of the deceased went into the yard attached to the house, leaving the deceased and a baby in the dwelling. About five minutes later, the mother heard screams, and as she ran into the house by the bank door, the child ran out at the front door enveloped in flames. A neighbour named Mrs Johnsln wrapped the girl in a shawl and extinguished the flames. The girl who was wearing her nightdress at the time was severely burned and Dr. MAcLennan attended her until her death. A verdict of " accidental death" was returned. Immediately on assembling the Board went into com- mittee, and on the renorters being called into the room, the Chairman asked bra motion.—Mr. Lightburn said the matter had been practically settled in committee,and it was now a formal matter. He would move that Mr. Wm. Fisher be appointed a member of the Board in place of Mr. E. Humphreys, resigned.—Mr. Flankinson seconded the motion, which was carried. Mr. Leach voted against and Mr. Lea did not vote.

MERCIFUL MAGISTRATES AT RUNCORN.

A youth named Thomas Harrop was brought before Messrs. Taylor and Norman at Runcorn Police Court on Wednesday chrged with stealing seven pairs of socks from the shop of Fred Blythe, High-street. P.C. Gregory apprehended the prisoner with six pairs of socks in his possession. He had soil one pair to a man at the Blue Bell Lodging house for 33. lime defendant told a pitiful tale. Be had worked oft the Ship Canal for nearly four years, but for many weeks he had been out of employ- ment and had existed on a few coppers ho had earned by carrying parcels at ,the station. Be was driven to commit the robbery hy hunger, ;ilnl in order to obtain a nights lodgings. In reply to Vie Bench the prisoner said he had a father somewhere in Mauchester. As this was the prisoner first offence the magistrates bound him over tc come up for jod,Tment when called upon. Ho Fah] he would try to .find his father if he the means and Mr. Taylor and Mr. Norman each handed Superintendent Atherton as. for the prisoner's use. A constable pur- chased the prisoner a ticket, saw him safely in the train for Manchester and then handed him the balance. Ma. J. S. OILLIAT, M.P., IT ROBY.

' There was an attendance of about sixty on Monday evening at the Stanley Arms Hotel, Roby, on the occa- sion of the annual hotpot supper in connection with the Huyton polling district of the Widnes Conservative As- sociation. Supper over, Lieutenant Strongitharm pre- sided, others present including Mr. J. S. Giiliat, M.P. for the division ; Mr. Mackenzie Smith, chairman of the association ; Colonel M'Clure, Major J. Royden, and Dr. Hall. During an interval in the programme of music, the Chairman submitted the toast of " Our Member, Mr. Gilfiat." He observed that since Mr.Gilliat's elec- tion that gentleman had worked hard in the interests of his constituency. He had during the last session of Par- liament attended 270 divisions in the house. So long an their member placed his services at their disposal they would return him to Parliament with increased majori- ties. Mr. Gilliat, in response, predicted that the next general election would take place in the present year. He described the Employers' Liability Bill as a measure without any liability whatever to the employers. Touching upon the work of the past year, he said the whole twelve months had been spent in endeavouring to force upon the country a bill which nobody wanted— namely, the Irish Home Rule Bill. Over 8,000 delicious loaves sold every week et C OLLIER.S. —Advt.

div.head: WESTON CRICKET CLUB.
div.p: WESTON CRICKET CLUB.

The annual dinner was fie!d on Friday evening, at the Royal Oak Hotel, Weston. About 60 members and their friends partook of a most substantial and well served repast, prepared by the lancilady,Mrs.G'reen. During last season the team played 14 matches, of which nine were won, three drawn, and two lost. In the batting aver- ages in the first team, the Rev. G. H. Kingston occupit d the head of the list, with 3887 ; whilst Mr. John Light. foot gained the same honourable distinction in the A team, with an average of 12. The number of runs scored by the first team was 1,283, with the loss of 144 wickets average 1125 ; the respective figures of their opponent* being 858, 129, and 6 65. The A. team secured 785 runs for 101 wickets, average 7-77 ; and their opponents 686 runs for 104 wickets, average 6.59. The club is in a good financial position, having a fair ha4nce in hand. The list of membership stands at over 60. A new field has been secuttd, and is being prepared for the com- mencement of next. season, which is expected to be a very successful one. The president of the club, Mr. T. T. Sill, occupied the chair, and was supported by the Revs. G. H. 'Kingston and IV: H. Stables, and the officers of the club. An interesting toast list was gone through. ST. EDWARD'S CATHOLIC CHURCH, RUNCORN.

Or Tuesday evening an excelli.nt entertainment was given in aid of the above church by the scholars attend- ing the school in Bethesda Lecture Hall. The room was crowded. The infants, who had received careful train- ing at the hands'of Mrs. Hardie,went through a musical drill, and gave a chorus in a hi4hly praiseworthy man- ner. S. BillinE;tm recited " Little Bess," and Master J. Finegan and Miss K. Burke gave "Dolly's mamma and the d ctor." After a recitation by five girls entitled " Grindina " had been given, a children's play in two acts, entitled " A real fairy," was gone through. The characters were nicely sustained by M. E. Englesfield, M. Davies, J. Conlon, K. Cain, M. A. Smith, J. Ford, M. A. Mutheran, F. Warred, J. Hun, and M. Dver. The second part consisted of a farce in one act, "The Irish Lion," the dramatic person w in which were Messrs. J. Durr, R. Williamson, J. H. Leigh, A. Hardie, J. Quinn, J. Parker, and J. Feeney ; Mrs. Hardie, Miss Leigh, and Miss R. Caskey. Mr. Williamson and Mr. J. Parker contributed songs. Subsequentl7 a number of those present engaged in dancing.

div.head: CONORI2T AT WESTON CHURCH SCITOOI3.
div.p: CONORI2T AT WESTON CHURCH SCITOOI3.

On Tuesday evening a very successful concert was given in St. John's Schoolroom, in aid of the day schools by the Runcorn Parish Church choir, assisted by Mr. Kershaw aAd Mr. Maddock. The choir, under the leader- ship of Mr. James Littler,gave several glees in a manner richly enjoyed. Songs were contributed by Master E. Newton, Mr. Branch, Master Wilkinson, Master and Mr. M.tddocks (comic.) In several instances encores were aaarded. Mr. Kershaw gave a c-uple of recita- tions, and received a well-deserved recall. Duets were interpreted by Messrs. Littler an Branch. The chair- man, the Rev. W. H. Stables, curate-in-charge, during the interval alluded to the Government regairements having compelled the School Committee to expend £6O in cert,a in alterations. He hoped this sum would soon be cleared off, and that the c,urse would be clear for the great work which was coming rapidly upon them, and which he felt sure would In due course be accomplishei. He referred to the provision of a new church.—Cheers were given for Mr. Littler and the Parish Church choir, as well as for Mr. Kershaw and Mr. Maddock. The accompaniments on the piano were played by Mr. Moor- house.
RUNCORN CO OPERATIVE SOCIETY.

The half-yearly meeting was held in the Co-operative Hall on Tuesday night, under the presidency of Mr. R. Royle. The balance sheet thowed that the total sales amounted to £44,080 94 4d, and the net amount for dis- pos4l was £6,501 17s sd, after charging all expenses, including depreciation and interest on capital and reduc- ing the Ship Canal shares £5O. A dividend af 2s lid was declared, which would absorb £8,423 19s 21, leaving the sum of £B4 183 31 to be placed to the reserve fund. A discussion took place as to the auditor's fees, with nw tangible result. Mr. Clark inquired whether the recorn- mendation of the last meeting with respect to the wages of the employes had been carried out. He understood that neither the general manager nor secretary had received any increase in their salaries. The Chairman pointed out that the Management Committee had no power to alter the salaries of these gentlemen. The matter lay with the members at the general meeting.— In reply to Mr. Worthington, it was stated that the society received 3-.1.> per cent.for the monQvdeposited with the Board of Commissioners. Eventually the balance sheet was adopted. A proposal was made that the next meeting be held in Widnes but it was lost by a large majority. Subsequently a special meetisg was held to consider the Society's rule with regard to the invest- ment of capital, and Mr. Royle said Counsel had advised them that under this rule the Committee could not legally invest money with the United Alkali Co.—lt was stated that the United Alkali shares held by the Society were worth mare than had been paid for them. The ruie was rescinded.
ALLEGED ATTEMPTED SUICIDE BY A LOOM OVERLOOKER.

Albert. Ward, for four • yea's and until recently a loom overlooker at. Cockhedge Mills, Warrington, lies in the Oldham Infirmtry, suffering from wounds inflicted with a knife on his throat and breast on Monday. ,The unfortunate man is now recovering although the injuries were of a severe nature. Ho was well known in Warrington.

div.head: SUSPECTED BURCILARS.
div.p: SUSPECTED BURCILARS.

As is well known, the police tidy,' good reas ons for stvpecting that a gang of burglars are in the town, as there have been so molly attempts of late to enter houses and other buildings during the night time. One night during the present week, a pane of glass was taken out of the back window of a house in Milner-street,and about the ground under the window, there was a large number of clog marks. An entrance into the house, however, was not affected, the burglars, if such they were prob- ably having been disturbed.
PrzßoLEust OILS,—GARLAND, 51, Bridge-street, Warring- ton.
DEATH OF AN EX-TOWN COITNCILLOR.

On Wednesday night, Mr. N. B. Percival, grocer, Buttermarket-st., an ex-town .councillor of War- rington, passed away, at his residence, 6 Salisbury- st., at the ago of 61 years. For a long time, he had suffered from a complication of the heart, and lung disease, but his health had greatly improved, and hopes hqd been entertained that he would recover. He grew worse again, however, on Tuesday, and rapidly sank and died the following day. He leaves a widow and two daughters to mourn his loss. Al- though of a retiring disposition, he has held a large number of public offices in the town. He was a member of the Town Council for a number of years, but retired for a time. In 1887, he was again re- turned for the old S.E. ward, and upon the rearrangement .of the wards, he was appointed to the 'Howley ward. Upon the expiration of his term of office in 1890110 contested theward in the Conserv- ative interest, but was defeated by Mr. Arthur Browne, the Liberal candidate, by a majority of 70. Mr. Percival was also the elmitrnan of the Blue Coat Brotherly Society Committee,and a life governor of the Warrington Infirmary and Hospital. As a Churchman. he took a deep interest in the affairs of the Parish Church where he held the office of rec- tor's warden for a prolonged period and in the ful- filment of his duties was most assiduous end earnest. He was also on the committee of management of the national schools in Church-st., in the work of which ,he took deep interest. Since his defeat in the municipal contest of 1890;he has taken a very small part in the public life of the town, but he leaves behind, a large circle of private friends.

div.head: Br AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.
div.p: Br AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

The freeholders of Runcorn are standing idly by, while Runcorn Hill, that once most pleasant resort is being completely ruined by quarrying operations. Cannot the Commons Committee of the Board of Commissioners take some action ia the matter.

There are not many magistrateA who will enhance the value of their leniency by lending a helping hand to the erring one. Mews. Taylor and Nor- man dealt with a young thief under the Pint Offenders Act on Wednesday and then gave him the means to readi his friends in Manchester. Thrice blessed are the merciful.

The Vicar of Norley is a most persistent man and one might say " cotnprete letter writer" so vol- uminous are his communications to Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority with respect to his schools. In the long run Mr. Nunn will find that the Autiionty backcd by the strong arm of the law, will conquer, and his besit plan would be to suend the time in devising means for satisfying the Authority's demands instead of penning long epistles that do little else but excite a feeling of hilarity.

The marriage of Miss Mabel Brunner, daughter of our respected member, Mr. J. T. Brunner,. to Mr. ff. Parker Lowe, at Allerton, on Tuesday, was a most.brilliant affair. Lord Borthwick, who was groomsman of his friend Mr. Parker Lowe, is the thirteenth holder of a title in the peerage of Scot- land, which was created more than four centuries ago.

At the meeting of Runcorn School Board. on Tuesday night, a hint was given of some consider- able change in the provi*ion for teaching elemen- tary education in the town, that would necessitate not merely the enlarging of Greeuway-road school, but the construction of another large school. Per- haps the next few days may throw more light on the subject.
Mr. Gilliat, M.P., for Widneg, has had a busy week. During the seven seven days he has visited almost every part of his eo nstitueney and has spoken at numerous gatherings, of most diverse aurae. et%

div.p: RUNCORN' 1UU114.1. SANITARY AUTHORITY

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr. Mclntyre presided, and there were present the Rev. 3. W. N. Tanner, and Rev. J. Hanby, Messrs. J. Knowles (vice- chairman),J. Weir, T. Lewis, E. Aaron, 11. E. Hey- wood, Jas. Whitlow, J. M. Williams, J. Bra.ndreth, C. T. 11; hitley, Thos. Ford, T. Baxter, C.C., C. Mn- field; J. Ashton (clerk), G. WATF.R SCHEMES FOR RELSBY.

At a meeting of flelsby Parochial Committee on Satur- day night, Mr. J Brandreth in the chair, schetnes for a water supply for the township were received, as follows: Beloe and Priest, Liverpool, £2,715, exclusive of land engineering and legal expenses ; Moorsotn, Manchester, £2,801, exclusive of land and wayleaves ; Radford, Not- tingham, £3,429, exclusive of land and' professional fees; Timmins, Ruficorn, £3,200, inclusive of land and en- gineers a.n.i law charges. It was resolved that the Clerk be requested to prepare a summary of the schemes giv- ing a comparative statement of, and setting, out in detail, the dimensions, mode of construction, and cost of the different portions of the works, and fOrward a copy thereof to each member of the Committee ; and that the further consideration of the schemes be adjourned to a special meeting on the 17th February.—The minutes were approved on the motion of Mr. Brandreth.
THE CLOSING OF KINGSLEY SCHOOLS. IMPORTANT CORRESPONDENCE.

Mr. Alfred D. Adrian, assistant secretary to the Local Government Board wrote stating that the Board had received from the Education Depart- ment a copy of a letter from the Rev. A. P. Rey- Hold i,appealing against the closing of Kingsley and Newton National' School by the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority. The Board had also received a copy of the authorities' letter of the 12th inst. to the Education Department and of its enclosures. The 11,-)ard had not received from the Medical Officer of Health the report which under section 18 (15) of their order of 23rd March 1891 it was his duty to send them when recommending the closure of the school in question (with others) in November last, and they had no infor- mation as to the ground upon which the closing of the school, rather than the exclusion of children from par- ticular houses, was considered desirable. The Board observed that the notice which the Rural Sanitary Authority on the 26th ult., ordered to be given to the managers of the schools, was not in accordance with article 88 of the Education Code was instead of requiring the closing of the school for a specified time,it requested that the recommendation of the Medical Cfficer of Health might be complied with, no time being specified. The Board requested to be furnished in the observations of the Rural Sanitary Authority on this matter and with an immediate report from the Medical Officer on the subjeat—The following extract wag given from Mr. Reynolds' letter to the Education Department. "At a meeting of the Sanitary Authority held on the 9th January, the Medical Officer Dr. Adams wrote' If the Kingsley schools are re-opened the greatest care must be exercised to see that no children attend from infected houses.' Instead of acting upon this injunction ot the Medical Officer, merely warning us to exercise the care he enjoined, the Guarkian of the parish (who is' not the medical officer) moved a resolution seconded by the Rev. Mr. lienby that the schools be further closed. Before receiving the new notice we had opened our schoels on the Bth.and during last week had 148 out of our average of 160 in attendance, proving that there is no widespread sickness among the child- ren. We have two medical men, Dr. Burton,the parish doctor, and Dr. Selby, a club doctor, dividing between them the work of the parish ; both of these gentlemen have asse:ted that from their knowledge of the parish there is no ground whatever for a notice to close the school so far as the health of the parish is concerned. If I may he permitted to add my personal testimony from daiey visiting in the parish, I have failed altogether to discover any ground for this new notice to cloe, so far as an epidemic is concerned. My point is that Mr. Woo- dward (the Guardian above named) is not the medical officer—if Dr. Adams had said remain closed' I would he the first to respect the notice, but as reported at the meeting he merely suggested the exercise of care, a suggestion always observed here. I beg, therefOre,on behalf of the managers, to enter a protest against the said notice, and respectfully request that some inquiry be made ac to the necessity of observing it. In the meantime, to the serious detriment of school work, we remain closrd."

THE CAUSE OF THE CLOSINO. In reference to this correspondence the Medical Officer (Dr.Adains)stated that scarlet fever occurred in Kingsley as early in last star as July and in Saptember,October and November there were outbreaks in twelve families, in one house there being five cases. It was only after the failure of keeping the children from infected houses in preventing the spread of the disease became apparent. and in view of approaching holidays, that after a con- sultation with the head teacher and the Guardians, I decided to recommend the closing of the schools for at least six weeks. On December 12, one fresh case was reported and on the 16th another fresh case, white later its the same month three fresh 'eases occurred in houses already infected. Li January 1894, however, a recrud- escence of the out break occurred, three fresh cases being reported on Jan. 3:d, four fresh cases on Jan. 4tn, two fresh cases on Jan /Mand one on Jan.lsth,and one case of diphtheria on Jan. 12th. In reply to the Rev. A. P. Reynolds, I would state that these eleven cases were , notified by the two med;cal gentlemen alluded to, ten of them being reported by Dr. Selby on the dates mentioned, they all occurred, however, in houses which' were already infected. Under these circumstances,l con- sidered it advisable that the utmost care should be exer- cised in reopening the schools. During my investigation, I found that there were many cases of " sore throat," and that one of the teachers had suffered from this. The district being a widely scattered one, closure seemed the more efficient method of dealing with the outbreak es- pecially as fresh cases continued to occur even after those known to came from infected heuses were excluded from the schools. I have to express my regret that owing to my unfortunate attack of influenza, by which I was confined to bed. and away from home for three weeks, I omitted to forwari a copy of nry report on the matter to the Local Government Board. 1 have every reason to 1, believe that the outbreak is now subsiding,no fresh cases having been reported for a fortnight. WOODWABD ABSENT. . Mr. Woodward writing on the fifth inst said that " Since 'La Grippe 'has got me, and I am in bed, I can- not possibly he with you to-morrow. I am therefore writing to ask you that in the event sf a reply from the Education Department re loss to schools through com- pulsory closing 'being read, you will be kind enough to , ask that the same be reported in full. I hope I may be sufficiently recovered to be with you a fortnight hence." THE SCHOOLS TO BE REOPENED. Mr, Heywood Said the question 'arose were the Achocls to continue to be closed.—DrAdasns said no fresh cases had been reported from Norley or Kingsley since the last meeting.—Mr. Heywood i Are there any cases P Dr. Adams repliel that there were certainly cases which were capable sf spreading infection if they were allowed to attend school, He should recommend that the mana- gers of the schools receive the official sanction of the Authority to re-open, subject to'precatit ions tieing taken to prevent children attending from inlected houses.—

Mr. Heywood asked would it not be desirable to keep the schools closed a little longer.—Mr. Brandreth pointed out that it was three weeks since the last case was notified.—A membei said this continued closure was a great interference with school work. Mr. Hey wood : We have not to consider the schools but the health of the district.—Dr. Adams said he thought the schools might now be opened providiag children from infected houses were rigorously excluded.—Mr. Bra ndreth moved that the clerk write to the managers of the school that they could re-open on Monday next, with a proviso that those children attacked by scarlet fever since Christmas be not admitted for another month.

THE SCHOOL GRANT QI7ESTION. In reply to the question as to whether a school could possibly lose grant, through being closed on the order of a local authority, Mr. J. W. J. Stephenson, of the Edu- cation Department, write stating "The calculation of tke annual grant is not affected by such closing, the grants for cookery, laundry work and dairy work under article 101 (g) (h) (i) of the Code being pcssible excep- tions."

POLLUTION Or SHIP CANAL. Mr. A. IT. Whitworth writinz under date 26th Janu- ary, stated that early in December last, the attention of the Company was called to the filthy state of the water in the Ship Canal at Haystack Cutting which it appears was causeal by the passage of tanneries refuse down an open drain into the canal. It appears that impure liquid constantly flows down this drain and he was directed to bring the matter to the notice of the Authority and also of the Improvement Commissioners with the object of an abatement of the nuisance. The drainage flows down an open ditch and is no doubt injurious to health.—The Nuisance Inspector said there was an intercepting sewer to intercept all the sewers at a low level at Runcorn, and he understood that the Canal Company were going to extend this intercepting sewer to catch this tannery re- fuse. He had found on inquiry that this had not been done.—Mr. Brandreth said the Canal Company had to deal with all these sewers during the construction of the Canal, and as they had not put A sewer underneath the Canal, because it would cost too much, they now wanted the Authority to do so.—Mr. Aaron said he attended every committee meeting and the Ship Canal Company undertook that every nuisance arising from sewers from Folly Brook, Weston, throughout the whole of the Sani- tary Authority's district they would abate. The Com- pany kept trying this thing on.—The Inspector said it was also mentioned that these liquids would never be- come a nuisance because the outfall was so near the tidal openings that they would get quickly away int) the river.—Mr. Brandreth said the Company ought to ar- range to take the liquid under the Canal.—Eventually it was decided on the motion of Mr. Aaron, seconded by Mr. Brandreth, that a copy of the letter be sent to the Authority's engineer, Mr. L. B. Wells.
TEE VICAR OF NORLEY

The Clerk read the following letter addressed to the Chairman, hr the Rev. C. R. Nunn, vicar of Norley : The report of the discussion re Norlev school at the last meeting reveals further inaccuracies which I beg to cor- rect. It was stated (1) Mr.Nunn will not put his "house (school) in order," whereas I have frequently pressed this matter upon the notice of the managers, and now believe improvements will be made. Moreover, on Dec. 12th I notified that certain alterations would be affected. Again, on January 9th I took upon myself the responsi- bility (in the absence from Norley of two colleaeues) of assuring the Authority that the recommenclatim - ef Dr. Adams' further report would be carried cit. .t as it merely stated that the offices were too el eto the school I inquired whether the Authority would insist upon their removal immediately as the managers might prefer not to build at present, the tune of year and other reasons being against it, unless absolutely neces- sary. One Guardian with his usual wisdom advised the Authority not to say what they required to be done! Again, it was said (2) the Vicar of Norley admits there is no supplvof drinking water for 135 children. Nothing of the kind. There has not been any difficulty in get- ting water when acquired for the 100 children or so in average attendance (not 135). But to satisfy the Autho- rity as far as possible I distinctly stated as far back as' December 12th, 1893, that an adequate filter, regularly filled with good water would be placed in the school. (This has been done). Notwithstanding this promise, it is reported that there is no water supply, and a notice was issued last week to supply it! I have no wish to be involved in any dispute with the Authority, but I maintain your committee has not been well informed of the facts of the case, and that consequently your action has been most unfortunate. I hoped, and am glad to know that my protest will be sent to the Educa- tion Department, and I shall consider it my business to learn from the Education Department or from the Local Government Board what protection there is against per- functory investigations and incorrect reports. I res- pectfully submit that it is the bounden duty of the Authority to siatisfy themselves that the reports of their officers are based upon adeqnate and personal investiga- tion before taking the serious step of closing schools for weeks ; and that if an officer by reason of illness is unable to perform his duties a deputy might prevent inconvenience to the public, and probably save schools from being closed longer than is necessary on reports which are not true to fact.--P.S. Mr. Woodward has apparently climbed down as far as Kingsley school is concerned, and no wonder his henchman, Mr. Hanby, hoped nothing more would be heard of the matter. Their irresponsible levity may be suitably described—as they rightly suggested—on foolscap. It is hoped they may have sufficient grace to do the next most " fitting " thing—put it on. (Loud laughter.)—Mr. Heywood said after hearing that letter, he thought they bad best hold the next meeting at Norley, and then they could be per- sunally responsible for what happened.—The Clerk said he hoped Mr. Nunn would not write many more letters. They took up a lot of time reading and a lot of space in the minute book. (Laughter.)—The Inspector reported that he had served Mr. Nunn with a notice to provide a water supply for the schools.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THURSDAY. —Before Messrs. E. K. Muspratt and J. Birchall.

FINED FOR DRUNRENNESS.—GetIfge H. Moore, no fixed abode; John Rooney, Alpha-street; William Moran, Victoria-street; James Lewis, Dock-street; Michael Fallon, Cromwell-street; and Michael Griffin, Derby- road.

BREACHES OF THE PEACE.—Mary Blond, Elizabeth Lewis, and Catherine Lewis, all residents of Dock-street were summoned for having caused a disturbance ot the peace on January 27th, and were bound over to keep the peace for three months, or in default of finding two sureties of £5, to go to gaol for 14 days. THEFT OP COKE.—John Beelis, Thos. Curley. and John Allender, lads residing in Dock-st., were charged with stealing about lewt. of cokc.. from the Liverpool Silver and Copper Co.'s works, Ditton-road.—Heelis was fined 10s., and the other defenaants were bound over to come up for judgment if called upon. THEFT OF TIMBER. —TIIOMAS Howard, Appleton-st., Thomas Burke, Catherine-st., Patrick Daley, Elizabeth- st., and Patrick Fallon, Victoria-st., were charged with stealing a quantity of timber from an unoccupied h-,use in Pearson-st., the property of the L.Sr,N W. Rail- way Co.—Howard was ordered to receive six strokes; Fallon, 12 strokes ; and the other two were bound over.

div.head: FRODSHAIsi.
div.p: FRODSHAIsi.

PAROCHIAL CommyrrEEs.—The monthly meeting of these Committees has been held, under the presidency of Mr. A. Thomas, J.P. Mr. Chad, s E. Linaker gave a verbal report as to the state and condition of the main sewer from the Bear's Paw to the Sea Flatt's outfall, and presented for consideration the several levels from which it appeared that there were unmistakable signs of a breach in the sewer in the main street, possibly caused by the quicksand through which a short length was laid A small sub-committee was appointed to confer with Mr. Linaker as to rectifying the defective length. With regard to the lighting district of Frodsham, it was agreed that the gas Inspectors should be advised that the Authority take over the duties of such inspectors as and from the sth instant. A letter was read from the Public Works Loan Commissioners informing the Committees that the sum ot £3,600 would be lent to the Authority on the security of the rates of Frodsha.ni, to be repay- able in thirty years. ALLEGED THEFT DY A SERVANT.—On Monday after- noon. at Frodsham Police Court, before Mr. A. Thomas, Alice Foyer, ag:id 21 years, domestic servant, a native of Frodsham Bridge, was charged with stealing £3 in gold from a writing desk in a bedroom, the property of George Davies, farmer, Frodshaun, between the 13th of January and February 2nd and also with stealing two hen eggs, value 2d., -belonging to Mr. Davies. The prisoner keenly felt her position, and wept whilst in court.—Prosecutor stated that he saw the money safe on ' the 13th January, when he placed six sovereigns in a 1 writing desk in his bedroom. He missed it on Friday, having no occasion to open the desk between the dates. Be saw Sergeant Thomas and reported the matter to ' him. The same evening the officer saw Foyer, who at first denied the theft, but when he was proceeding up- stairs to examine her box, she promised to get the money and return it. Ultimately she acknowledged taking it.—A remand until Wednesday was granted.
AGED PEOPLE'S TREAT AT RUNCORN. -

The annual treat to the old people of Runcorn took place on Tuesday evening in Runcorn Pubiic Hall. The arrangements bad been made on the usual complete scale. Subscriptions both in money and kind had beesa gathered and a good repast was spread before the 400 guests who assembled.

A warp dresser at Dudley Hill, Bradford, named Les- ter Bastow, was on Wednesday discovered to have mur- dered his wife akd a fifteen-year oki daughter by cutt- ing their throats, and to have afterwards committed suicide. Bastow had been out of work for some time, ' and there was evidence of extrvine poverty in the house.

div.head: TOWN CoUNUIL NOTES.
div.p: TOWN CoUNUIL NOTES.

lAl3errnan Francomb, the Deputy-Mayor, presided at the rneetinp. of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday evening (for the Mayor is still enjoy- ing the milder climate of Mentone), and at the very outset he excited, but did not gratify, the curiosity of his auditors—of those at all events who are not in the " inner circle." He announced that he had received a letter from Mr. John Crosfield anent the gates that are to be erected in front of the Town Hall, but as the subject was not mentioned on the minutes and as Mr.Crofield was labouring under a misappre- ' hension—so said the Deputy-Mayor—the letter would not be readmut the Town Clerk would under- take the work of answering it. No questions were asked, and then the matter droppeu for the time being.

There did not seem to be much room for develop- ments on the minutes of the Watch Committee. A few licenses to haekney carriage owners and drivers, and marine store dealers, the appointment of a small sub-committee to carry out the onerous work of selecting policemen's clothing, and that was all. But Councillor Monks pronounced in fa- vour of aboiishing the cabstand in Cairo-street. He pointed out that the street was narrow, that there was sometimes a whole string of cabs standing there, and that residents in the street and worship- pers at the Unitarian Chapel alike complained of a nuisance. The Deputy-Mayor explained that the cab-owner who has the benefit of this tittuid was strictly limited as to the manner in which he was to make use ot the privilege, and that the cab in- spector was expected to keep his eyes open and see that these limitations were not over-stepped. It they were—well, lie thought he might promise that that cabstand would be non est. Having been thus placated, Councillor Monks withdrew his proposal. Then Councillor Jas.Fairclough inquired if there was anything in the nature of municipal law to keep carts and lames on their own side of the street. He complained that dilatory drivers were in the habit of enjoying the rilxious weed on the footpaths, while the animals of which they were in charge perambulated along the centre of the road- way, thus obstructing the passage Gf vehicles corn- ing at a brisker pace behind. The Corporation drivers, Mr. Fairclough confessed, were the worst offenders. It was explained that the law was equal to the emergeacy. and that it was the plice through which the law operated.

There was little now between the Council and the chief dish of the et ening—or shall we call it the pica de resistance. This was the proposal of the Sanitary Works Committee to increase the salary of Mr. Dees, the manager at Longford, by £lOO a year, that is to say, from £2OO to £3OO. But, first of all, Coun- cillor Monks, the chairman of the Committee, pro- posed that the Council should go into Committee to discuss that particular subject. This unusual pro- position seemed to take the majority of the Council by surprise, and, though it was supported by a num- ber of members, it was rejected by a decisive majority. :qr. Monks then moved the Committee's recommendation in an admirably arranged and lucid speech. He alluded to the past difficulties at, Long- ford, the confusion that prevailed there at one time, the improvements both in methods and machinery that have . been introduced by the present manager, and the remarkable savings that have been effected in the working expenses. For these reasons and others he was strongly of opinion that the additional £lOO should be granted.

Councillor Flood who is also a member of the Sanitary Works Committee moved, on the other hand, that the proposal should not be carried. It as soon evident that there was to be plenty of support for the amendment. It was seconded by Councillor Shaw and supported byCouncillor Davies the latter gentleman contending that a rise of .£lOll was too much after only two yearh'• service under the Corporation. Councillor Muir suggested thht recourse should be had to the eminently commercial device of" splitting the difference," by giving Mr. Deas £5O instead of the £lOO. Councillor Roberts declared that he would vote for the £lOO, and if, that were rejected, for £75, and, finally, if need be for £5O, according to the maxim that half a loaf is better than no bread. The next speaker was Alderman Harrison, who, in the course of the meeting, performed some intricate uyrations. He had, he said, come with the inten- tion of voting fur the £lOO, but having beard tkv.r it was not by any means a unanimous proposal on the part of the Committee, he pronounced against it and in favour of the £5O. In the end, however, be voted for the Committee's prvosal as it stood on the minutes.

Councillor Skelton was in favour of the amend- ment, and so was Councillor Longton, Alderman Sutton backed the Committee as did Councillors R. T. Fairclough and Greening, while there were ar- rayed on the other side Councillors Smethurst (whose opposition was of the root and branch order), Heaton, and Shaw. Councillor Shaw was in a particularly militant mood and seemed dis- posed to carry the war into the enemy's country. An accusation that some of the Councillors took care to" get over the border" from the heavy rates of the town led to a lively altercation between him and Councillor Roberts, in which some of tee choicest flowers of debate were introduced. The Councillor who lives in Bewsey but represents St. John's alleged that Mr. Roberts' qualification as a burgess rests upon a stable; and Mr. Roberts admitted that he had a stable but added that he wanted a donkey for the stable and he should apply to Councillor Shaw for it. This sally raised a laugh but Councillor Shaw dec:ared he had not heard it. If Mr. Roberts would, how ,ver, repeat it to him private he would " square accounts," or something to that effect. Councillor Beaman next supported the committee, but a rote that was taken went, against them, and in favour of Mr. Flood's amend- ment. by fourteen to eleven.

Thesubject was, however, not done with, for Councillor lie.pherd a; once prepo.,,ed an in- crease of £5O. To this proposition there was prac- tically no opposition, but in the debate that ensued Councillor Roberts and Councillor Shaw again came into collision and the" scene" that followed affords some lively reading. The only part of the remain- ing business was the raising of the salary of the cashier in the gas offices from £l5O to £2OO a yea-, and of the chief clerk in the same offices from £lOO to £llO.

div.head: GARDENING AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: GARDENING AT WARRINGTON.
FORMATION OF A HORTICULTURAL SOCIETY.

For some weeks a number of gentlemen have been agitating for the formation of a society for the encouragement of the growing of flowers in War- rington and the neighbourhood, and on Monday evening, a meeting to consider the subject wa, called, at the fown Hall. Alderman R. W. Francomb (the, deputy-mayor), presided over the meeting, which was attended by a good number of gardeners, amateur and professional. The Chairman said that he was ask& to preside over the meeting by Mr. Ryan, who appeared to be an enthusiast in the matter and deserved to be encouraged. In manufacturing towns like Warrington, there was little else to look at but chimneys and black smoke, and the object of the proposed society was to encourage the working-classes to grow flowers in their windows and in their back yards and even to have small greenhouses. It was quite a mistake to think that flowers could not be grown in a manufacturing town, for some years ago a gentleman at Warrington produced some specimens of auriculas which beat some of the first gardeners in the kingdom. He thought there was great ' cause for encouragement, for there was a great /lumber of flowers grown in the neighbourhood of Warrington, particularly chrysanthemums, in fact Mr. Ceosfield's houses were equal to any in the county of Lancashire.— Mr. H. Isherwood proposed that a society be formed re be named the Warrington Floral and Horticultural Society.—Councillor Bolton seconded, and Councillor Smethurst said that he would give a copper kettle to the I best flowers grown in a cottage.—The motion was car- ' rid d unanimously. —Mr. Fairhurst proposed that Mr. James Ryan be appointed secretary. He took a great interest in the formation of it, and they could not hay, a better. With reference to greenhouses ii heel, N aria. Ihe (the speaker) would advise the people '.o as the powers that be " before getting one, as It was neces sary to have so much space in the varce—Councillor Bolton seconded the motion,but quite disagreed with Mr. Fairhurst as to the bye laws concerning the back yards. Greenhouses helped to make them healthier, and he I therefore did not think th at they would get into any ! trouble by having greenhouses in their yards. (Laugh- ter.) The motion was carried. —Mr. Wm. Gill proposed I that Mr. Fulton Smith be treasurer, Mr. Thompson seconded.—Carried.—The following gentlemen were I elected as a committee :—Alderman Francomb, Coun- cillors Bolton, Dr. Cannel!, and Smethur,t, Messrs. I. Parker, Hipps, Joseph Grounds, Handles, Heasom, Skel- ton, H. Isherwood, Lockhart, and Starkey.—The sub- scripti en was fixed at 2s. 64. per annum.— the meeting I then terminated, and Mr. Ryan wassuccessful in ttiml f good number of names of persons intending to jo. the: society.

I have been supplied with a few particulars of the Penketh Penny Bank, which seems to be a 1 uzcfal ani flourishing institution. It is mentioned that this is one of the very few penny banks that have survived since the opening, some thirty-nine 1 years ago, and it is, therefore, amongst the oldest existing. The object of the bank is to encourage the deposit of small sums, and especially by young people,so as to promote habits of thrift and saving, i and, judging by the amount of business done, the object must be pretty well secured. During 1893 there has been a total number of 1373 transactions, and the ampunt deposited in that period was £395 13s. Bd., the amount withdrawn being £343 16s. 9d. The sum credited to depositors in the ledger is. £1,667 Bi.ld. Tile treasurer, it may be mentioned, are Mr. It. Garnett, J.l',. and Mr. D. Garnett.

The meeting to consider the formation of a floral society was a successful one in point of numbers,' and now that a society has been formed there will ,be some encouragement for gardeners, whether' they be amateur or professional to cultivate witts greater diligence the various kinds of garden pro- duce. It is expected that a show will take place in August or thereabouts. The laws regulating back yard-4 evidently need considerable explanation, for Mr. Fairhurst,the borough treasurer,was of opinion that it would be wise on the part of those wishing to have a greenhouse in thcir back yards, to take the local authorities into their confidence. Coun- cillor Bolton on the other hand thinks that it would lft; absurd to prosecute a man for having a green- house in his yard. As the town clerk was not pre- sent, the question remained unsolved. However, to judge from the nember of amateur and profes- sional gardeners present at the meeting, there is every prospect of success before the venture.

The following letter from the member for War- rington should prove interesting to your readers, for it is a curiosity in its way. The attempt ta formulate a joke at the expense of the Gladstonians is really superb. The letter, it should be explained, was read at the meeting of the Warrington Debating Society on Tuesday evening, having been sent to Councillor Bennett, one of the secretaries. It reads es followa ;—" Shepf!eard's Hotel, Cairo, Egypt, Jan uury 26th 1894.—Dear M r. Bennett,- -It was only last evening, in my arrival here, that I got your letter of the 13th. I hope that, long before new, you have found out that lam aboard. You will see that I must with regret excuse myself from being preeent at the coming meetings of the Debat- ing Society, I think that you and my many other friends in Warrington will grant that, after a ses- sion beginning on the 31. t ofJanuary, 1893, admit- ting of but. little holiday. I claim (I do net say I have a riht) to a real helidly, both for pleasure and for health—and these tw,)go together—eveci- ally as when one gets to the larger England which begins (say) at Gibraltar, the stray Gladstomians are eo scarce that the few that there are who may be hunted down and caught might well, alter being stuffed with the dry speeches of their leader,be put into the museums where they keep antique curiosities, or strange seal for mations. lam here for cnly a few days—afterwards I go probably to Syria and Asia ninon—Yours very truly, ROBERT PIBB.POINT."

Another addition has been made to the publica- tions issued from Warrington. The first of a new series of the "British Nat uralist" magazine has been published this week under the joint editorship of Councillor L. Greening and Mr. Joseph Smith, A glance at the new issue shows that it contains promise of being a publication of high merit, both in regard to its " get-up," and in the selection of its contents. The editors promise, he- ides matter from their own pens—and they are both writers of some weight on subjects of natural history—contributions from several well known naturalists, and locally from Dr. Charles While, Dr. B kiwden, D. Langflaie. and Mr. A. J. JAley. Of its kind the magoitne claims to he one oi the most extensively eirilate,,d puhlications in the British Isles, and that so much of its management should t-ntrusted to Warrington naturalists is no moan tribuie to the reputation they have won.

Berry stated that he met the defendant on Saturday nieht. He had the quilt (produced) in his possession, and as he could not give a satisfactory account of it, witness took him to the Police Station and charged ;him with having stolen the article, when he replied " I must have stolen it, but I de not remember."—Oh the application of Superintendent Keighley defendant was remanded for a week for the police to make inquiries. The Warringten fifteen set out on Saturday, on their annual tour. They journeyed to Birmingham, meeting Moseley in the return match at the Redding,s. There was a capital attendance, and both sides played their best available fifteens, the most conspicuous absentees being James Bate, Jolley, and Nevins from the Warring- ton side, and Byrne fram Moseley. Only two thirties were played, and Bate, winning the toss, took advant- age of the high wind, which blow from goal to goal. The kick-off was finally charged by Taylor, who cleared Rogers, and nearing Rowlands he passed across to Bailey, who failed to take the proffered chance. Byrne piloted out of danger, and vigorous forward rushes by the home front rank realized neutral quarters. Thorniley Berry, and Turner, ably led the way back to the attack, and Dakin made one desperateeffert, being checked when only a few inches off the goal. Warrington were exhibiting capital combination, and after Barber and Potts had made unsuccessful essays te get through, Evans got possession, and easily dodging Stone he rushed over the line, gaining a meritorious try, which he failed to enhance. Tne drop-out was met by Heesom, and for some informality Warrington were penalized, but the kick did not serve Moseley well, for Heesone piloted back to the local 25 flag. Rogers struggled hard and cleared slightly, and handing back to lamas, Handles stepped in, and cross dribbling by that player, laerry and Bailey gave Rowlands trouble once more. Another round of passing by the Warring- ton backs was checked in its finishing essay, but Barber kicked neatly to Rogers who failed in fielding the oval, and in the general melee which followed Berry took the leather over, but again Evans was at fault with the place. The home custodian saved repeatedly, and after three miners had been ehrenicled in as mazy minutes, a grand spell of passing betweea Evans, Bate, Potts, sad Barber saw the latter held a yard inside, Rogers using unnecessary vigour in tackling the visitors. Again did Moseley relieve oaly to see Taylor effect a fine dribble, Which should have been turned to good account. Rogers got clear but failed to pass Potts, arid then Broady made his niark,Turner tryieg to shot at goal from a difficult angle. The leather travelled wide of the mark, hut several opportunities were lest by the leaders owing to a want of judicious play in the final essay. Rowlands again saved from a forward rush, and after Lomas had effect- ed a run to half-way, the home forwards by the aid of the tactics already mentioned gave Hi436OM trouble. When half-time was called, with the score—Warrington Warrington, two tries ; Moeeley, nii. The earns was speedily resumed, and exchanges between Evans and Rogers ended to the formers' credit. The outcome of the prolonged attack was a minor. After Turner had spoiled Rogers in taking a pass from Stone, Potts, Carey,and Broady passed neatly,and the sequence beiug assisted by a free dribble by Berry and Thorniley, Mose- ley were hard pressed. Rain now fell in torrent, and Warrington were at a double disadvantaee in having to face the heavy downpour. However, they continued to attack, mad Rowlands was lucky he saving after Turner, Thorniley, and Evans dribbled to the line. Tee locals made another effort, and the visitors failing to check their progress, the ball was taken ever ancr Fount:ley scored a try far out. Tide was the lest chance Moseley had, for Warrington new displayed their fine stamina, and their opponents began to show signs of distress. A round of passing started by Potts and tekan part in by Bate, Carey, and liarber saw the latter racing over anti putting the fini:;lnal touch to an excellent bit of dem- bination. The locals were now beaten completely, and after the drop out Warrington renewed the attack through the instrumentality of Bates and Evans. Carey scored uner the close of the game andWarringten won by 4 tries to 1. Teanas :—Warrington: Hoesom,b-acli; Broady, Potts, Carey, and Barber, three-quarters ; Bet e and Evans, half h-aek Turner, Taylor; Dakis4, rhornl!ey, Berry, Donohue' Bailey. and Bandies, fotwards. Moee- ley : Rowlands, back ; Rozers, Byrne, and Lemas,threa- quartets ; Stone and Challinor, half backs ; Rogers,E.R. Lycett, Pountner, Rossitor, Insworal, flunaphreys,Cat- tell, Allan, and Dods, forwards.

WARRINGTON A V. D11071.1:5M107 HORNBTS. teams mot at Wilderspool Causeway enclosure on Satur- day, but as the visitors arrived three quarters of an hour late, the spectators ideelme soieewhat impatient,. before the match began. rho game was commenced at four o'clock, and owing to the strong wind prevailing, it was divided into four quarters. The visitors won the toes and tsok advantage of the wind during the first quarter' but for a time Warrington were very dangerous until the Hornets threct•quarters repelled the attack, and llampson did his side a good turn by reaching past the centre line. The first quarter was finisheel without any scare, although Drnyleselen ha,d had the best of it, but were unable to penetrate the good siefenco of Warring- ton. With the wind at their backs, Warrington quickly set to work, and after a short spurt by tho Hornets, Haughton did some excellent work, and by a neat pass to Burton, enabled that plaaer to score, after a dodgy run round his opponents, the place kick failing. War- rington continued to have the best of the game until the close of this quarter, which brought half-time with the score of Warrington one try to nil. Droylesden again attacked after the interval, and faun a long pass, Reed got the better of the Warrington players, and romped over, and the place kick put the Hornets two points ahead of Warrington. Desperate efforts to score were made by Burton, but in vain, and tho third quarter arrived with the visitors leading by a goal to. a try. Immediately after the commencement of the last quar- ter, Burton scored his second try, but Warrington again showed their need of a goal kicker, for the place hick was again a failure. The Hornets from this point to the end of the game, had slightly the better of the game and matters looked dangerous when they had a shot at, goal from a mark, but this failed, and Warrington ran out victors by the narrow victory of two trios %six points) to a goal (five points). WARRINGTON ST MARY'S Y. WIGAN RI4CRISA.TION.--ThlS match was played at Warrington on Saturday in rather boi,terous weather. The visitors arrived late, and two half-hours were decided upon. Wigan kicked off against the strong vrind. and were soon called upon to emend, but kept their opponents at bay for a considerable time, when, by sonic neat passing by the Saints' backs, War- burton ran in at the corner, the kick at goal failing. After the drop-out the Bees, played up with determina- tion, but could make no head way against the wincLand on the call of half-time the score stood St. Mary's, 1 try; Wigan, nil. On changing ends, the Saints had to play against the wind, but they soon made affairs look rather dangerous for the Recs. Bennett and Berry being tackled on the line, only to gain a minor. This brought but short relief to the Recs. as P. Hill made a grand run and scoreel, the kick at goal . again failing. Shortly after this, the Recs. made a forward rush and scored, but the point was not improved. The ball being again put into motion, both teams played a hard and vigorous game, and on the call of time nothing more had been scored, and St. Mary's retired winners by 2 tries to 1, this being tne thirteenth match that the Saints have won m suc- cession. SWINTON.—Owing to the action of Swin- ton, in refusing to play their fixture at Runcorn on Saturday, football was at a discount. However, a match was hastily arranged between players from the Ist and "A " teams. An enjoyable game was played, in which the juniors showed some excellent points, and with care- ful training will quickly develop into first class players. Robinson and Warder scored for the Ist team, Butter- worth converting one of the tries. The "A "team failed to notch a point, although they experienced hard luck on several Occasions. A great amount of feeling was manifested in football eircles in Runcorn on Satur- day, through the action of Swinton, in refusing to play their fixture on the Irwell-lane enolosure. Referring to the matter, the" Athletic News" has the following re- marks, which are in no way too strong :—" It is not often that a football fixture is abandoned, unless the weather is unsuitable, and, as a rule arrangements made between clubs are sacredly honoured. Therefore we are all the more surprised to find that Swinton re- fused to go to Runcorn on Saturday on the fiimsy pre-i text that, having two men playing for Lancashire, 1 they were unable to raise a team. This excuse is so palpably frivolous on the fate that we cannot but re- gret that an important organisation like Swinton should have descended to such a paltry and mean subterfuge in order to get out of an engagement which they had no liking far. Runcorn have our sympathy in this matter. They have never shirked their responsibilities, and when the county calla upon their members they don't make silly excuses te their opponents. During the semen Runcorn have won 15 matches, drawn four, and loot three, and have scored 27 goals and 37 tries against six goals and seven tries gained by their adversaries."

CHARGIR AGAINST A TRADESIftN. At the Borough Court on Monday, H. Green provision dealer, 4, Lyme-et., was charged with haying on the 19th January exposed for sale a certain quantity of margarine without having attached a label " mare:tr- ine," and ha was also charged with seiling to Bliss Hill, some margarine in the name of butter.—lnspector Nor- man said he saw in the defendant's window'some large parcels of what bethought was butter, as they were not labelled. He instructed a Mrs. Hill to make a purchase for him. She did so, and he took the purchase from her and told the man he would have it analysed, and he would leave him one third. The defendant replied that be needn't have it analysed, it was margarine, and he bad sold it as margarine. There were eleven other par- cels of margarine not labelled which made the defendant liable to a penalty of £220, but he had only bummconed him for one parcel. The defendant told him he hoped he would not be very hard with him.—Mrs. Hill said that acting upon instructions from Inspector Norman. she went into the defendant's shop and asked for a pseend of Bd. butter. She then handed the parcel to lespector Norman .—Mr.Forsha w ,soli eitor, who appeared for the defendant said, with regard to the charge of aelling the margarine in the name of butter, the woman was toid that they had no eightpenny butter, but they bad margarine, and the woman made no reply. With regard to the other charge, he admitted that a technical odence had been committed. Friday night •xas the defendant's cleaning up night, aid the label had not been axed on when the Inspector came in.—lnspector Norman said there were five parcels in the windowwith- eat labels, and the defendant told hi ne he had no labels. —Evidence for the defence supporting Mr. Forshaves statement was given by the defendant and his brother. At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednes- day, Samuel Lee, Watkin-street, Warrington, was charged with stealing one cock and six hens from the hencote of Margaret Ann Faircloueh, value £1 3s. Prisoner pleaded guilty. The complainant sti-,ted that she lived in Crow-lane, Great Sankey. On the likh January she saw her fowls safe in the hencote,—P.C. Cooper said he met this prisoner and another man in Hallam-lane on Saturday, the 26:h January. Notichu.' the prisoners' pockets very bulky,he asked him what he had in them. The prisoner replied " Nothing." Wit- resa told him of the fowls' legs protruding from his poc- beta, and he then replied that he had just bought them. Soon afterwards the prisoner became very rough, and eventually got away. He was re-captured the same piglet. The prisoner had served fourteen days in gaol for the assault.—P.C. Dugdala deposed to receiving the prisoner in custody from the Warrington police. In reply to the charge. the prisoner admitted taking the fowls, and said he threw some in the Sankey (lanai as they were too heavy to carry. He was committed to gaol for two months' bard lat-aiur. William Henry Monks, 41, Knutsford-road, was sum- *toned before the Warringt.o magistrates yesterday, on the charze of assaulting and bating Robert Flatman. 1.0.3, Mersey-road, on Feb. sth. Mr. P. Davies prose- cuted, and Mr. A. Browne defended. Before the open- ing statement, Mr. Browne a/lred Mr. Davies if he was going on with the case. eA Ain. Monks, the defendant's Mother, and Flatman had cnuie to an agreement.where- by tman bad accepted lO—r. Davies said that his ineruct'ons were that thero war; no settlement, and that the case must go on. The Mt. would be returned to Monks. The present ease reee out of an unfortunate

owl's which was heard a fortnight ago, in which Mr. Fleming. was the defendant, and Mr. Monks the corn-' plainant, and in which there was also a cross-summons. On that occasion, Mr. Jenkins appeared for Monks, and made an application for all witnesses to leave the court. Flatman was a witness on that occasion, for M. Flem- ing, and left the court, hut it was net found necessary to call him. That was the only cause of animus that could possibly exist in Monks' mind against complainant for there had previously been no quarrel of. any kind be- tween them. Flatman was a blacksmith in the employ of Mr. John Fleming, contractor, and on Monday morning he was tout by Mr. Fleming to Monks' premises in Arpley to repair a cart arm which was brolten. He took the cart arm away 4nd after repairing it, he came beck and found the cart turned upside down. He asked Monks who bed done it, and Monks replied that he had not. Monks then told Flatman that he dared not have a drink with him or he would get the "sack." Flattnan,however, said he dared, and they went across to the " Ring-o-bells," where Flat- man got two pints of beer, and as he had had some pre- viously, he became very drunk. When they returned to the rope walk, they began "sparring, "and Flatman told Monks that he had told a lot of lies at the castle; on the occasion of the above mentioned case. This vexed Monks, and in a temper he struck Flatman a violent blow in the face, krakeking him to the ground. Danbob- bin, a worktnan of Monks, lifted Flatman up, and he was knoeked down again. This was done three timee. Thomas Ward, a labourer of Flatman's was near by, but dared not come to his assistance. After Flatman had recovered from the blows, Monks asked him to come and have a drink, but Flatman told him he would have to pay for it, and engaged Lim (Mr. Davies). The in- juries he had received were of a very serious natere,and he contended that the complainant had made a mistake in not sunimonsieig for a more serious offence than as- sault —After anotlier ineffectual effort at settlement by Mr. Browne, Robert Flatman, and Thomas Ward gave evidence in support of the clearge.—Dr, Peacoeke said that he saw the complainant on Mooday, .and his eyes were " bunged np." His chest was also severely bruised and he might have received some internal injuriee.—Mr. Browne contended that the whole affair was a stand-up fight between the two parties,and said that Flatmate had endeavoured to tear Monks' mouth with his hand.—Wm. Dunbobbin, sen., gave evidence in support of this state- ment, and said that he had tried several times to separ- ate them.—The magistrates retired to consider their de- cision,and on returning said that they had decided to fine Menks 10s. and costs, and order him to pay a guinea and a half for the doctor's fee, and a guinea for the solicitor's fee.
