INDUSTRIAL SCHOOL ORDERS.--JOIHI Henry Houghton was summoned to show cause why an order should not be made upon him to contribute towercis the mainten- znce of his son in Chester Industrial School.—Superin- tendent Atherton said the defendant had promised to pay is. per week, but he was now 29 weeks in arrears. He asked for an order.—The Bench made an order of 23. 61. a week.—Michael Phillyn, of Mersey-street, was brought up under similar circumstances. His son is an inmate of Bishop Brown's Industrial School, Stockport, and he agreed to pay Is. per week. He was 31s. is arrears.—An order of is. 64. was made. ALLEGED CRUELTY TO A HORSR.—John Murphy was summoned for cruelly ill-treating a horse whilst in an unfit state.—John Baguley, foreman, Hallwood Farm, 1 Balton, was summoned for causing the horse to be 1 worked.—Percy George Luff, an inspector of the R.S.P.C,A: at Warrington, deposed tc seeing the horse drawing a load of manure in Church-street, Runcorn. ' It was very lame on both forelegs, and there was an old sprain of the back tendon. After walking a few yards, the horse blew and sweat a great deal, and was evidently in great pain. The animal was a perfect cripple.—ln reply to Mr. Baguley, witness said the horse was in good condition.—lnspector Cooper corroborated.—Mr. Bagu- ley denied that the horse was is pain, and said if there had been pain the horse would have lost flesh.—Mr. Lancely, veterinary surron, Frodsham, said he ex- amined the horse on the 24th inst., and found that a shoe had become displaced, and caused extra weight to be on the foot. Pain would thereby be caused. The horse would do very well for farm work on soft land,but he would not stand on a hard road.—Mr. Reynolds said Mr. Baguley probably did not know he was putting the horse to pain, and they would dismiss the case. He must confine the animal to farm work ;he muss not work it on the road.—Mr. Baguley said he could not work the animal en the farm without taking him on the highvray.—Defeadants wore ordered to pay costs ss. Eld. in each case. A QUARREL BETWEEN BOAT-PEOPLE. —Samuel Bailey and Lucy Bailey, of the boats Rose and Loretta, were summoned at the instaece of John Threlfall for assault- ing him on the 20th January.—A cross-summons was taken oat again Threlfall for assaulting Lucy Bailey. In thefirst case complainant stated that he was assistiag to

take a boat clown the locks, when Mrs. Bailey struck him and kicked him several times. Her husband then got held of him and shook him, at the same time threatening that if it were not for the law he would throw him into the canal.—A constable named Molyneux said he wit- nessed the assault.—ln the case against Threlfall, Lucy itailm, stated that tha defendant was the first to strike. her with a rope across the mouth. She struck him back, and in self-dafence repeated the close.—The case against fbrelfall was dismissed. and Samuel Bailey and Lucy Bailey were each fined 59. and 13s. costs.

div.p: NAWTON BOiRD OF COMMISSIONERS.
MZDICAL OFFICERS REPORT.-A HIGH DA en! BATE._ _ _

The monthly m;e—til-g—ol. the Newton Board of Couenai.s,sioners was bald at the Town Hall. Earles- town, on Monday. Tnere were present : Messrs. J. W. Emmett (chairman) T. Orreand, P. McMahon, P. ' Thompson, G. Ratcliffe, T. For6ter, Dr. Watkins (medical officer), J. E. Woraley (law clerk) R. Itrierly (surveyor.) T. J. eILLESPITSS RESIGNATION. The Chairman read a letter from Mr. T. J. Gillespie who regretted to inform the Board that owing to the . little time which he was able to devote to the business • of Lie position among them, he found it necessary to send in is re-signation. 411 hairman said he was ex- ceedingly sorry that Mr. Gillespie had tendered them his resignation. He had been a member of the Commis- ! sioners for 14 or 15 years and be could safely say that during that time Mr. Gillespie had discharged the duties that devolved upon him with ability and conscientious regard for what lie thought was the best for the rate- payers. (Applause.) He therefore sincerely hoped— end he was sure he only expressed their unanimous feeling—that Mr. Gillespie would withdraw his resigna- tion and give them the further benefit of his long and valuable experience. (Applause.) Of course they all knew that Mr. Gillespie had not always been able to , vote with the majerity—indeed, he hoped the day would come when the interest in public affairs should be killed by such harmony if agreement—but then he had voted with conscientious regard for his views and feelings on the matter. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Gillespie was one of their most reispe.cted and eapahle members and he sincerely hoped he would be aisle to see his way to with- draw his re.signation. (Haar hear.) Mr. G. Ratcliffe expressed his regret that Mr. Gillespie had sent in his resignation, and he proposed that Mr. Gillespie be asked to withdraw his resignation.—Mr. Forster seconded the proposition, which was carried unanimously.

GAS AND WATER COMMITTER. A :netting of this Committee was held on January 15. The Gas Manager's report then submitted gave the quantity of furl used during- the past six weeks as 603 tons at an average cost of 121. 6d. per ton. It was also ordered that Mr. Brierly confer witm the Law Clerk upon the contract with the Whitecress Co., respecting the con- tract for cannel nuts. The carleonizing account for the pat month was read giving fuel used 439 tons 12 cwts, gas made 4,409,000, being an average of 10,027 kt. per tom of fuel used. Mr. Briefly having certified for £4OO due to Messrs. Woodhouse and Rawson in contract for gasholder, it was ordered that a cheque be drawn for that amount. The minutes were adopted.

meting of tt7i7C-o-i-nria-itiTde was held on the 15th of February. The application of the postal authorities for permission to erect a pillar letter-box on the footpath opposite the Post Office, Earl-at., was considered. It was felt that such an arrangement would create a nuis- ance and would not supply the accommodation which the public required. It was therefore decided not to grant the application. It was further reported that in compliance with the request from the county authori- ties, Mr. Briery had submitted his estimates for the /maintenance of main roads and secondary roads for the year ending 1895, and which amounted to £1,350. It was desided to forward the estimates on to the County Council. Bans for the erection of the following property had been submittwd and approved: Four cottages, in Duke-st., for Mr. Thomas Williams; six houses in Crow- lane, for Messrs. Fitzgerald Brother 3 ; three houses in Quecia-at., for Mr. Thomas Williams. - The minutes of this Committee were approved.

div.head: TRU FINANCE COMMITTER.
div.p: TRU FINANCE COMMITTER.

At a meeting of this Commitzoe held on the 15th of February cheques were signed for the payment of vari- ous accounts amounting to £1,225 9s. sd. Tim minutes were adopted. :MEDICAL OFFICBa'S IMPORT. Dr. Watkins, medical officer, submitted his annual re- port for 1393, which showed that the number of deaths . registered was : mates 251, females 220 ; births : males 126, females 133 : e::coss of births : 125 males, females 82. The infantile death rate was 771 per thousand. In the course of his report Dr. SS atkins aqucied to the death rate as being one of the highest they had experienced in Earlostown, and this had been greatly due to the hot weather. In speaking of the sanitary conditions of the town, he alluded to the ill-paved and badly sewered streetx,as being ehje,cts for the Board's careful attention. Respecting the reinoval of excreta he was glad to see that in many cases the water carriage had been introduced in the town, in place or the dirty and objectionable pails. He hoped they would give this a more extended trial. It would he a great aivantage te dispense with the abominable smells which arose from pails. (Hear. hear.)—The Ciaairrman said he was sure they were all sorry to hear that the death rate during the past year had been one of the highest known to Barlestown. Of course, as Dr. Watkins had told them, the extrerem heat had had much to do with the 'high mortality. Some allusion had also been made by the doctor to the defec- tire water supply during the summer, but he (the chairman) might tell him that that had been caused through the company sinking a new well just as the hot weather commenced. That however had now been remedied. With respect to the sewage of the streets he might explain that they had applied to the Local Government Board for powers to borrow money to carry this work out ; and they had not yet received the necessary sanction. Of course they could compel the property owners to do their own work, but this would only mean a temporary improvement, and when the real work came on would mean a second burden on the shoulders of the property owners. (Hear, hear.) Be did not think that such a course would be fair. How- ever, it Was to be hoped that they would soon receive the sanction they had applied for, and then the work could be done completely. (Hear, hear.) Mr McMahon thought that some of the streets were in a most disgraceful state. For instance there was Water Street. Their Board bad made an attempt to' sewer it and now it was in a much worse condition than ever. In wet weather there were puddles of water in the street six or seven inches deep ("shame") V and all day long there were something like a thousand children going to and from school, along that street. It was something disgraceful. He hoped that Dr. Watkins would go and see the street.—Dr. Watkins: Oh ! I have seen the street time after time.—Mr. Brieriy : I do not think it is any worse than the other streets.—Mr. McMahon: It is a great deal worse, and what I con- tend is that this Board has no right to go and interfere with a street and leave it in a worse condition than it was originally in. (Hear. hear.)—Dr. Watkins' report was then approved, after which upon the proposition of Mr. McMahon seconded by Mr. Ormand, it was de- cided to consider the sewage of Water Street and other streets, in comtnittee.—This concluded the public business.

RUGBY. WARRINGTON v. MOSELEY.

ST. EBLENS v. TYLIDESLIM—PIayed at Tyldeslsy,before a good number of spectators. Tyldoslev were fully represented, but the visitors were short of Foulkes, who was assisting Lancashire against Devonshire. A power- ful wind was blowing, which TyWesley started agaiest. Immediately the visitors started. a hot attack, and Cross getting hold, ran in under the post, but a scrimmage was ordered, from which St. Helens get a free kick, but May's attempt at goal was charged down. Almost in an instant May got a free kick, and landed a Rice goal. Pearnley here about got in a nice run and kick, but Appleton relieved. Play still raged in the Tyldosley 25. Eventually, from a cross kick, the ball was passed back to Bancroft, who mulled, and Appleton grounded under the Vest, but the try was again di6allevved. Half-time score :—St. Helens 1 dropped goal, Tyldesley nil. Though Tyldesley had many opportunities after the restart,. nothing was seared. Final result :—St. Helens 1 goal, Tyklesley nil.

ST: BRUINS RICRIATION V. WAEBVIIIILD TRINITL— Played at St. Helene, before abet 4,0110 spectators. The visitors were short of five fret team players, while Ellison, an old player, attain played three-quarter fcr the Recreation. A strong wind was blowing along the field, aed, the Recreation having lost the toss, Seddon started against the wind. Trinity paid a flying visit to the home lines, but Ducker, mulling a pass, Hughes made good use of the chancy and sprinted to the centre. rilkington received and further improved matters, only being prevented from scoring by Ducker. Trinity worked back to centre, and Goodaire, receiving a pass from the scrimmage, made a splendid run, Crossley bringing him down on the line. Wakefield, assisted by he wind, had floe beet of the play, but the Recreation showed good defense,. At half-time nothing had been scored. Dolan afterwards got an unimproved try, and from a free kick by Seddon, Melyneaux pieced a goal. Final result Helena Recreation 1 goal 1-try, Wake- field Trinity ail.

RIINCORN RECROATION T. ST. BRUINS RECNHATION A MAlL—This match was played at Runcorn, on Saturday St. Helens won the toss, and Whitney kicked off up hill. At the onset the home men Pressed, tont St. Helens relieved, and play was transferred to the centre. From a good kick Matthews followed up well, and Worrell and Hughes failing to gather the ,ball, the St. Helons man scored an easy try, from which a capital goal was kinked. After this easy reverse the home men warked hard, and front some keen play in the visitors' quarter Pendlebury got over near the corner. Worrall made a good attempt at goal, the ball just grazing the post on the wrong aide. Half-timo arrived...with the bcore— Runcorn, three poles; St. Helens, five points. In the second portion the game was of a very desultory char- aster for a long time. The home forwards played up well, but the basks played a disappointing game' and missed several easy chances of scoring, Towards the close play brightened up wonderfully, and the Runcorn sido put in Some nice paseing, but the visitors' defence wa,s equal to the occasion, and prevented any further score being made. This final, result was: St. Helens Recreation, one goal, one minor; Runcorn Recreation, one try, four minors. WARRIMITON T. RIIIIRY.—POIIIIWiIItg their match with Moseley the Warringtonians journeyed to London en Sat- urday evening. Sunday was spent in a quiet way, and the 'match with Kent Wanderers on Monday being can- celled owing to the inability of the Wanderers to raise a team, ample opportunity was afforded the Lancashire men of seeing the many places of interest. Originally the Warringtonians intended returning on Wednesday, but an application by Rugby to have the match played on Tuesday was acceded to, and Warrington called at the Midland town in order to play off the return fixture. James Bate and Jolley superseded Evans and Berry, otherwise the visiting team war similar to that which accounted for Moseley. Warrington won the toss,., and playing with the wind, soon had the Rugby naea on the defence, and after several essays Taylor scored. The Warringtonians were superior at all points, and though there was a laxity of that dash which marks League fixtures, they maintained the attack. Fine kickaig by Heesom was followed by capital passing amongst the Warrington backs, and eventually John Bate scored, our , local team leading at half time by two tries. Resuming the Warringtonians again isplayed their aggressive tactics, and after Turner had been disappointed he suc- ceeded in gaining a legitimate point. Rugby now bad a spell or attacking. and when' looking dangerous Barber secured possession, and a run the whole length of the field saw him maintaining his consistency for scoring tries,the brilliant performance being cheered to the echo. Potts kicked two goals. Near the close Rugby pressed, and good vrork by Woolf resulted in Wynne scoring. Final—Warrington, 2 goals, 2 tries; Rugby 1 try.

div.head: ASSOCIATION
div.p: ASSOCIATION

*A.URIMGTONT. PENXIITH:—A large crowd assembled on the cricket ground, Arpley, on Saturday, when the above dabs met to play off their first fixture of the season. The Penketh men came with a good record, and their supporters were confident of victory. Connor started the ball, and Evans was called on early to relieve, which he did in fine style. The visitors however, put on further pressure, and for a time the home backs had , plenty of work. Penkath conceded a corner, but the hall was kicked behind. Mather was next conspicuous by some excellent play, and then Elliott for the visitors stepped an ugly rush. Half-time arrived with a blank sheet. On the re-start the Warrington men showed up much better, and the Penketh custodian, an able limn, had several warm shots from the right to deal with. Mather was now called upon to relieve, and Add sent in , an excellent shot, which was put behind, a barren corner resulting. The ball rested in the home half for some time, but at length Antbonr, who Was playing a pod game, gave toFennelly, who, after a neat dribble, passed to Linnaker. That player transferred to Reid, who shot past the goalkeeper amidst great excitement. This was the only score, and the final result was Warrington, one goal; Peuketh, nil. The visitors' team contains some excellent men, the right lull back—Elliott—especially shining. Forrest had very little work to do, the visitors shooting badly, but the visitors' custodian got through an amount ef work in excellent style. Mr. C. Spinks officiated as referee: ST. MARYS A.F.C. v. PARIS& CEUJECIL—The above

match was played on the ground ef the latter on Satur- day: r' rho- homesters kicked off against the wind and the visitors at once began to press, a fruitless corner resulting; but, not to be denied, Hayes with a good shot scored the first goal for the visitors. Still keeping up the pressure 3 more goals were scored by Hayes, Richardson, J. O'Neil, half time arriving with the score St. Marys 4 goals, Parish Church nil. The second half, with the wind in their, favour, the homesters began to press, and from a throw in Baines scored. Even play tollowed but the homesters again broke away the same player scored number two. The visitors now exerted themselves and taking the ball down the field Gilloav scored. The kemesters again became dangerous but the visitors' defence was found to be safe. Nothing further resulting the game ended St. Marys 5 goals; Parish Church 2 goals.

ORFORD CRESCENT T. LYMIL ReseavE.—This match was played on Saturday at Marsh House-lane. During the first half the home team managed to score thrice.the Lymm forwards rarely going past half-way. Orr the change of ends it was expected that the • visitors would show up better, but the Crescent scored four goals. Re- sult—Orford Crescent, 7 ; Lymm, 0.

RUNCORN V. WARRINGTON LONDON AND NORTE- WESTERN Au:dm—Played on Saturday, on the ground of the former. Score: Runcorn, four goals; Albion, nil. LYMM GRAMMAR SCHOOL---rAST V. PRESENT.—The above match was played on the ground of the latter in fine weather, resulting in an easy win for the Present by six goals to one. EARLESTOWN T. LIVERPOOL Rasnays.—Played at Earlestown, in the Liverpool and District League. Liver- pool started with only 10 men, and Earlestown kicked off with the hill and wind in their favour. Correct shooting was out of the question owing to the high wind ana Earlestown were able to confine play in the visitor's quarters during the whole of the first half. Within a few minutes of the start, Earlestown secured a corner. which was fruitless.' The Reserve did their utmost to break away, but although 'they played a sturdy game, the eould not get beyond the half-way line. Rennie,the visitor's goal keeper was kept fully employed and he was instrumental in saving some stinging shots. After a quarter of an hour's play, Conway secured a' goal, and shortly afterwards Lee notched a second point. From a scrimmage a third goal was obtained and with a long kick from the right, Clarke sailed•the ball under the bar. Another swift shot from the right was cleverly saved by Rennie, but he was shortly defeated by Hughes and at half-time the score stood Earlestown 5 goals, Liverpool nil. Turning round Liverpool had all the advantages which Earlestown had in the first half, but they were unable to score, and the game ended with Earlestown 5 goals, Liverpool nil.

div.head: ST. ItELENS THEATRE ROYAL.
div.p: ST. ItELENS THEATRE ROYAL.
MOROCCO BOUND.

As will be seen from our advertising columns,the latest burlesque success "Morocco Bound "will be presented to the patrons of the handsome Theatre Royal and Opera House, St. Helens, next week. The piece itself scarcely needs recommendation, as its uninterrupted ran of suceess wherever produced has more than testified to its popularity. The company is under the control of Mr. F. J. Harris, from Shaftes- bury Theatre, London, and the strong cast includes the well-known performers :—Messrs. Wilfred Shine, G. King, Morgan, Willie Drew, Misses Florrie Schuherth, Constance Wallis, Clare Greet, Kittie Harcourt, Ray Vivian, Flo. Gracey and 'Violet Lloyd. The burlesque is replete with hilarious entertainment, and combines the rarely associated qualities of fun and magnificence.

A fact in connection with the special fund which the Tories are raising in order to prosecute "a vigorous campaign" in London should be noted. The principal contributors as yet are the great ground landlords of London. These persons evid- ently regard the campaign as intended to be in defence of their interests against the men who would tax ground rents. The general body of wealthy Conservatives, aingularly enough, have held aloof.

div.head: WEDDING OF MISS BRUNNER.
div.p: WEDDING OF MISS BRUNNER.

On Tuesday the 'marriage ef Miss Mabel Alicia Brunner second daughter of Mr.J. T. Brunner,M.P., to Mr. Henry Parker Lowe, was celebrated at All ,Hallows. Church Allerton, with full choral service. 'The ceremony was performed by the Rev. 11. F. Y. Kemble, rector of Allerton,and witnessed by a large and fashionable gathering, comprising many repre- sentatives of the highest local circles. • The church was beautifully decorated with white flowers and palms and .he aisles were spread with crimson cloth. The altar, pulpit, and choir rails, were festooned with ear- lands of greenery, and almost hidden beneath masses of white .azeloas, lilies of the valley, cyclamine, and Nile 1111 lea. The font was similarly adorned, the gasaliers were hung, with white ribbon, and at intervals clown the whole length of the body of the church were placed tall, spreading tree palms. The morning was cloudy and grey, but the church with its dual row of painted win- dows, the picturesque arrangement of white blooms and foliages, the tints of the ladies dresses, in white and rose colour, violet and primrose,and the numberless bouquets of early spring flowers carried by the guests haal a bright- ness and sweetness ef its own.

div.head: ST. MARTS SCHOOLS, NEWTON.
div.p: ST. MARTS SCHOOLS, NEWTON.

In'aid of the above schools a concert was given in St. Mary's and St. John's Hall, Newton, on Tues- day evening. There was a very large andience,and a IA iscsll4neou,4 programme of songs was ably sub- mitted, each item being duly applauded, and in the same instance encored: Some interest was occa- sioned. by the fact that a local young lady, who at present attending the Liverpool School of music, would make her debut/ as a singer. The young lady in queFion, Mist; Beatty,: met, with an'encourag,hag .reception, and considering this was her first Dilate, 'appearance, she fulfilled th.e expectations of the audience. She, has a good voice of much compass, and high range, and with careful attention to minor parts she will prove an acquisition to the concert platform. Her songs were " Kathleen Mayourneen,' and "Dear hearts," for each of which she was deservedly encored. The songs were very sweetly and correctly rendered, although the', artiste gave signs of being. somewhat nervous and was perhaps a little too abrupt in her style. IThe programme ineluded a couple of violin solos by ' Mr,-,Peplow •, songs,. "The Bell Ringer," and - " The Buglar,-',Mr. J. Hiehatn, which ,were excellently sang; Ora•nr6 noble" and" Killarnev," which Miss Bartley; sangwith good taste and finish ; " The Holy City," and "To the Woods,"' which Miss L. Gorse, gave sweetly, but lacked expression; "Molly Sawn," and " The Fisher Draid,P by Mr. S. Highatn. Mr. J. Williams filled the; post" of hurnourist, singing "My wife's relations," and " Ilat was enough for both of which were duly -encored. During an interval the Rev. F. J. Lennon took an opportunity of thanking the artistes for their services.and, the audience for their presence,whieh showed that they t.,:ok an interest in the work of educa- tion:, TWe Catholic Church liked to give as much learn. lug and light:to her children' as she could. Dr. O'Reilly, the Angliqau Bishop of Liverpool, said whoever neg- laded it, the RoMan Cathblics would not neglect their childrentdrthat wherever they saw a church, they would invaediately see a school rise for the children of the poor. (Hea,r, hear.) Our great trial and strife was, net to educate children of the rich, who could take care of themselves their duty was the care of the poor.' children, therefore it was that they laboured. He hadt offered the management of his school to his people, and/ said he would give them £2O per year, as his subscrip- tion, but they had thought it best to leave well alone. It was their principle to give their children a good soznd secular and religious education, because they felt that the first of all subjects they had to study was Almighty God. Others perhaps did not study the Vestion as the Roman Catholics did; they simply said why not leave religion to the Sunday School. They (the Roman Catholics), said that religion should be mixed up,with every duty of the day, and. the children should be actuated and taught by the high Principle of religion., In their school they had met all the requirements that a 1 Board School had to meet, and in addition to that; they,. did more, they gave a religious training as well as all I Government required. How did they stand, in that district. They had school boards in Croft, and Bunton- wood,and what was the result of the examination. They had met all the requirements of the Government, in a • strict Board School examination, and they stood higher than any Board School within a radius of 20 miles. 'rhey had earned a grant of 215. 6d. for gulls and 203. for every bay„ which was the highest grant that could be made by any school. If their friends in, Earlestown I should let well alone, uad say if the Catholics,Wesleyans, land Church would pay for their schools they would be I satisfied. If they thoroughly understood they would simply say, "we are grateful to these denominationalists who are willing to tax themselves to meet the require- ments of the Education Act by subscriptions, and carry on their schools without troubling no.' If they had a School Board, after having educated their own children, the working man, would have to pay for well-to-de parents, who had insisted upon a Itoard School, and who could well afford to send them to a grammar or Eigher grade school. Many of the working men had not n alizeci that side of the question, and he advised them to go icto it before it was too late. (Applause.)

div.head: SIR ARTHUR SULLIVAN ON "GETTING
div.p: SIR ARTHUR SULLIVAN ON "GETTING
ON."

"You knot*, I hate being interviewed," said Sir Arthur Sullivan, the famous composer. to a " Chums " represeatative. "In fact, I never will submit to the ordinary general interview, but I don't mind saying a few words to the boys, and telling them some 'anecdotes of my earlier days. It is very hard to say anything when you ask me my advice to boys—there is so much one would Wish to say, and it has all been said over and over again before. Perhaps the thing that I—and, is fact, all men who have got on in the world—feel to be one of the greatest things to boarin mind is--' whatever YOU do, do it as welras you possiblyetn.' It is the old Proverb over agairt—' What is worth doing at all is worth doing well.' Always aim to do your present occupation to the very beet of your ability. It is a first-rate thing for a boy when he has done anything to feel—' Well, that is the best thing 1 have ever done.' It may not be —very often is not—and very soon he will get dissatis-- fied with it and try to better it. But all the same, he Should always feel on its completion—' I could not do it better ;it is the best lam able to do.' It shows he has thrown himself into his work or xahatover it was. He Should be pleased with it whets it is done—his own con- science should praise his effort. Tf,at is a great thing, and it goes a leng way towards success. It is a thing, too, that the dullest can aim at. Do their beet always, nothing but their beat. Never mind how had it is, if it is their best. Everyone can do that. I remember once in my earlier days, I was doing some little stage music for the opera at Convent Garden, and I was worried be- cause it took me so long and gave ma so much trouble. I could not do it superficiaily. It was only a little thing and yet I felt I had to put my whale being luta it. I took as much pain with the orchestration as if it Lad been some great work, a symphony or an oratorio, and the consciousness of title bothered me,and I one day said aS much to Beverley—you know the great scene painter. He was then doing some work far Covent Garden. His reply has stuck to me ever since. That is how it should be. If I had to paint a brick wall I should take as much trouble over it as if it were a miniature of the QiEeen.' That is the spirit in which to set about life.

div.head: REORGANISATION OF ST. HELENS
div.p: REORGANISATION OF ST. HELENS
FIRE BR IGADE.

IMPORTANT RECOMMENDATIONS. f- The special committee appointed to inquire into and report upon the working and reorgant6ation of the St. Helens Fire Brigade have made the follow- , ing recommendations :—That one fireman, in addi- tion to Superintendent Rutherford, to devote the whole of • his time to the work of the brigade, be appointed, his wages to be 255. per week, rising yearly at the rate of a is. per week. That a capable man for driving the steam fire-engine be always at woz k in the daytime in the workshops at the Town Hall. [hat one Police-sergeant and six constables be employed as auxili- ary firemen, the sergeant to receive, in addition to his Pay, 3s. per week and 3s. for attendance at each fire, and tho constables 24. per week and 2s. for each fire,and also seventeen firemen, at the following allowances : Two sergeants each £4 per annum, is. for practice, 35. for attendance at fire the first hour and is. fld. every hour after ; one ongiueer £3 per annum, Is. practice,2s. , attendance at fire first hour and is. ed. every hour after • , __ _ ,

and fourteen firemen £2 per annum, is. practice. 2s. attendance at fire first hoar and Li. every hour after, and is. for calls in all cases where their services are not required. That members of the brigade be required, as far as possible, to reside in the houses belonging to the Corporation in Bryan-street. That fire boots be pro- cured for use of the members of the brigade. That each !member, with the exception of. the police-sergeant and constabl' es who have a claim on the superannuation fund be insured against accidents at the expense of the Cor- Poration in the sum of £250, with allowances for dis- ablement. The steam fire-engine has been sent to the makers for examination; the manual engine has been repaired, and a quantity of hose purchased. The Watch Committee of toe St. Helens Corporation, who have Charge of the Fire Brigade, have received a communica- tion from the Home Office stating that the Home Secre- tary had directed that there should be annually paid to the Police Pension Fund from the fund or rate applicable to the purposes of the Fire Brigade or Fire Police whose 'constables are employed exclusively as firemen, a SUM equal to la per cent, of the pay of such constables,and 'where they are employed partially as firemen a sum equal to 20 per cent, of any extc a pay allowed to such constables. The Watch Committee have approved of the recommendations of the Brigade Committee.

div.head: VEGETARIANISM.
div.p: VEGETARIANISM.

Sir,—There has lately been inanif2st a very great in- terest in tile subj-ct of Vegetarianism as a part of the important fOod question,ao interest in which Warrington and neighbourhood doubtless fully shares. In many households an increase of variety in their ordinary fare by the occasional use of a pleasant vegetarian dish would be much appreciated, while here or there may be one who, for the sake of health, economy, or some other reason, would like to put this system of living to a fuller practical test. The advantages of the system and the interest attaching to it would take too long to dwell upon in 3-our pages, but to any of your readers who wish to know more about it I wilt be glad to send some papers with a few simple reeipeA on receipt •,f recraes t. —Faithfully yours, JOSEPH KNIGHT. t3i.c. Veg. Soc. 9, Peter-street, Manchester, Feb. 7th, 1394.

A FORGOTTEN FACT ABOUT LONGFORD. Sir,—As the disciples of economy were loud in their , protestations on Tuesday evening, I venture to draw their attent on to a forgotten fact about Longford which ought to have directed and ought still to direct their energies into a proper channel. Only two years ago the Bcriugh Surveyor had his salary raised from £4OO to £5OO, and I remember well one of the main arguments adduced for this increase was that he was largely taken up with the management of Losigford depot and its accessories. This was shortly after the appointment of the present manager at Longford, but Mr. Dims, after a short experience of the then many masters at Longford, insisted upon exercising his sole individual authority with retard to the management. The result was that the Borough Surveyor ceased to have any connection with the concern. This was as it ought to have been but it ought not to have ended there, for, if the Longford duties were an argument for raising the Borough Sur- veyor's salary,their cessation is an argument, for having that salary again revised. Like Councillor R. T. Fair- clough I think on strictly commercial ground alone the present manager and engineer was worthy of the rise to £3OO, hut with the above fact staring me in the face, I rail to see why the £lOO or the £5O increase should come out if the rates. Are the economists afraid of taking the right bull by the horns, or are the ratepayers for ever to sue the true interest of the borough fall sublimely to the floor be- tween the snappishness of one member and the vulgarism and street cornerism of another, a mcst humiliating and une,diiying spectacle.—Yours, OPEN SECRET, Warrington, Feb. 3, 1894.

div.head: 11ATIONALP=N1 VERSUS REASON.
div.p: 11ATIONALP=N1 VERSUS REASON.

. Sir,-1 am very sorry to see by Mr. Peer's letter of this week, that he has totally misunderstood my position in this coaroversy ; and through doing so, is simply wast- ing his strength and beating the air. I hold no brief for what has aptly been termed "fragmentary Christianity," but only for the Catholic church. What is the use of flinging out hooks baited with scraps of evolution, to one who in commen with most thinking Catholics accepts evolution in toto. The Catho- lic church has never defended the "origin of developed species by special creation," consequently she cannot come under the ban of Mr. Peers for doing so. Like a great many more people he simply does not know what the Catholic church does, or does not, teach! The single proposition I put forward in defence of a primeval fail or as it is called, "original sin" is only oRe a series of cumulative proof which is simply resist- less ; but even this one, your correspondent has failed utterly, as anyone can judge, to refute! And I wkuld point out, not only to Mr. Peers but to all your readers, science has not in one single instance upset one of the doctrines of the Catholic church, nor does she attempt tow to do so. We know, that, as regards Biblical cri- ticism, the "higher critics" have been doing nothing else lately (through the exigencies of newer evidence) but "climb down" from their much vaunted positions; that the earlier Darwinism and the present doctrine of Evo- lution are very distinct; in short, scientists are not now an riak. to accept on slender evidence, marvellous and f.s r reselling generalistns. All this only shows the truth of my original point, i.e.,t hat Mr. Peers, notwithstanding ' tis dogmatism, is neither novel nor ingenious! The school of thought to which even I have the honour to be- long cic, not "accept jumbles of assumptions," norhave I put torward any. If Mr. Peers is unable to estimate the A'alue of an a priori argument, so much the worse for As to the concluding joke! (sic), I must leave your readers to judge of its value.—' am, sir, yours faithfully, JOHN S. HOWELL. 9, Montgomery Road, Chiswick W., London, 611 Feb. 1394. HARRY ESMOND AND HIS "PERPLEXING

div.head: PROBLEM."
div.p: PROBLEM."

Sir,—l was something more than perplexed in reading the above correspondent's letter in your issue of Satur- j dae last. That any intelligent man should have allowed years to pass over his head with an unsolved problem j troubiing his brain " putting questions to others whom he thought better informed than himself," and seeking satisfaeticn to his questionings, but finding none, is to me be th a perplexity and an a ma,zement. One would have thetent, that his disturbed understanding would have led him to refer to some reliable authority or other in botany, whose merest elementary work would have supplied him with the easiest solution of his difficulty, if be had only been sufficiently in earnest to find one. In this case there would lave been no necessity to refer to Christ's authority in the passage from the 12th chapter ef St. John's Gospel (not Matthew's, as he incorrectly quotes) ; and still less occasion to exhibit his own ignor- ance, and want of comprehension, by casting reflections upon the knowledge of Christ. Now, every scientific botanist well knows that the "corn of wheat " whea buried in the soil" does die," and let me say that the use our Lord nukes of this fact is one of the most beautiful and apt illustrations of His divine prescience and wisdom. But here allow me to ask what is meant by the corn or grain of wheat ? Have cavillers never bethought them of this simple but nec.cessary question ? Is it cenceivable that any one but the merest dullard could overlook it? Does the " corn of wheat "then mean the living germ only ? And is there nothing about it,of which it may be said very truly that" it dies." In fact, do our Lord's words need to imply for an instant that :Ile conceived the living germ dies? I answer : No more than we conceive that the soul of man dies when his body is corvigned to the grave. Yeur perplexed corres- vondent will find the needed illumination in one of the elementary works of the Professor of Botany in the Uni- versity of Edinburgh. On page 105 ol his •1 First book of Botany," Dr. Baliour says "The great bulk of the " grain of wheat is composed of nutritiou s matter "separate from the plant or embryo. This matter must "all be changed, and dissolved, in order that the plant 41 may spring. Unless it dies and undergoes solution "there can be no nourishment convered." Such a dying of a " corn of wheat "as this is simply all that is re- quired in the undow ted meaning of our Lord's beauti- ful parable. "The great bulk of the grain "—the ex- ternal wrappings, or investiture of the germ, undergoes separation of parts, dissolves, and dies. The grand point of our Lord's asserthm is, what every tyro in botany knows, or may know, if he is only gifted with common Wee and ordinary discernment—that unless the body of the" wheat corn does eass through this actual dissolu- tion of its substance—correctly called death—the living germ can never manifest its life, or come to perfection, and bear its large increase of fruit. That it Ghould be possible for any man seeking to understand the truth o so blindly miss the object of his search passes my comprehension.. I have heard however of this craze in other quarters, and in most instances have set it down to that malignant Gpirit of hostility so rampant in our day, to everything connected with revealed religion. A song a class of literary triflers and smatterers scienee nothing is too sacred to lay their Philistine hands upon; and the very Lord of life Himself must be arraigned at their hyper- critical bar, unless Be hays so coestructed His formulas of speech that mere pedants and cavillers should be left without a subterfuge or an excuse. Yoors truly. BEN CHAYIL,

Churches be sufficient to induce us to accept sas the sum of those numbers. Equally simple is the answer to the question "Does a seed die ? in a3cordance with the text Jphn xii. 21 : " Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone ; hut if it die it bringeth forth mush fruit." In every nature and fertile seed we have two parts—a living germ or embryo—possessed of latent vitality— and a dead part—the nutriment for this germ—in the case of wheat this is starch. Now the starchy we may dismiss from our consideration ; that, never having been alive, ceuld not die ; and as to the embryo, the most fatuous resurrectionist would hesitate to say that this dies ere it becomes a living plant. Indeed, from the first grain of wheat—the ancestral Tritieum—down to that of the last harvest, we have the evidence of an unbroken chain of close-linked vitality. It will be time enough to accept the doctrine of seminal resurrection when addle eggs produce chickens. Until then I shall defer ad- hesion to this dogma. And now as to the " perplexities " of this problem. These come by trying to get a sane mind to accept both of these antagonistic ideas. There is no perplexity in the mind that " believes " without reasoning ; and none in the mind of him whoreasons without regard to belief. It is the mixture that does the mischief. Now there can surely no honour occur to the .God of Truth by our per- verting one of His attributes. And yet the history of ecclesiasticism reveals to us the case of men engaged in perverting words and facts, ostensibly in the service and for the glory of God ! In the namnof the God of Truth let us have no quibbling with words and no perversion of facts ! But man seems to nave an inherent objection,to the acceptance of whole truths at once ; they like to be let down easily, from the fools' paradise of mythological fiction to the plain level of plain facts. Unitarianism has been defined as " a bed to catch a falling Christian " ; I regard it as the half-way house toward thorough reasonableness in matters relig- ' ious. In like manner the modern dogma of the limitation of Christ's knowledge is, to many, the ledge of salvation to which they cling,to save themselves from too precipi- tate a fall into the dread abyss of truth. It is nothing to them that the facts of the case rather indicate that these' limitations" were inherent and could net be got rid of, rather that that they were assumed. With the blindness natural to this state of mind they get out of one difficulty by getting into a worse. "Jesus," say they," used a popular illustration to ensure popular appreciation of his doctrine of the resurrection of the body." For myself, I say it is inconceivable that God, or any person accredited by God, c•-uld make such a statement for such a purpose; nothing but truth could come from its source. But to me, whilst Jesus was a man merely, still he is a splendid example of many qualities which it would be well for us to follow, and it would he much better for the world did we do so. I care not that Jesus borrowed the Chinese philosopher's maxim "Do unto others as ye would have them do unto you." He it was who inculcated most thoroughly this golden rule. I need not imagine him divine to revere him for this. That he was a man and shared some of the ignorance of his time, does not prevent me from admiring the great lesson of his life and death—self-sa.crifice for the good of others; a lesson the world is too apt to read inversely.—Yours, &c.,

div.head: February 7th, 1894. DOES THE SEH:D DIE? A PERPLEXING PROBLEM.
div.p: February 7th, 1894. DOES THE SEH:D DIE? A PERPLEXING PROBLEM.

In other words he tries to reason upon belief—a sure source of mental entanglement. lam more concerned about the last half of H. He who depends upon tradition will be emphatically affirma- tive, the mind that prefers truth to tradition will give a ver 'let on the negative side. div.head: JOHN PEERS.
div.p: JOHN PEERS.

TWO CRITICS OF SOCIALISM. Sir,—l• was interested on seeing in your last issue that Socialism formed the subject of a debate at the first meeting of this session of the Warrington Debating Society ; and also in a letter on the subject from Mr. T. Y. Howcroft, of Middlesbro'. The Rev. E. C. E. Carle- ton evidently entertains very curious notions as to the character of leading Socialists. Men who "go in for Socialistic legislation," says the rev. cleric, "obtain a cheap reputation for generosity, and for giving away ether people's money,"and that Socialists generally are a bad lot, their private conduct " throwing doubt upon their sincerity." This is just the sort of rubbish which makes intelligent men disgusted with the average par- son. Does Mr. Carleton really contend that men should revel in luxury and splendour, while the pro- ducers of their wealth should live a life of slavish toil and want? If so, then I am not surprised that the masses do not attend church. Either Christianity sanc- tions or does not sanction this condition of things. If the former then I want nothing with it. If the latter then Socialism and Christianity are in agrecment,and the Socialist who advocates legislation on the basis of his doctrines is doing the work of Christ. Says Sir Thomas More, " What justice is there in this, that a nobleman,a banker, or any other man that either does nothing at all or at least is employed at these things that are of no use to the public, should live in great luxury and splen- dour upon what is so ill-acquired, and a mean man, a carter or smith or ploughman who works harder than the beasts themselves, and is employed in labcur so necessary that no Commonwealth could hold a year without them, can only earn so poor a livelihood and must lead so miserable a life that the condition of the beasts is much better than theirs." When the reverend gentleman talks about Socialistic legisla' inn being tan- tamount to " giving away other people's money," it is quite evident he has not studied his subject. Socialism aims at preventing "other people" from getting what does not belong to them. This makes a very great difference. When the Church recognises this and uses iher influence accordingly, her capacity for usefulness will be increased. The Rev.E. C.E. Carleton was not far wrong when he said that " Sccialism dealt only with material wants, but the Church considered man as being made for eter- nity." Just so ; and that is where the Church has been wrong. In other words,Socialistn has something to offer for this life ; as the judicious Hooker says, " Unto life many implements are necessary." You cannot live a righteous life unless you live, and you cannot live a life worth living unless it has in it joy, comfort. delight. Socialism deals with life, far the living of which" mate- rial things " are necessary, and it may be that the pre- sent life is a preparation for the "life to come." The Church has too frequently offered a stone when the hungry one has asked for bread. She has taught him to carry himself reverently and humbly towards his betters (who they are God knows ; I don't), and when he has exhibited a healthy dissatisfaction with his sordid existence the greatest consolation she has offered him has been a " reward hereafter." Well, this is not good enough. Either the Church has been as Dean Stubbs says of the country clergy, "too much busied in trying to alleviate particular symptoms of social distress rather than dealing with its general causes," or else she has wilfully held herself aloof from an attack upon a sys- tem which even the Bishop of Manchester,since his con- version, says, will "no longer be tolerated in the world." I am glad, however, the Church—and I mean the Church in the broadest sense—is waking up to a sense 'of her responsibilities, but she requires a good deal of shaking up, and perhaps a galvanic shock or two will be necessary to stimulate her to real Christian effort. Of Mr. Howcroft, whom 1 have not the pleasure of knowing in any way, I have a few questions to ask. He starts out with the declaration that the active principle of all socialism is selfishness, and then says he has never seen a " real socialist." He lets heard people profess socialism (the " active principle " of which is selfishness) " but a little probing has revealed the weak- ness of their professions." Have we to infer from this extraordinary declaration that they who profess social- ism are not as selfish as their socialist principles ? Is selfishness an essential qualification for a real socialist. If not, what does lie mean by a " real socialist." Or did he not make a mistake when he said that the active principle of socialism is selfi.shoess,and that he meant he had never seen a real socialist because he had not seen a man who was not to some e:•:t era selfish. Is that what you mean Mr. Howcroft? If so please say so in your next letter, and then we shall better understand each other. Mr. Howcroft thinks that socialists have an antipathy to capital. Let me assure him that this is not so, What the socialist however, objects to, is that wealth which is made by the worker should be appropriated by those who do not produce it. He has no quarrel with the product of labour, but with its distribution and method of utilization. " Are not the people of to-day "Mr. Howcroft asks, as a whole better off than at any other 'period of the country's history." Not that I am aware of Mr. Howcroft. The development of machinary not- withstanding. Hallam in his "Europe during the middle ages" says under Henry Via labourer earning threepence a day or eighteenpence in the week could buy a bushel of wheat at six shillings the quart,er,and twentyfour pounds of meat for his family. A labourer's wages of 15s. wont buy so much now. A fat sheep in 1500 was worth is. Bd. and the wages of a common labourer were Is. a week, so that he mold have purchased a whole sheep and four fat geese. whllh were then selling at 4d. a piece. The com- mon labourer could not buy half so much with his 'wages te-day. And yet we have had " development of machinery !" If machinery is not invented for the good of all, but only for a few, what is the use of it? Even Mr. J. S. Mill doubts wh6ther machinery has been beneficial to the working people. Mr. Howcroft declares that " true socialism recognises neither king nor country but the whole human race as one family." We socialists do not quarrel with that asser- tion. Socialism,of s,ourse,is a question of time and growth: It is growing; read of France,Germany and Italy,but let I me point you above all ta New Zealand where they have a Socialist Government with a Socialist programme, enough to make your teeth water, The Socialism of the individual quoted by Mr. Howcroft is, if I understand the somewhat vague definition, pure and unadulterated individualism—" the good old rule, the simple plan ; that lie may take who has the power and he inav keep who can." The Socialist recognises the injustice of that system, though, of course, he cannot dissociate himself 1 from it until ha own doctrines have, is application, superseded it. It is a system of this sort that breeds selfishness,i , and it sno argument against Socialism that the foreigner's labour is so cheap. Socialists would have the foreigner raise the price of his labour, at d they are helping hun to do this all the world over. All the Socialists Mr. Howcroft has seen, want their share and as much snore as they can get. Mr. Howcroft fails to see that the Socialist by a foolish self-sacrifice in business would benefit those who stood least in need of it, and cripple his own capacity for usefulness. S .cialism is not a question of the spontaneous exercise of personal bene- volence, though not opposed to it, but is broadly speak- ing a scheme of national co-operation, conducted by the State for the benefit of all. One would have thought we had got past the necessity for a 16ssou so elementary, but it appears not. Yours, &c., COMMON JUSTICE.
THE EX AMIN ER, SA T RD Y, FEBRUARY 10, 18)4. ' NOTES ON GAMES "AD POLICE COURT AND PRISON GATE ATHLETICS. MISSION.

A ercwded and successful meeting under the I uvices of the Police Court and Prison Gate Mis- sion (Livrpool diocesan C.E.T.S.), was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-st., on Tuesday evening• The chair was occupied by the Rector (Rev. F. W. kVillis), and there were also present, Revs. Canon
Penrllyn (rector of IVitiwick), Dr. Porter (All

Saint's, Southport), G. H. Spooner (rector of Wool- ton), J. Hirst (dioce3an klecretary), J. I.irtlan, and G. D. Mason, Alderman Sutton, J.P., Messrs. R. Garnett, J.P., E. J. Guest, J.P., John Fairclough, J.P., S. B. Stringer,and H. Taylor, P.C.M., and Miss Bessie Dutton. After hinging and prayer, The Chairman, in his opening address, congratu- lated the Society upon having such a number pre-

sent that evening-. He would like to impress the classes to join together in the greAt effort to stem the tide of drunkenness. (Lfea.r, hear.) It was the bounden duty of the clergy and also he thought of the laity to do so. They ought to he the very foremost in every effort to promote true temperance. There were certain legal steps which he thought ought to be taken. There should be rebtrictions in the number of public-houses. (Hem., hear.) They all knew that where there were many house,: together they formed a too great attraction for work- ingmen. He also thought that the hours of sale should be restricted on Saturdays. He was not, however, in favour of closing them entirely upon Sundays. There should be a restricted time to enable people to get what they needed if they did need it, but there should not be facilities of drinking. He asked all those present ear-

nestly, to agitate for the abolition of grocer's licenses. Those licenses led to a good deal of drinking privately —(hear, hear)—ancl lastly, there ought to be a Bill passed for tho prohibition of the sale of drink to children. The clergy should strive to have parochial institutions r (flubs wo ere they could provide reading rooms with papers and books for workingmen, and have adult terns eerance societies, and juvenile abstinence societies. The children ought to be brought up never to touch drink and he was sure that they would not begin when they eet older. He wished to speak earnestly on the subject. He once did believe earnestly that it was absolutely neceesare to one's health to take something. He had , altered his opinion now and hardly ever touched it. , Mr. Henry Taylor (police court missionary for the Warrington, Newton, and IVidnes Courts), next moved the following resolution : 'That it is the testimony of judges, magistrates, gaol chaplains, and others that a great proportion of crime is produced by excessive drinking, and this meeting gives its cordial support to the work of the police court- and prison gate mission." He said that he had ereat pleasure in moving that resolu- tion. He wished at the outset to take the opportunity of tendering his heart-felt thanks to the magistrates, magistrates' clerks, chief constables, and to all the police officers with whom lie came in contact in his district,for the kind manner in which they had received him during the fifteen months he had been in Warrington. During the past twelve months the number 4of visits paid to courts in this district was 378, the number of prisoners conversed with was 1,454, number of pledges taken 178, and the number of visits paid to the homes of prisoners charged at the police courts, 1,710. Twelve men had been sent to the firewood factory at Bootle. Three lads had bean sent to their parents or friends, and there had been 14 women sent to homes in Liverpool ; 92 letters had been written with regard to cases brought before the court, and 50 cases had been attended to at the request of the magistrates; 104 cases had been sent to the clergy or ministers in various districts. 69 meetings had been addressed during the year and various race courses, agricultural shows, etc., visited, at which men had been spoken to, and suitable literature distributed. With , these facts before them, they would all realise the great need there was for this work. Th, work of the mission was extending all over the country, and it was very desirable that this work should be carried on, and he ' appealed to the meeting to do their utmost in their power to help it on. Mr. Taylor conclueed an interest- ing speech by giving a number of examples of the work done in Warrington and the neighbourhood. Mr. Rohert Garnett, J.P., seconded the resolution. He said that, he was not sorry that Mr. Taylor had come first, as he had given a very interesting account of the work. A mission like this, had been required a long time. He was glad to see that the church had for some time been moving earnestly in this direction. People had been slow in learning that men, women, and chil- dren had bodies as well as soul. They had been de- voting themselves almost exclusively te the spiritual work, but he believed that Christ intended them to do good to the bodies as well as to the souls. With regard to the resolution he attached the greatest importance to the success of this society. It seemed to him like some one trying to brush back the waves of the Atlantic. , While they were trying to stop the little leaks' they had , the manufacture of drink going on largely throughout the land. 'They were looking hopefully for some legis- lation which should materially diminish the supply of that which produced so much mischief and misery to the land. having spoken in high terms of the work by Mr. Taylor, he said that he trusted the meeting would support the mission which deserved all the support it could get. The motion was carried unanimously. Alderman Sutton then moved a resolution to the effect that it was desirable for Parliament to establish homes for habitual inebriates, where they could be sent by magistrates for a space of time, and also that it was desirable that rich inebriates should pay the expenses of , their habitation in these places. He said that he was very pleased to propose that resolution, because it was entirely in accord with his own feelings. As a magis- trate he had often expressed the wish that they had some other method of dealing with habitual drunkards to the one of continually sending them to prison. When they came out of prison, they repeated the same 'offence and were dealt with Urn* after timo. Sending them to prison for drunkenness was not a bit of use in his ex- perience. (Hear, hear.) The Rev. Dr. Porter seconded the petition. He said that if people did not drink, there weuld be no toners (Laughter), and these places would not then be needed. They wanted to see fewer public houses in the country. He was quite sure that Warrington had more than its share. They also wanted them closed on Sundays, for this was the time that meat of the drinking took place. He was also of opinion that when a man was put into the dock on a charge of drinking, the publican who served bins with the beer should be placed by his side, in fact after the fashion of the Employers' Liability Bill. (Laughter.) 'The Rev. G. H. Spooner in supporting the petition said that the proposed bill was not a class bill for it operated on rich and poor alike. He next went on to examine possible objections to the scheme. Mr. E J. Guest, 3.P., also supported the motisn. rle said that he knew nothing of the prison gate mission except through Mr. Taylor. He was very glad to know Mr. Taylor, as he was a very kind, genial, and sympa- thetic man, and lie should consider it a great loss if he were taken at any time from the police court. His work was a work of mercy. He did not say that the magistrates exercised their power without mercy. He believed that they had mercy in their hearts, but their object was not so much the reformation or regenera- tion of the criminal as to award the punishment neces- sary be the guilty. Mr. Taylor's work now came in, for he spoke to them in the court or at the prison gate and was gladedfeTwitwh3tlfideP.ChuHro wi o Church Eng- land Temperance Society, which was an admission that that te tthhee m ra itstri on rightwa connected e of intemperance was at the root of the evil. He believed that the opinion of the people of England was more in favour of temperance day by day and year by year. He believed that in the future they would be a more tem- perate people than now. Let them stop the tide. Let them decrease the public-houses. When people had lost self-control, they should be put under the control of other peeple,and he therefore bad great pleasure in sup- porting the motion. The motion was put to the meeting and carried unanimously. At the latter part of the meeting lantern views cf various police courts, missions, missionaries, &c., con- nected with the society 'were thrown on the screen. The lantern was manipulated by the Rev. J. Hirst, and Mr. Henry Goldstone. The hymns were accompanied by Miss Lydia Evans. The usual votes of thanks closed .1 the meeting. .893. I

Paosnicirs.—lt will be noticed that a prospectus is advertised in our columns of a new company to be called The Douglas, Llandudno, and Liverpool line of Steamers Limited. As the name implies, the company is being formed for the running of a line of passenger steamers from Liverpool to the watering places mentioned, and also along the Manchester Ship Canal. The share capital of the com- pany is £lOO,OOO issued in 95,000 shares of each and 500 founders' shares of £lO eactiovith power to increase. The 500 founders' shares, do not rank for dividend, un- til Th per cent. is paid on orkiinary shares. Another feature to be considered by intending shareholders is that debenture holders of £lO, and ordinary shareholders of not less than £lO are entitled to a free first class coupon pass for five years on the comp iny's steamers available between Liverpool, Llandudno, and Douglas. These coupons :are transferable. In addition there will be transferable first class return co-oper- ative tickets available for Douglas and Llandudno (one return vocage) further particulars of which will be found in the advertisement. The steamers of the company will also run on the Manchester Ship Canal uring the season. A. one half of the capital of the company is al- ready arranged, there seems every prospect of the com- pany being floated. The share and debenture lists for application are now open, and will close on the 17th inst.

div.head: RUGBY FOOTBALL.
div.p: RUGBY FOOTBALL.

The Warrington Football team has just terminated its annual tour. It has been a very enjoyable tour. In- deed I believe it has been the most enj!)yable tfAir that has taken place in connection with the club. This is so, there is no doubt, because it has been said of every tour that has taken place. Without being, as the famous Artemus put it " 2 skarcastic," it is quite truthful to say that all of the 25 members of the team who went on the journey enjoyed themselves immensely.

The party left Warrington at ten to tan on Saturday morning and arrived in" Brum," in ample time to carry out the engagement with Moseley. Without alluding to the character of the game I will get along and speak of the tour as a holiday trip. Although two of the club do not speak of it in that sense, at all. Moseley is a very aristocratic part of the town and the " War- rington boys " had their hearts gladdened by seeing on every hand the palaces of the modern commercial princes of" Brum," and on the field the figures of some of these princely adherents to the great King Comtairce. After the match they journeyed still further unto the great capital yclept " the Smoke." Having traversed the city along to Covent Gardens on the top of a 'bus,to an accompaniment of the " Rowdy Dowdy Boys," an hotel was fixed upon and invaded. Then a substantial meal was demOlished and rooms were chosen. The party then broke up and in various fragments separated its Elf among the rush and turmoil of the" Giddy Strand." My informant then lost sight of the party until next morning,

He and several others had foregathered on the landing I before going down to breakfast. Suddenly they were ! startled by one of their party rushing up to them with a bowl of water, and the very excited query of " Wheer shall I wash myself." Upon being told in the room where he had got the bowl irom he observed that" he wern't such a foo as to get washing himself at a clean table with a new cloth on it." However, things were explained, and after that the excited one took every opportunity to do " a bit o' floundering abart a clean . table." Breakfast having been sent the way:of all good things, the party sauntered down to Hyde Park, and took a view of the Albert memorial—and they took also some other things, after 12.30. A bright idea occurred to one of the party, after dinner ; which may seem strange. He suggested that they should pay a visit to Hampton Court Palace.

They said " We will," and promptly rushed down to Waterloo Station, and were just in time to see the train passing over by Vauxhall. Then somebody else had a bran new idea born upon him. What a glorious thing it would be to visit Greenwich Hospital? " How strange" they all said " that we did not think of it before. Of course we'll go through the hospital." So they boarded a bus, and in the course of time they mate unto the place of Time and Delapidated Seamen. And with one accord they marched up to a policeman, and said " Tell us where is the hospital." He told them—and he also said that the hospital had been closed some ten minutes ago. This was very distressing, certainly, but the party made the best of their way back t- the city, and passed the remainder of the Sab- bath in a quiet manner. Tile next day they ought to have met the Kent Wanderers, but the match was post- poned. This gave tl), party a chance to enjoy themselves, which they did. The tower was visited—and the old Beef Eaters looked very scared when they saw such a formidable troupe invade their domain. A great many other public places of interest were visited during the afternoon. In the evening the party broke up again— some went to seethe wonderful "Constantinople" at the Olympia. and others visited various theatres.

The next day the patty were up betimes and away to Rugby. After paying a dying visit round the town,they met the local team and alininiAtered to them a somewhat vigorous licking. The homeward journey was commenced after tea, and at 10.10 the party arrived at Warrington, singing " We've had a rare old time of it." Which I do not disbelieve.

The Swinton football team have just comraittel a most unsportsmanlike action. They were due at Run- corn on Saturday to play the team of that town, but at the last ro•ment, they sent word that " having two men playing for Lancashire, they were unable to raise a team." A more flimsy excuse could scarcely be found. Where was their A team ? A first class club can surely have at least two men to fall back upon. It appears as though Swinton did not relish the thought of defeat. But if a club is afraid of defeat, they a:e net worth much. Runcorn have frequently to find five or six men at once for the county, but they have never shirked their en- gagements on that score. Needless to say a great amount, of feeling has been aroused in Runcorn over the matter, and the" Athletic News" characterises the excuse as " palpably frivolous," and as a " paltry and mean sub- terfuge in order to uat out of an engagement they ha d no liking for."

Lancashire got the best of DevenslAire at Swinton on Saturday, after a very desperate struggle,by three goals to a goal and two trie. It was a most energetic struggle throughout,and had Devonshire the choice of ends at the commencement, it is not unlikely that the result would have been different. A noticeable feature of the match was the passing between Bate and Valentine,who had re- peatedly bad luck in being pulled up near the line. Lan- cashire's forwards were over-played by Devonshire's, and one paper asserts that there will have to be three or four changes in this department.

The championship of the " nations is becoming an open matter. When England beat Wales at Birkenhead,. it was expected that the championship was practically decided, so well did the Englishmen play. On Saturday however, they in their turn had to" bite the dust," and that from the" Sons of Erin" who had only beaten Eng- land once previouslv,while Wales were engaged in taking down the brawny gcotchmen. The net result so far is that England, Ireland, and Wales had won a game each while Scotland had lost one. It would be difficult indeed to predict the champion " natbn " from these as yet. The result of the Irish-English match must be very galling to the Yorkshiremen who had seven na6n in the English team out of the fifteen, and yet like Oliver Twist itliev "wanted more." The very department of the team in which they had half the men, viz., the forwards, was where England failed most conspicuously. Perhaps, after this, the English Rugby Union (to quote the words of a contemporary) will find out that " there are other places besides Yorkshire where football is played."

div.p: BOATING

Boating' does not corns. within tha ordinary ken of thio athletic column. It is not a game and is not usually re- garded as a branch of athletics. Nevertheless it comes in the general categvw of sport. Nis is just the time of the year that the Warrington Sailing Club is heard of, and in accordance with custom the members are now bestirring themselves for the purpose of arranging the annual sailing tlaatch, the Saturday after Good Fri- day.
