div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
THE FATALITY ON THE OPENING DAY. . -THE BODY FOUND. .

The Bittern On proceeding down the canal from Man- chester, on Saturday, disturbed the body of Mr. Row- bottom, the chief engineer of the. Norseman, abiut a mile from Latchford locks. The deceased it will be re- membered was drowned on the night of Saturday, Dec. 30th, at the locks, having missed his footing while mak- ing ,in towards the yacht in a thick fog. He fell into the 45 feet lock, and though the services of a diver were ob- tained, and every effort was made to recover the body, it was not until Saturday afternoon that it Was found. The body was observed coating on the top of the water near the higb level bridge at Latchford. A rope was secured round it, and a flat towed it to the locks, whence it was conveyed, under the direction of the lock mas- ter, to the Latchford mortuary, to await the inquest.— An inquest was held en Monday on the body at the Latchford Hospital, before Mr. Yates, county coroner, and a verdict of ^." Accidentally drowned," was turned

div.head: MAN INJURED AT RUNCORN.
div.p: MAN INJURED AT RUNCORN.

On Sunday morning as the iron schooner, Olwyn, of Chester, was being brought through the Bridge Water Lock, at Runcorn, the tow rope slipped, and caught Joseph Bridgson crushing his thumb and fingers of the right hand seierely-. He was attended by Dr. Mackenzie and is progressing favourably.

div.head: THREATENED STRIKE OF. FLATMEN.
div.p: THREATENED STRIKE OF. FLATMEN.

The Ship Canal Company are at present involved in a dispute with the fiatmen at the Salford Docks. A con- siderable number of flats are employed ih lightering goods from the ships at Salford to Water-st. on the old" Mersey and Irwell Canal and to Castlefield on the Bridge- water Canal. The rate allowed by the company is 2d. per ton, and the men through their association—the Upper Mersey Watermen's and Porter's Association,— have put in a demand for 20. per ton to Water-st. and 3d. per ton to Castlefield. The difference in the'rates.is explained by the fact that to:Water-st. there are no locks to pass, while in journeying to Castlefield‘thres locks are encountered. There is also a further grievance. The flats are frequently sent with no more cargo than two or three tons, and some days are kept altogether idle, and the men contend that it is altogether unjust to send them with such small cargoes. They desire that a minimum cargo should be fixed. Another grievance of the men is that they have to undertake the entire work of loading their flats from the vessels, whereas at Liver- pool the stevedores send from four to six men on board, and the master of the fiat practically acts as foreman and sees to the proper, placing' of the cargo. The men placed their demands before the directors a fortnight ago, and two deputations from the executive committee of the watermen's association, with Mr. Ellis Gatley,the secretary, have also had interviews with the representa- tives of the Company, but no definite reply has, as yet, been received. Another meeting of the executive com- mittee Of the association is to be held during the week, and some decisive step will then be resolved upon to en- force the men's rights. It is probable that a strike will be ec ided upon. Between 500 and 800 men are affected.

div.head: CANAL AND THE RAILWAY COMPANIES.
div.p: THE CANAL AND THE RAILWAY COMPANIES.

On Wednesday; before the Railway Commission in London, with Mr. Justice Collins sitting as president,the case of The Manchester Ship Canal Company v. The Cheshire Lines Committee and the Lancashire and York- shire Railstay Company came on for hearing. Mr. Bal- four Browne, Q.C., complained, on behalf of the Ship Canal Company, that the- Cheshire Lines Committee, which had been receiving the canal traffic at Cornbrook sidings, had suddenly declined to forward it, at all events on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway, the latter Company refusing to receive the traffic in that particular way. It looked as though the Lancashire and Yorkshire Company were trying to keep cargoes at Liverpool, so that they could get the railway traffic for themselves. Mr. Littler, Q.C., said the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Company found it very inconvenient to deal with the traffic in the mannerdesired, and it was simply a piece of pig-headed obstinacy on the part of the manager of the Ship Canal. The case was fixed for hear- ing on the 16th inst.. but Mr. Littler said his Lordship would probably not be troubled with the matter again.

div.head: DUES QUESTION AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THE DUES QUESTION AT RUNCORN.

The-adjourned meeting of the General Purposes Com- mittee of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners and the traders and ship o*ners of the town, with respect to the Ship Canal dues and tolls, was field on Wednesday night under the presidency of Mr. James'Pritchard. The sub- committee presented the report they had drawn up, in which the grievances of the traders and ship owners were fully set forth. After over an hour's discussion, it was resolved to forward a copy of the report to the directors of the Manchester Ship Canal, accompanied by a request that they would receive a deputation on the subject. In the event of the directors intimating their reaainess to receive a deputation, the following gentlemen were ap- pointed to act :- .Messrs. S. Taylor, J.P. (chairman of the Board), P. Speakman, J.P. C.C.,J. W. Lightburn, James Pritchard, Fred A. Smith, and F. A. Lake (Law Clerk to the Commissioners). The meeting determined that the

report should not be made public through the press. One grievance was removed by an order issued on Thursday morning. It is well known that ships, traversing the Canal to Manchester are freed from all ships' dues, both on the inward and outward passage. On several occa7

sines owners of steamers have desired to pick up small cargoes at Runcorn in addition to what have been loaded but they were prevented from doing so, by the fact that they at once became liable for full ship's dues on the whole of the cargo. This was looked upon as a great injustice and hardship, and the Company have now de- termined that such vessels may call at Runcorn and com- plete their cargo without incurring the charges mention- ed. This will be received with great satisfaction by all concerned.

div.head: RUNCORN GRAVING DOCK.
div.p: RUNCORN GRAVING DOCK.

The Committee of Runcorn Board of Commissioners, appointed to deal with this subject, have caused a com- munication to be addressed to the directors of the Ship Canal Company drawing their attention to the fact that they are under agreement to construct a graving dock at Old Quay, Runcorn, within twelve months of the opening of the Canal and asking thein to proeeed with the work without delay. Shipbuilding was at ono time an important industry in Runcorn, and it is believed that capacious graving docks might do somewhat to- wards reviving the trade.

div.head: RUNCORN PORT SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN PORT SANITARY AUTHORITY.

It will be remembered that some months ago a Port Sanitary Authority was constituted for Runcorn district after exhaustive inquiries for the Local Government Board by Mr. Jemser Fust. The object was to deal with cholera-stricken ships, and with imported disease gener- ally. The public bodies included in the Authority were Runcorn Board of Commissioners Runcorn Rural Sani- tary Authority, Widnes Town Council, and Warrington Town Council. The Runcorn Commissioners have re- ceived a communication from the Llcal Government Board informing them that owing to Manchester having been constituted a port, the whble matter will have to be re-considerocl and asking them to appoint two repre- sentatives to a conference ,to be held shortly, and to suggest a suitable place at which to hold the same. Messrs. J. W. Lightburu and E. Imison have been ap- pointed to attend the conference, and Warrington has been mentioned as the most suitable place of meeting.

div.head: ____.,•.______ PE N KETH.
div.p: AMBULANCE CONCERT.—On Monday night the concert in connection with the Penketh branch of the St. John Ambulance Association was held in the St. Mary's Sun- day school, Sankey. The Vicar, Rev. E. S. Jackson, was in the chair, and there was a large and representa- tive audience, the room being too small to accommodate the whole of the people. The Rev. J.ll. Jones was also present, and the energetic secretary, Mr. E. W. Clarke. The vicar in opening the concert complimented the class on their pregress and urged them on to further exer- tions. The Misses Edith and Lena Mclver then rendered their duet" The Gazelle Galop " on the pianoforte in a very skilful manner, and were followed by Miss Emily Jeans, with the "Lady of the Lea" in which she , showed her beautifully rich voice to perfection. Rev. J. R. Jones then sang" The Village Blacksmith "in a manner that elicited a hearty encore. Mr. Ralph Foster favoured the audience with two violin solos, "The last rose of summer," and " Home sweet Home," with all his .well known skill. Miss Lena Mclver sang "Dolly," in a very pretty manner, and in response to a hearty encore, sang" The cows are in the clover." She also sang " The very worst girl in the school." The humor- ous items were in the hands of Messrs. Leonard Foster and R. Scarisbriek. The former with " Dotty on the Ditties "and " The Cat came back "enlivened the pro- ceedings somewhat. " Dick" Scarisbrick bad his laughter Provoking marionettes, which he worked to perfection, and created much amusement ree.eiving a hearty encore. This was followed by an exhibition of ambulance work by certified members of the Association the splinting and bandaging being performed with great neatness and despatch, and interesting the audience greatly. Miss Hubi-Newcombe charmed the audience with her rendering of " The Children's home." Mr. Norman sang" Dimon the Cellarer "in a very pleasing manner, and Mr. W. H. Ireland sang" The Holy City" in his usual good style though suffering from a slight cold. The lengthy programme was obliged to be cut down, hi consequence of the frequent encores demanded from the artistes, the audience being greatly pleased with the entire affiar. The concert ended with the ren- dering of the Welsh National Anthem, "God bless the Prince of Wales," he being the President and Grand Prior of the Order. MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION.—On Wednesday, the weekly meeting was held in the Wesleyan School. The paper for the evening was " Work and its reward," the lecturer being the Rev. Owen Watkins. Mr. R. Garnett, J.P.' was in the chair, and there was a large attendance. The lecturer spoke of work in its literal sanse and also of working for the cause of the church. He showed the reward to be received for work and ; exhorted his hearers to do their duty in whatever branch ! they were labouring. At the conclusion a vote of thanks wa4 passed to the essayist and several members briefly discussed the paper. The following took part in the discussion : Messrs. R. Garnett, Barlaw, IN bite, Snoddy, and Parker.
LOVAL TEA. PA Et rms.
BT. ANN'S CHURCH •PAROCHIAL TEA.

The St. Ann's annual parochial tea and concert was held in the schoolroom on Tilesday, when about 350 sat down to an excellent tea. The tables were presided over by Mrs. Gorton, Mrs. Glover, Miss Davies, Miss Jeffer- son, Miss Hawley, and Miss Drioley, amisted by a large number of friends. After tea the company adjourned to the large room for the concert, Mr. T. Morris, F.G.S., being in the chair, and Mr. Higbey in the vice-chair. Mr. Morris in opening the proceedings said his first worth would be addressed in a spirit of welcome to their new pastor, Mr. Davies. (Cheqrs.) He considered that Air. Davies, who had not been in this locality quite six months, had been exceedingly successtul in his work,

inasmuch as he had collecte'd In that short time the sum of £247. (Applause.) Now this sum Was enormous for the reason that it had not come out of the pockets of the working people, but out of the pockets of tha lords of the manor who owned property about here, and they had responded nobly to his solicitations. Mr Davies' sister was also an excellent worker, and if they kept on they would soon lift this parish ft.= a state of apathy to one of great succes.4. He now wished to give them a hearty welcome. (Loud cheers.) The pro- gramme which was an excellent one, was then pro- ceeded with, and was taken part in by the band, under Mr. Randall, Misses Bate and M. and R. Taylor, R. Rigbey, Randall, Messrs. Seed, F. Taylor, IP'. lirimelow, Dell, and F. Meld.

div.head: ST. BARNARAS' CHURCH.
div.p: ST. BARNARAS' CHURCH.

In connection with St. Barnabas Church, Lovely-lane, the annual tea meeting and conversazioney was held in the school, Bostock-at.,. an Monday evening. About 200 persons sat down to tea, and the tables were presided over by the following ladies :—Mesdames Allton, Roscoe, Looker, Trevett, Griffiths, Jones, Prinsep,Hassall,.Parr, and the Misses W'lmshurs.t, Allton, Lansdall, Steward, G. Steward; and Short. Amongst those present in addi- tion to the vicar of the palish, we noticed Mr. Grilffiths (vicar's warden), Messrs, Trevett, Prinsep and John

Looker (sidesmen), Dr.. Tanner (Manchester), and Mr. Smith (Newcastle). After tea,. the Rev. G. Allton deliv- ered an address. A vote of thanks to all those who had lent their services in providing the tea was proposed by Mr. Griffiths, and unanimously carried. Dancing was atterwards indulged in until a late hour. The room was crowded.

div.head: WESLEYAN HOME MISSIONS IT' RUNCORN.
div.p: WESLEYAN HOME MISSIONS IT' RUNCORN.

The annual services on behalf of the Wesleyan Foreign Mission,,were commenced on Sunday morn- ing in St. Paul's Chapel, when the Rev. John Hanby preached an appropriate sermon. In the evening the Rev. T. Wilkes preached in support of the Mis- sions. There were good congregations at each ser— vice. On Tuesday afternoon, the Rev. H. J. Pope, President of the Conference, preached a sermon on the text Mark ix., 28;.t0 a good. congregation. In the evening the annual.meeting.was held under the presidency of Me.. F. Jt Norman, .LP., who was sup- ported by the Revs. H.', J. Pope, Chas. Garrett (Liverpool),. T.. Wilkes, J. Hanby, W. Arrowsmith and 11. Posnett ; Messrs. John Simpson, S. Taylor, J.P., A. It Norman, liniveton, J. Povah, S. Pope, R. Rawlinson, T. Simister, and J. D. ,Jones. The sacred edifice was completely filled. The Rev. W. Arrowsmith submitted the report showing that the in- come of the societywas £30,092 15s. 9d..0r £538 6s. 9d. more than the expenditure. There was a balance of £67, 9s. 4d. in the hands of the treasurer... The fend assisted more than half the circuits-in Great Britain. The total amount raised by, the Rimcorti Circuit on behalf of the society during the pastyear was £6B 75., compared with £B6 18'3. 7d. 124nonths ago. In his address,the Chairman said the great problem of to-day was the Social one,and was being tackled by every school of thought. In his opinion the great Christian Courch was the true one for dealing with the problem successfully. The Wesleyan Home Mission was a.distinct branch of the Christian Chnrcli and its most peculiar advantages were suitable far dealing.with all conditions of society. (Applause.) The Rev. H. J. Pope said the subject of that meeting waS exhilarating to him for it showed they had graspea the importance of the subjectand were prepared to place Home Missions in their right position in their minds. Although the society only dated back 38 years, the Wesleyan Church had carried on home missions all along, for Wesleyan Methodism from the hour of its incept' m to that hour bad conducted operations with great suc- cess. He strongly advocated the return to the old sylitem where the village chapels were associated with the towns, and alluding to the grand Manchester Mission, said they owed a dcep debt of gratitude to Runborn Methodism: They had reared the man who had been instrumental in the hands of ded in doing a great work. He did not know what they should have done without Samuel Collier. (Applause.) He was full of enthusiasm and had the spirit of unselfishness. which caused him never to ask anyone to do anything he was not prepared to do himself. The Mission under him was growing in a marvellous manner and the city and dis- trict were infected with it. (Applause.) The Rev. Charles Garrett in the course of ax able speech drew attention to the marvellous changes which had taken place dfirieg this century in the moral and social life of. the people, and alluding tothe drink trade said if they must have public houses they ought to be placed amongst the homes of the wealthy. (Applause.) On the motion of the Rev. T. Wilkes, votes of thanks were accorded to all who had taken part in the meeting. During the evening the united choirs of St. Pauls, Halton-road and Camden ren- dered several anthems in a most efficient manner under the leadership of Mr. R. Morris. Mr...Grice was at the organ. The collections' including those of Sunday .realiivid £32 3s. 2d., or £l2 in advance of the sum ob- tained last year.

div.head: NEW FEMALE CASUAL .WARD.
div.p: NEW FEMALE CASUAL .WARD.

In accordance with notice, Mr. Brandreth moved that the Guardians consent (1) To the erection at the Work- house of the Union of a casual ward for females in accordance.with plans to which; the Local Government Board have affixed their seal subject to such modifica- tions thereof,.as that Board may hereafter direct. (2) To the expenditure of the above mentioned purpose of a sum not exceeding three hundred and thirty-five pounds. (3) To the borrowiry, of the said sum of £335 or such part thereof as may be necessary for the purpose afote- said, the repayment thereof with interest to be secured by a charge on the common fund of the Union,in the manner provided by the statutes in that behalf. Ile further moved that the sum of £335 be borrowed for the purpose, and that the sum so borrowed be repaid by such equal half yearly payments as reckoning principal and interest together will repay the sum borrowed in twenty years.—Mr. Heywood seconded.—Dr. Gastaldi suggested that in this new ward beds and not planks should be provided.—The Chairman : lam afraid that would increase the tramps.—Mr. Brandretla : Must it be a feather bed?—Br. Gastaldi :. It ought to be a bed.— The motion was carried.

div.head: COUNTY RATE.
div.p: THE COUNTY RATE.

Mr. Brandreth presented the report of the Finance Committee who recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £3,478 104. 71. Mr. 13randreth explained that this sum included £3,32675. 7d. for county rate,but as the County Council had to pay the Union somewhere, about £2,000 back, the Committee proposed that a cheque should be drawn and that the County Council te informed that the Guardians wouldexchange chevies. The balance in the treasurer's hands was £2,553 108.3 d., and of course if the County Council paid the Union, they would have sufficient to pay the courity calk—Tne laccounts were passed.

div.head: LIVERPOOL, ST. HELENS, AND SOUTH
div.p: LIVERPOOL, ST. HELENS, AND SOUTH
LANCASHIRE RAILWAY.

The report of the directors of the new Ltverpool, St. Helens, and South Lancashire Railway ice the half year ended 31st December last states that dtrcing the past. half year fair progress has been made with the Ashton cutting, the viaduct near St. Helens, and the several bridges on the line, notwithstanding that the works have to some extent been retarded by causes connected with the long suspension of the coal trade. It is antici- pated that the arrangements at preseV in band for obtaining possession of the whole of theibecessary land affording access to St. Helens will be shortly completed. The *directors have considered it desirable to introduce a bill in Parliament jointly with the Manchester, Sheffield,- and Lincolnshire Company to empower the latter company to subscribe further capital and to enter into agreements with the conaPany respecting the priority of the same. The statements of accounts shows that the capital authorised was £733,000; capital created or sanctioned, £280,000 balance of capital, £453,000. Of the £280,000 created, £221,286 had beeu received; calls in arrenr, £228; amount uncalled, £56 ; amount unissued, £58,430. The amount expended up to June 30th, 1893, was £218,643 150. 4d. ; amount ex- pended during six montks to 31st December, 180, was £25,237 Os. 10d. ; total, £243,681 ss. 2d. The receipts showed :—On ordinary shares, £81,26; on 3-4 per cent. guaranteed shares £100,000; and on 4 per cent. pre- ference shares, £40,000; total, £221,286, leaving a bal- ance to ho raised of £22,595 ss. 21. The total estimated further expenditure during the present half year is £30,000, and in subsequent half years £459,000. The new line wss commenced in January, 1888, the first sod being turned by the late Lord Derby, on land near the St, Helens Town Hall.
DEATH AND" FUNERAL OF MR. MOLYNEUX, OF RUNCORN.

The mortal remains of Mr. Thomas Molyneux, of 1, Cooper-street, were interred in their last resting place at Brincorn Cemetery, on Wednesday after- noon, amid surroundings betokening Much respect. Born in St. John,street, the deceased was a native of Runcorn, and for 16 years he was employed asft captain under the old Bridgewater Trustees. His father before him was employed as a mason by tile same irm in the construction of the dock, at Old Quay. The deceasedwas an earnest Wesleyan,and had had an official connection in the denomination. list was a class leader, d teacher in the Sunday School and a visitor. Twenty six years ago he was ap- pointed chapel keeper at St. Paul's, and during that lengthened period he had only been absent from his position on one occasion. A most conscientious and painstaking Man he had the respect and esteem of all. He died on Monday, after a brief illness, from erysipelas ,in the head. The funeral procession Proceeded from the deceased's late residence to St. Pa-ut's Chapel, where the Rev. T.:Wilkes read the first portion of the burial service.
